documents.ai_summary: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation Working Group discussed the PY 2027–2028 seasonal LOLE study, which maintains a 0.1 days/year annual target with seasonal 0.01 days/year floors across four seasons. The study incorporates seasonally differentiated ELCC values for wind and solar, improved load-forecast modeling, and Capacity Import/Export Limit (CIL/CEL) calculations by Local Resource Zone. Notably, MISO documented unprecedented winter and spring load growth across its footprint, with peak-demand patterns shifting away from summer dominance; stakeholders were asked to comment by July 7, 2026 on revised load-forecast uncertainty parameters that may reshape planning-reserve-margin requirements. Hydro operators should monitor: (1) seasonal ELCC methodology as applied to dispatchable resources, since seasonal accreditation drives RA value; (2) load-growth findings and their impact on reserve adequacy for winter/shoulder periods (classic high-scarcity windows for dispatchable hydro); and (3) CIL/CEL results in September that will constrain interregional transfer capability and affect hydro export value in neighboring zones.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Resource Adequacy Subcommittee is advancing three substantive accreditation reforms: (1) solar accreditation will remain on fixed hours until demand-limited operating levels (DLOL) take effect in PY 2028/2029, when mismatch with actual system risk will be addressed; (2) MISO proposes reducing the 24-hour lead-time threshold for offline resources to either 12 hours, zero availability within 48 hours if lead time increases, or a sliding-scale reducing availability 5% per hour from 4-hour baseline—a FERC filing is planned for October 2026; (3) PRMR allocation to LSEs will shift to a three-year weighted average of actual demand during Tier 2 RA hours (filed by end of 2026, effective PY 2029/2030). The lead-time proposal is most consequential for hydro: tightening the online-availability threshold and penalizing lead-time increases during stress periods will lower the accreditation value of conventionally operated run-of-river and reservoir hydro that cannot flex dispatch commitment rapidly. MISO's wind-profile enhancement in the Loss of Load Expectation model will materially alter accreditation for all resource classes, including hydro, by improving meteorological alignment of wind modeling and reshaping the marginal contribution of dispatchable resources to seasonal adequacy. Stakeholders and affected resource owners should engage on the lead-time proposal before October 2026 filing and on wind/solar accreditation impacts at the August 19, 2026 RASC meeting and continuing LOLEWG discussions.

Load conformance in real time dropped dramatically—from 1,400 MW average in January–February 2025 to 50 MW in the same months of 2026, improving FMM–RTD alignment. For pumped-storage hydro, this signals that battery-scale short-duration storage is saturating the regulation market where PSH historically competed, narrowing the revenue niche to longer-duration discharge (evening peaks exceeding 12,000 MW) and forcing PSH operators to compete on state-of-charge management and peak-placement timing rather than ancillary-service volume. The CAISO tariff will update default variable operations and maintenance (VO&M) adders in early June 2026—hydroelectric facilities currently have only a 0.77 $/run-hour/MW adder, the lowest among renewable and fossil technologies, which may be revised during that triennial review. Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) performance monitoring begins in July 2026, with monthly public reporting expected to drive long-term visibility into multi-state hydro deliverability and pricing.

For reservoir and pumped-storage hydro exporting across seams or managing internal transfers within Markets+, this creates new operational flexibility in how interchange can be scheduled and priced — reducing reliance on pre-scheduled bilateral contracts and allowing market-cleared transactions to flow through the MPSP mechanism, potentially improving dispatch optionality and revenue capture on short-notice export opportunities.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ has adopted MIR81-R, which introduces separate Normal and Dynamic transaction types for Market Transfer Interface (MTI) and Market Opt-In Transfer Interface (MOTI) scheduling constraints. Normal MTIs/MOTIs are used in the Day-Ahead Market, RUC, and Pre-RTBM SCED and become fixed in real-time; Dynamic MTIs/MOTIs apply only in RTBM, allowing BAAs to adjust constraints post-DA without overturning the prior commitment plan. This separation allows a BAA to restrict incremental market transfers in RTBM (via Dynamic constraints with tighter limits) while preserving the DA-optimized dispatch and avoiding the artificially high real-time prices and binding constraints that would result from post-DA constraint tightening. The presented example shows how Dynamic MTI constraints in RTBM permitted flexible generation (including BAA3's cheap generation via Dynamic MTI2-3) to respond efficiently to a load change in BAA2, whereas a static constraint would have choked off that supply. Protocol sections 4.2.7, 8.2.1.1, 8.2.2.1, 8.2.6, and 9.4.1 were updated to operationalize Normal/Dynamic tagging and submission requirements. This is relevant to hydro owners in SPP Markets+ because tighter real-time scheduling constraints (historically a pain point for use-limited resources) now have a structured mechanism to coexist with DA efficiency, potentially reducing artificial scarcity pricing and improving dispatch-following opportunities for flexible hydro.

documents.ai_summary: Dominion proposes a Load Entity Large Load Addition (LLA) Sufficiency Incentive to restructure PJM's capacity market: load entities serving incremental large loads must procure or contract for new capacity (or capacity-equivalent alternatives such as demand response or provisional interconnection service) to meet 70 percent of their LLA obligation prior to the Base Residual Auction, or face a penalty equal to Point A of the VRR curve applied to the uncovered portion. The penalty is phased in over a 5-year transition (calculated but not assessed in Year 1, 50% assessed in Year 4, 100% in Year 5), with delivery years 2028/29–2033/34 covering the implementation window. Hydro owners and flexible generators benefit if this shifts PJM's market from over-reliance on the centralized BRA toward bilateral contracting and tighter alignment of generation investment with load growth — which would raise investment signals in the energy and ancillary-services markets and reduce uplift — but face revenue risk if it accelerates retirements or cannibalization of existing capacity through reactivation of retired resources to meet the LLA obligation. documents.ai_summary: MISO is executing a multi-year Reliability Imperative with five strategic pillars. On capacity-RA, MISO is aligning accreditation with peak risk periods and further refining seasonal accreditation including external resources through 2029 — directly affecting how hydro's contribution is measured and valued. On storage, MISO is optimizing storage-resource participation in markets (initiated 24–36 months) and advancing storage integration with market optimization in subsequent years — bearing on PSH charging-energy treatment, AS stacking, and state-of-charge rules. On flexibility, dynamic reserves initiatives are underway to improve local reliability. On interconnection and load growth, MISO is accelerating large-load integration ('reliable speed-to-power'), expediting generator-interconnection studies (ERAS/EPR), and reforming its queue process — expanding the addressable market for hydro's flexibility and firm capacity, but also increasing operational constraints. Stakeholder feedback is requested by September 4, 2026, on alignment with member needs, gaps, and support required.

documents.ai_summary: Constellation presents root causes of PJM's resource adequacy crisis: structural barriers (doubled construction timelines, escalated capital costs, regulatory uncertainty, lack of revenue certainty) exacerbated by unprecedented load growth and political sensitivity to capacity prices. The presentation emphasizes that the Base Residual Auction (BRA) was designed as residual, with load hedged through bilateral contracts, but now functions as primary procurement vehicle — exposing load and supply to extreme price volatility (clearing prices ranged $28.92 to $329.17/MW-day across recent delivery years). Constellation argues out-of-market interventions (price caps, RMR bidding as price-takers) undercut price signals needed to incentivize both new construction and retention of existing resources, including relicensing costs for hydro ($100M+) and nuclear units. The presentation proposes hedging mechanisms that shield ratepayers from volatility while allowing spot-market prices to reflect fundamentals — a framework that would restore revenue certainty critical to investment in new and existing hydro capacity in PJM.

documents.ai_summary: GridLab (via Executive Director Ric O'Connell) presented a market-design workshop to PJM arguing for elimination of the RPM capacity market in favor of scarcity-based energy pricing coupled with bilateral contracts for reliability and investment incentives. The mechanism matters to hydro owners because eliminating RPM would erase hydro's capacity-market revenue stream (currently a major hedge for use-limited resources with seasonal energy profiles), transfer revenue risk entirely to scarcity pricing and bilateral contract negotiation, and potentially reset deliverability standards in interconnection—reducing the network-upgrade burden on new hydro but eliminating a protected accreditation pathway for existing fleet. Most exposed are pumped-storage operators whose RA contribution is currently framed through ELCC accreditation; large reservoir hydro with bilateral-contract scale would benefit from scarcity pricing if water availability aligns with winter/system peaks. documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Manual M14D revision 71 establishes mandatory reactive power (voltage support) operating requirements for all generators in PJM, directly affecting hydro's ancillary-services revenue stream and operational obligations.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual M14D to strengthen reactive power control requirements for all generators, mandating automatic voltage control mode as the only acceptable default (with documented exceptions) and defining acceptable volt-var boundaries and VAR control ranges per MW output. The revision, triggered by NERC's May 2026 lowering of IBR registration threshold and motivated by the 2025 Spain blackout (insufficient voltage control from offline synchronous generators) and emerging PJM low-voltage constraints, clarifies D-curve submittal requirements and establishes a three-party investigative process (PJM, TO, generator owner) for reactive control performance issues. The timeline shows first read/review in June 2026, education and Q&A sessions in mid-to-late June, and endorsement expected July 23, 2026 at the Markets and Reliability Committee, making this a mandatory compliance obligation for all hydro and PSH units. Synchronous hydro — the canonical voltage-support resource — faces both an operational requirement to maintain automatic voltage control and potential PJM direction to alter AVR settings or reactive control parameters if systematic fleet analysis identifies non-compliance; this consolidates and clarifies PJM's enforcement authority over a revenue stream hydro has historically supplied.

documents.ai_summary: PJM has established a new Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT) — a parallel, temporary fast-track process outside the standard PJM Cycle for generators meeting three criteria: written siting authority support, 36-month path to commercial operation, and ≥250 MW accredited UCAP. The process compresses Application Review (~180 days), Study (~60 days), and Final Agreement Negotiation (~60 days) into a single 360-day path. FERC accepted the tariff revisions on June 9, 2026 (Docket ER26-1563), effective July 31, 2026. Manual 14H (PJM's interconnection procedures manual) is being updated to conform to OATT Part X changes and was first-read by Planning Committee on June 24, 2026, with Markets and Reliability Committee endorsement on July 28, 2026. Large hydro and PSH projects meeting the eligibility criteria now have a material option to bypass the standard queue and compress pre-construction lead time by roughly half — particularly valuable for projects that can secure state/utility siting endorsement and have shovel-ready engineering. The qualification threshold of 250 MW UCAP excludes most run-of-river and smaller reservoir projects but opens a strategic path for large reservoir and pumped-storage facilities.

documents.title: Item 01 – 1 Flexible Resource Loc Eligibility – Presentation

documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes refining the definition of 'Flexible Resources' to require that all available schedules have combined startup and notification time ≤2 hours and minimum run time ≤2 hours; currently, resources may be flexible on some schedules but not others. The effect: a fast-start hydro or PSH unit committed day-ahead on a flexible cost-based schedule because it failed the transmission-security test might have been eligible for LOC credits if held out in real-time; under this proposal, if that unit's market-based schedule (the only one available in real-time) is not flexible by the new standard, the unit forfeits LOC eligibility even if physically capable of starting quickly. This tightens compensation for units day-ahead-committed but left idle in real-time. documents.ai_summary: PJM presented a pro forma Reliability Must-Run (RMR) agreement framework for generators (including potential hydro units) that PJM requests to continue operating beyond market deactivation to resolve transmission constraints until upgrades are complete. The pro forma streamlines compensation by pre-approving non-rate terms and conditions at FERC, allowing RMR units to either pursue a Formula Rate (Deactivation Avoidable Cost Credit under Tariff Part V, Section 114) or file for Cost-of-Service rate recovery (Tariff Part V, Section 119), eliminating the need for hearing and settlement-judge procedures. Key feature: RMR units remain outside RPM auctions and RPM penalty regimes, but energy/capacity/ancillary-services revenues are credited against RMR charges, making the net compensation dependent on market realization. Hydro and other dispatchable generators retained for transmission reliability under cost-of-service rate schedules will now be treated as automatic zero-bid capacity sellers, exempt from non-performance charges and performance-ratio calculations, with all capacity revenues credited to the zones paying for their continuing operations rather than to PJMSettlement. This eliminates discretionary pricing authority for retained units and locks their capacity value into the zonal load that funded the retention order — a structural change to how use-limited and must-run resources participate in capacity markets. documents.ai_summary: PJM's Part V tariff revisions establish the procedural and financial framework for generation deactivations and reliability-driven continued operation. The multiplier structure (110% Year 1, 120% Year 2, 135% Year 3, 150% Year 4) reimburses avoided costs of continued operation, with credits offset by actual net revenues. Hydro and PSH owners—especially those facing transmission constraints or holding reserve obligations—are directly exposed to these rules when plant economics deteriorate but system reliability demands continued operation; the 12-month notice window and escalating multipliers create both timing and valuation risks for retirement planning. This tariff revision is on the Markets and Reliability Committee calendar for July 2026; stakeholders should monitor for any changes to how actual net revenues are calculated, as that directly impacts the credit floor.

documents.ai_summary: Constellation proposes amendments to PJM's pro forma RMR Agreement to clarify cost-recovery rights and termination conditions before operating units under RMR. Separately, Constellation opposes blanket inclusion of RMR resources' UCAP (Unforced Capacity) values in the RPM (Reliability Pricing Model) auction, arguing RMR resources are not Capacity Resources and inclusion should require crediting all capacity-market revenues back to entities funding RMR operations. documents.ai_summary: PJM is updating its default Gross CONE (Cost of New Entry) and Gross ACR (Avoidable Cost Rate) values for the 2030/2031 delivery year, using EIA 2026 cost data and 2025 Quadrennial Review financial assumptions (9.506% ATWACC, 20-year life, 55% debt at 5.8%, 16% equity rate). August 2026 MRC/MC Advisory Vote will ratify the updates, with FERC filing by October 1, 2026. documents.ai_summary: PJM's tariff amendment adjusts the MOPR floor-offer-price methodology for the Base Residual Auction starting in delivery year 2023/2024 by replacing the bonus-depreciation adjustment factor with a revised federal tax law–based factor: 1.022 for nuclear/coal/gas and 1.01 for solar/wind/storage. The mechanism works by adjusting gross costs of new entry (CONE) downward to reflect declining effective capital costs as bonus depreciation schedules change; the new 1.01 factor for storage will lower the MOPR floor for battery and pumped-storage resources. For pumped-storage hydro owners, this reduction in the entry-level offer price in the capacity auction narrows the cushion between allowed offer floors and actual economic entry cost, potentially compressing offer discretion and revenue if the tax law assumptions underestimate PSH's true cost structure or if PSH's tax treatment differs from battery storage. The redline is in tariff amendment form at the Markets and Reliability Committee, indicating it is under active development; no comment deadline or vote date is stated in this excerpt.

documents.ai_summary: PJM and The Brattle Group have completed a 2026 update to gross avoidable costs (GAC) for existing generation, a key input to offer mitigation and resource retirement analysis. The 2026 analysis updates representative-plant characteristics and cost drivers compared to 2022 (with notable increases in coal GAC: +44%, onshore wind +29%, simple-cycle CT +23%, reflecting aging fleets and input costs), and introduces battery energy storage as a new resource type. documents.ai_summary: PJM is addressing workflow bottlenecks in its RPM (Reliability Pricing Model) planning-parameter process starting with the 2030/31 delivery-year auction. The issue: ER24-99 compliance expanded ELCC (Effective Load Carrying Capability) analysis to all resource types and introduced new verification steps, but RPM planning-parameter deadlines in the OATT and RAA have not been adjusted to accommodate the tighter data-availability-to-analysis timeline. The problem statement identifies three specific workflow pressures: aligning the resource portfolio for IRM/FPR computation with actual RPM participation; incorporating updated PJM load forecasts into demand-side uncertainty analysis; and calculating UCAP for every resource type (including hydro and PSH). If deadlines are not reformed, PJM risks missing mandated filing dates or delivering insufficiently verified ELCC-based capacity values. The Markets and Reliability Committee will be educated on key milestones and proposed reforms; no comment deadline or vote date is stated in this problem statement.

documents.title: Item 04 – 3 Planning Parameter Deadlines – Issue Charge
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: RPM capacity-auction planning-parameter deadlines affect the timing and accuracy of hydro accreditation data (ELCC/UCAP) submitted to PJM's capacity market, touching hydro revenue through RA accreditation and auction-parameter design.
documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes to reform RPM Planning Parameter deadlines, which have become misaligned with post-ER24-99 workload and verification requirements, creating insufficient time between data availability and analysis completion. The issue charge frames this as a 'quick fix' to be first read in July 2026 and endorsed in August 2026, with proposed edits to OATT Attachment DD 5.10 (Auction Clearing Requirements), RAA Schedule 9.2, and M18. Hydro and storage owners depend on timely, accurate planning parameters (including ELCC values used in capacity accreditation) to value their RA contributions; tighter or slipped deadlines could delay or degrade the data hydro participants rely on to submit bids and forecast RA revenue. The mechanism is direct: compressed deadlines reduce verification rigor, weakening the input data for accreditation; conversely, deadline relief could improve ELCC estimates' accuracy. Pumped-storage and seasonal-hydro owners with significant RA obligations are most exposed to deadline-driven data-quality swings.

documents.title: Item 05a – 1 Manual 14h Ieee 2800 Revisions – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM Manual 14H revisions adopting IEEE 2800 inverter-based-resource interconnection standards establish ride-through and frequency-response requirements that set technical standards synchronous resources (including hydro) must meet for grid support and that may affect how existing conventional and pumped-storage hydro are evaluated for voltage/frequency service obligations.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 14H to adopt IEEE 2800-2022 interconnection requirements for inverter-based resources in Phase 1, effective June 22, 2027, covering definitions, voltage and frequency ride-through capabilities, and primary frequency response parameters. The revision establishes default enter-service voltage criteria (0.9–1.05 p.u.), frequency criteria (58.8–60.12 Hz), and voltage ride-through times ranging from 0.16 to 6 seconds depending on voltage severity, along with droop and frequency-response deadband settings. While targeted at IBRs, the standard-setting precedent and interconnection requirements framework affect how PJM evaluates and credentials all resources for synchronous-machine obligations; synchronous hydro units will operate in a market where the baseline reliability expectations are rising. Endorsement is scheduled for August 19, 2026 at the Markets and Reliability Committee.

documents.title: Item 05a – 2 Manual 14h Requirements For Inverter Based Resources – Executive Summary
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM is mandating IEEE 2800-2022 inverter-based resource (IBR) standards including voltage/frequency ride-through and primary frequency response requirements, which extends PJM's operating standards to synchronous hydro resources serving the same grid and establishes a precedent for how storage and variable resources must behave; hydro operators need to track whether similar mandates will follow in their RTOs.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is adopting IEEE Standard 2800-2022 requirements for inverter-based resources (IBRs) in Manual 14H, effective August 19, 2026. Phase I adds new Section 9.15 and Attachment K covering general definitions, voltage and frequency ride-through, associated protection requirements, and primary frequency response. Although PJM has limited conventional hydropower, this sets a precedent across RTOs for synchronous-unit operating standards and frequency-response obligations; pumped-storage hydro with power-electronic interfaces and variable-output generators face similar mandates elsewhere, and this IEEE 2800 adoption pattern is spreading industry-wide. MRC voting date: August 19, 2026.

documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 14H (Revision 05, effective July 23, 2026) governs the New Service Requests cycle process for generation, transmission, and merchant transmission interconnections. The manual covers application phases, study procedures (Phase I–III), cost allocation, surplus interconnection service, and generator requirements including power factor rules and capacity vs. energy resource elections. Section 12 addresses surplus interconnection service — the pathway for uprates and efficiency upgrades at existing plants — and Section 9 covers generator obligations including power factor requirements and demand-response integration. Hydro and PSH operators rely on these procedures to pursue uprates at existing facilities, optimize interconnection costs, and understand whether their resource qualifies for capacity or energy accreditation; changes to surplus interconnection thresholds, cost allocation to legacy plants, or power factor mandates directly affect the business case for retrofit projects.

documents.ai_summary: PJM is publishing conforming changes to Manual 18 (Capacity Market Operations) reflecting approved FERC tariff filings, including revisions to VRR-curve parameters (ER26-455-000), new capacity-deficiency penalties tied to AUCAP derate factors (ER25-2002-000), DER aggregation test-failure charges (ER26-980-000), and clarified must-offer exception administration (sections 4.6.3, 5.4.1). The changes also remove environmentally-limited resources from winter-period capacity resource definitions and associated aggregation rules. These are conforming updates to already-approved tariff changes; the presentation indicates the manual revisions are being rolled out for member reference following FERC orders. Key updates include clarifications to ICAP definitions, refined ambient-condition and simultaneous-requirement testing rules with specified deadlines, a new Appendix A codifying test-data requirements, and expanded language allowing additional data collection for ELCC analysis—the methodology that directly sets hydro and pumped-storage accreditation levels. documents.ai_summary: PJM is updating Manual 21B (Rules and Procedures for Determination of Generating Capability) with administrative clarifications effective August 19, 2026, approved at the July 28 MRC meeting with voting scheduled for August 19. Key changes include clarified ICAP definition language, tightened ambient-condition and simultaneous-testing requirements with specified submission deadlines, and formalized test-data requirements in a new Appendix A. Section 9 was updated to permit additional data gathering to support ELCC analysis, and the Performance Adjustment section was revised for DER calculation. For PJM hydropower owners, these changes refine the technical and procedural rules governing capability certification — the foundation of capacity-market accreditation and RA showings; clarifications to ambient-condition testing and ELCC data collection could tighten or standardize how seasonal or run-of-river hydro capability is proven, affecting accreditation values. Most relevant to all PJM-interconnected hydro facilities subject to capacity-market participation.

documents.title: Item 05c – 3 Manual 21b Periodic Review – Redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Manual 21B governs the ELCC accreditation and capacity rating methodology for all resource classes in PJM, which directly determines hydropower and pumped-storage hydro accreditation, capacity revenue, and RA obligations.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 21B (Revision 06, effective June 24, 2026) is the operator's authoritative handbook for determining generating capability, ELCC classification, accredited UCAP, and capacity accreditation across all resource types including limited-duration resources (the category covering pumped-storage hydro). The revision reflects a periodic review cleaning up language, updating defined terms, and clarifying the capability verification process—particularly submission deadlines and ambient-condition rules that affect how hydro and storage assets demonstrate their rated capacity. Hydro owners must comply with these testing, data submission, and accreditation procedures to maintain capacity revenue and interconnection rights; no policy change to accreditation formulas is documented in this revision, but the clarified verification rules and ICAP definitions establish binding operational requirements.

documents.title: Item 06 – 2029 2030 BRA Fpr IRM Results – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ELCC accreditation methodology and ratings directly determine hydro and pumped-storage capacity revenue; this 2029/30 BRA analysis establishes hydro's accreditation factors and the shift toward higher winter risk exposure that degrades intermittent hydro's RA value.
documents.ai_summary: PJM calculated 2029/30 BRA Installed Reserve Margin (IRM) of 20.4% and Forecast Pool Requirement (FPR) of 0.9248, driven by higher winter peak loads (data center growth and electrification of heating) that shift the seasonal loss-of-load-expectation risk 96.2% to winter vs. 77.4% in 2028/29. Hydro Intermittent ELCC rating held flat at 35% (no change from 2028/29), but the Pool-Wide Average Accredited UCAP Factor declined 1.53 percentage points to 0.7681 due to worse winter-hour performance across the portfolio—meaning all variable resources, including intermittent hydro, face lower accreditation relative to nameplate. Hydro With Non-Pumped Storage (reservoir hydro) portfolio of 2,015 MW nameplate was assigned 1,945 MW effective capacity; 4–10 hour storage batteries (4-hr: 57%, 6-hr: 67%, 8-hr: 69%, 10-hr: 77%) saw small declines in ELCC rating but remain accredited. The system is tightening: UCAP Surplus shrank to −3,051 MW (a deficit of 1,635 MW vs. 2028/29), signaling scarcity conditions ahead that should elevate realized RA auction prices for all capacity suppliers, including hydro, despite individual resource accreditation pressure.

documents.title: Item 07 – Storage As A Transmission Asset Informational Report – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Storage-as-transmission-asset (SATA) rules define how storage resources (including pumped storage) are studied, operated, and compensated when serving transmission functions, directly affecting PSH revenue recognition, market participation eligibility, and operational dispatch protocols.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is finalizing a combined Phase 1–Phase 2 design package for Storage-as-Transmission-Asset (SATA) participation, presented to the Markets and Reliability Committee in July 2026 for informational review and first read. The design restricts SATA to transmission-only operation (no energy-market or capacity participation, no queue eligibility), with automatic discharge for identified RTEP violations, revenue-grade metering, state-of-charge telemetry, and cost recovery via Schedule 12 Transmission Enhancement Credits (TEC). This framework matters most to pumped-storage operators considering transmission-augmentation contracts: SATA explicitly forecloses revenue from energy or ancillary-services markets for storage deployed as transmission, requires PJM-coordinated charging after discharge, and mandates no harm testing during planning. The combined package moves to Markets Committee for endorsement in August–September 2026, with FERC filing targeted for October–November 2026.

documents.title: 2026-07-28 PAC A07.0 2025 LTTP RFP – Preliminary Preferred Solution
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: This Longer-Term Transmission Planning (LTTP) selection in New England directly affects transmission deliverability of hydropower and storage resources; the chosen solution (LTP A1, a Maine–New Hampshire AC transmission upgrade) alters the interregional transfer capability and geographic scarcity signals that determine hydro export revenue and strategic dispatch options for NHA members in Maine and New Hampshire.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE's Planning Advisory Committee is evaluating six longer-term transmission proposals to address three needs by December 31, 2035: increase Maine–New Hampshire interface to 3,000 MW (LT-1), Surowiec–South to 3,200 MW (LT-2), and accommodate 1,200 MW of new onshore wind at Pittsfield, Maine. The ISO selected LTP A1 (Central Maine Power AC proposal, $2.20B, in-service Q4 2032) as preliminary preferred solution after testing against energy standard, capacity standard, and transfer-capability requirements. LTP A1 was the only proposal passing all three RFP objectives — achieving 3,100 MW summer and 3,425 MW winter capability on Maine–New Hampshire and 3,300 MW summer and 3,725 MW winter on Surowiec–South. All other proposals (B1, C1, D1, D2) failed transfer or stability tests and were excluded. The increased transmission capacity and lower-cost, earlier in-service date of LTP A1 versus alternatives will improve export capability and reduce congestion-driven scarcity premiums for hydro generators in Maine and existing hydro/pumped storage in New England; the proposal now advances to PAC and likely Board vote for final selection.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO staff (Allie Mace and James Friedrich) are presenting the evolution of scarcity pricing reform efforts at the WEM Governing Body, following 17 stakeholder meetings and 97 sets of comments (Nov 2024–present). The working group is weighing two tracks: incremental changes to balancing-authority-level mitigation and scarcity rules (Track 1) versus comprehensive scarcity pricing redesign (Track 2). Four unresolved questions frame the decision: timing relative to EDAM implementation, whether scarcity signals or resource sufficiency alone drives reliability, the role of demand-side participation in maturing markets, and whether scarcity pricing must apply uniformly across the Western footprint. Stakeholder presenters (Six Cities, Calpine, Portland General Electric, and Public Generating Pool) will voice positions on urgency and EDAM interaction; no explicit comment deadline or vote date is stated in this briefing material, but the working group's parallel-track structure suggests imminent decision points.

documents.ai_summary: CESA urges CAISO to advance a comprehensive scarcity pricing design on the published 2026–2028 policy roadmap, arguing that robust real-time energy scarcity pricing is essential to correct longstanding price-signal failures (evidenced during Summer 2020 events) and to backstop imbalance reserve procurements that cover only 97.5% of uncertainty. CESA proposes defining an 'energy supply margin' of unloaded or flexible resources (excluding ancillary-service bids) whose relaxation would trigger gradual energy price increases above marginal cost in real-time, enabling voluntary offers from resources without day-ahead or reserve awards to dispatch during extreme conditions. The mechanism directly raises real-time energy revenue for all dispatchable resources—especially storage and hydro—during scarcity by pricing energy closer to true scarcity value rather than the marginal resource cost, and expands the margin calculation to include ramping resources across multiple timescales (30-minute and 60-minute starts/ramp capability). A WEM Governing Body decision is scheduled for Q4 2026; no comment deadline is stated in this letter, but the March 3, 2026 WEM Governing Body meeting is referenced as the next proceeding touchpoint.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO's scarcity pricing redesign (ORDC-style reform) directly affects real-time energy price formation and uplift/make-whole allocation, the two primary revenue mechanisms for hydro and PSH; PGE's intervention argues for deferring structural reform until post-EDAM stabilization, affecting the timeline and sequencing of changes that will reshape how hydro's flexibility and scarcity value are monetized.
documents.ai_summary: PGE argues that CAISO should implement only targeted interim scarcity-pricing improvements in 2026–2027 (load-shed pricing refinements, reserve-pricing consistency, shortage-logic clarification) and defer structural scarcity redesign (ORDC-style reform) until after EDAM stabilization in 2027+, citing risks to settlement mechanics and co-optimization during the 2026 EDAM launch. The concern is that concurrent objective-function changes during EDAM onboarding could alter core optimization and settlement logic while BAA-level market power mitigation, DAME coordination, and transfer mechanics remain under active development. Hydro owners should monitor this because scarcity pricing reform directly sets the value of real-time energy and uplift during tight conditions — the primary revenue source for flexibility; deferring structural change preserves the current DA/RT co-optimization framework that has historically worked in hydro's favor, but the post-2027 structural redesign will almost certainly reprrice hydro's contribution to scarcity and reserves. The trajectory suggests CAISO will eventually move toward a more explicit, reserve-demand-curve (ORDC) style approach, which may improve price signals for energy scarcity but risks depressing uplift payments if not designed carefully for use-limited resources.

documents.ai_summary: Vitol presented CAISO's Price Formation Enhancements initiative, specifically advocating for an enhanced Operating Reserve Demand Curve (ORDC) that ties real-time and day-ahead energy prices to the marginal reliability value of reserves (LOLP × VOLL). The proposal aims to move CAISO away from binary, sporadic price spikes during shortages toward a continuous, graduated scarcity-pricing mechanism that signals reliability value *before* reserves are exhausted—similar to MISO's recent implementation under ER25-579. Key design levers include LOLP measurement (probability reserves will fall below minimum within the next hour), VOLL calibration (customer willingness-to-pay segmented by load class), minimum-reserve thresholds, and reserve-requirement expansion to capture "economic shortages." For hydropower and pumped storage owners, a well-designed ORDC would raise energy-market revenue during tight conditions by rewarding flexible supply earlier in scarcity events and encouraging day-ahead hedging and long-term investment signals; a poorly designed ORDC could suppress price signals if VOLL is set too low or reserves too high. Comments are due through the Price Formation Enhancements proceeding (no explicit deadline stated in this document).

documents.ai_summary: Markets+ has established opt-in and opt-out procedures for transmission capacity, allowing Transmission Contributors to designate non-Participating TSP transmission service (both within and outside Participating BAAs) as available or unavailable for Markets+ optimization. Monthly-or-longer service on non-Participating TSPs within Participating BAAs can be opted in via RMS ticket submission for inclusion in Service Flow Constraint development; shorter-duration service does not formally opt in but may be coordinated directly with the Participating BA. Transmission outside Participating BAAs can be opted in as a Markets+ Opt-in Transfer Interface (MOTI) serving two BAs, requiring submission of TSR details and validation by the Market Operator. Hydro owners holding reserved transmission service or acquiring external transmission capacity must navigate these processes to ensure their inter-BAA transactions and day-ahead/real-time scheduling are honored under Markets+ optimization; failure to opt in monthly-or-longer service blocks formal inclusion in transmission constraints, and opt-out mechanics for MTSP transmission on reserved services require three-step eligibility/request/notification processes.

documents.ai_summary: PJM has formalized an Engineering and Procurement Agreement (E&P Agreement) process available to project developers in Phase III of the interconnection queue. The agreement expedites procurement of long-lead-time items (such as transformers, generators, and structural components critical to hydro and PSH projects) by allowing developers to begin engineering and procurement work before execution of the final Generation Interconnection Agreement. The E&P Agreement does not grant interconnection rights, priority, or construction authority, but allows developers to lock in equipment costs and delivery timelines early. Project developers must coordinate with their assigned PJM Project Manager and the relevant Transmission Owner on scope; PJM drafts the agreement, developers execute within 15 business days, the Transmission Owner has 15 business days thereafter, and PJM then files with FERC or reports in Electric Quarterly Reports. First batch of TC2 E&P Agreement requests closes August 14, 2026. For hydro owners with projects in PJM's queue, this reduces the risk of long-lead procurement delays and cost escalation between Phase II and commercial operation.

documents.ai_summary: PJM has filed and FERC has accepted (June 9, 2026) tariff revisions establishing an Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT) for projects supporting large load additions, effective July 31, 2026 (Manual 14H revisions endorsed by PC and MRC, effective July 31, 2026). The EIT imposes specific site-control, financial-deposit, and dynamic-modeling requirements including: 100% site control for 36 months minimum; acreage thresholds (10 acres per synchronous-generator facility, 1 acre/100 MWh for battery storage); readiness deposits of $15,000/MW; study deposits of $500,000; and combined dynamic models (PSCAD/PSS/E) for uprates. Hydro and PSH developers seeking EIT status must provide a Notice of Commitment from a Primary Siting Authority and critical-path construction schedules. The mechanism affects interconnection timing and strategic queue positioning for storage uprates, pump-back expansion, or run-of-river/reservoir projects co-located with or serving large loads (data centers, industrial); smaller hydro facilities that cannot meet 36-month site-control terms or acreage density thresholds may be excluded from fast-track benefits. The track is now open for applications in NextGen portal as of 12 EPT July 31, 2026.

documents.title: 20260727 LLWG Item 02 Interconnection Reliability Requirements (LLWG 2026 3) Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Large load interconnection requirements, especially for computational loads (data centers, AI/HPC), affect hydro's strategic options for co-located load, transmission deliverability, and competitive positioning against dispatchable resources in regions facing rapid load growth.
documents.ai_summary: MISO is finalizing tariff language (target filing mid-August 2026) establishing interconnection reliability requirements for large loads ≥50 MW, with differentiated standards for computational versus non-computational loads. Computational loads (data centers, AI/HPC, cryptocurrency mining) face full requirements including PMU, ride-through (voltage/frequency), and ramp management; non-computational industrial loads face basic facility data, modeling, and telemetry only. Transition provision exempts loads already in service before the effective date (November 1, 2027) unless they expand by ≥25 MW, while prospective loads approved in MTEP but not yet in service by December 2026 face ramp and ride-through requirements immediately upon service commencement. For hydro owners, this framework creates both risk and opportunity: rapid data-center expansion in MISO could constrain transmission for existing hydro exports and raise reserve/ramp requirements (which hydro typically supplies), while co-location rules or hybrid arrangements with large loads could open new revenue paths if tariff language explicitly allows behind-the-meter service or load-aggregation participation.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group has drafted tariff language (Section 37A) establishing baseline reliability requirements for loads of 50 MW or greater, with special stringency for computational loads (data centers, servers). New requirements include PMU installation, ride-through compliance during voltage/frequency disturbances, ramp-rate limits in the aggregate, day-ahead and real-time load forecasting, telemetry via ICCP, and modeling submissions — with compliance phased in by September 1, 2027 for existing interconnection-queued projects. Critically, the tariff explicitly addresses "Generation Resource(s) serving such Large Load that is located behind the same Point of Interconnection," triggering individual metering thresholds, and defines Computational Load *excluding* charging of Electric Storage Resources. For hydro owners, this opens a participation pathway for behind-the-meter generation serving large loads (potentially hydro-powered data centers or pump-storage charging paired with collocated industrial load), but the ramp and ride-through rules may constrain operational flexibility. The tariff is in draft form; no comment deadline or vote date is stated in this excerpt, but implementation is expected by September 1, 2027 for new large loads.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group has drafted tariff language (Section 37A) establishing reliability requirements for large computational loads (≥50 MW), with differentiated rules for computational loads (data centers, servers, etc.) versus general industrial load. Computational loads must install PMUs, meet ride-through standards during voltage/frequency disturbances, and comply with up/down ramp limits; all large loads must provide real-time telemetry, load forecasts, and detailed electrical models prior to September 1, 2027 (or service commencement, whichever is later). The tariff explicitly excludes from the definition of "Large Load" any load associated with charging of electric storage resources, preserving a separate category for PSH charging — but the ramp-rate requirements for computational loads and the modeling/telemetry mandates will likely set precedent for storage participation rules and co-located resource interconnection standards across RTOs. documents.title: 2026-07-23 RC A03.b Capacity Auction Reforms - Seasonal/Accreditation - Post-RAA Accreditation - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE is redesigning how it accredits capacity from hydropower, pumped-storage, and other energy-limited resources in its seasonal capacity auctions, directly affecting the rMRI (resource reliability measure index) values that determine what NHA members can bid and how much capacity value they receive.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is implementing post-RAA (Resource Adequacy Assessment) accreditation methods to determine Accredited Capacity (via MRIC = MCap × rMRI) for resources not included in the ~10-month-prior RAA modeling window. For energy-limited resources including pumped hydro, ISO will apply a proxy ES (energy-storage) rMRI-duration curve developed seasonally, with rMRI sensitivity to energy duration (1–100 hours), EFORd, and round-trip efficiency (84% used in proxy). For intermittent-power resources (IPRs), hydro will receive class-weighted average rMRI by SOG/non-SOG type and load zone. Hybrid resources sum component-level rMRI derived from applicable non-hybrid methodologies, then cap at facility limit. ISO will publish representative rMRI values ~5 months before each seasonal auction (e.g., June 12, 2028, for winter 2028–29). Stakeholder feedback is requested by July 31, 2026; Technical Committee vote and final design amendment are projected for Q3–Q4 2026, with FERC filing in Q4 2026.

documents.title: 2026-07-23 RC A03.a Capacity Auction Reforms - Seasonal/Accreditation - Accreditation Process Flows & DCap Follow-ups - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE's capacity accreditation reform (CAR-SA) directly affects how hydropower and pumped-storage resources are modeled, valued, and accredited in the region's capacity market—establishing the seasonal DCap (Dependable Capability) and MRIC (Marginal Resource Contribution) processes that determine RA eligibility and capacity payments for hydro assets.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is reforming its capacity auction to introduce seasonality and accreditation modeling through the CAR-SA project (proposed effective Q2–Q3 2027). The reform defines Dependable Capability (DCap) as a resource's expected availability during stressed system conditions, measured in the top 100 load hours per season; DCap is then applied in three RAA functions: capacity-zone formation testing, deliverability scaling (summer only), and rMRI assignment to aggregated resources. For non-energy-limited resources (including most hydro plants), DCap is calculated as MIN[median availability × performance factor, seasonal MCap], where performance factor for dispatchable units equals average (metered output ÷ DDP) over the past 12 months. The ISO released accreditation process-flow diagrams in this presentation showing how MCap, DCap, EFORd, and outage parameters feed RAA modeling to derive seasonal rMRI values, which are then multiplied by MCap to calculate seasonal MRIC (the capacity value used in auctions). Stakeholders have until July 31, 2026 to submit follow-up questions; technical-committee design finalization and tariff amendments are scheduled for Q3 2026, with FERC filing in Q4 2026. Most exposed are owners of traditional hydro and PSH facilities, whose seasonal accreditation and capacity revenue will depend on the ISO's measurement of DCap and the scaling methodology applied in summer resource-adequacy assessments.

The proposal recognizes that ESR charging for grid services differs fundamentally from traditional load consumption and is moving to the Planning Advisory Committee in August 2026 for tariff development, with feedback due August 7, 2026. For pumped-storage hydro, this lowers the cost burden on battery competitors in MISO's energy and reserve markets, eroding PSH's cost-of-operations advantage and potentially reducing PSH revenue from energy arbitrage and reserve provision when batteries can charge at lower net cost.

documents.title: BAL-001-TRE-2 Process
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ERCOT's primary frequency response (PFR) evaluation and performance-scoring process for generating units directly parallels hydro's obligations in NERC BAL-001-TRE; this document details compliance mechanics, performance thresholds, and exclusion processes that would apply to any dispatchable hydro or PSH in ERCOT, and serves as a cross-market reference for how frequency response rules are operationalized.
documents.ai_summary: ERCOT's BAL-001-TRE evaluation process establishes a rolling 12-month performance scorecard for all generating units' primary frequency response during Frequency Measurable Events (FMEs). Resources must maintain a rolling average PFR score of 0.75 or above; those failing to meet this threshold or scoring below 0.75 for three consecutive FMEs become subject to reduction in their Ramping Reserve Service (RRS) MW allocation based on past performance. Market participants have 30 days from MIS posting to request exclusions for legitimate operating conditions that impaired normal PFR performance; ERCOT makes final determinations, though the PDCWG may be asked to advise. This scheme links frequency-response performance directly to reserve-service capability — a dispatchable resource's ability to provide RRS is capped by its demonstrated PFR capability during disturbances, creating a performance-based ratchet on flexibility services.

documents.title: PDCWG Frequency Control Report for Jun 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ERCOT frequency control and inertia performance metrics establish cross-market comparison data on system frequency response and synchronous-inertia adequacy — hydro-rich RTOs use ERCOT's inertia trends and fast-frequency-response procurement (FFR awards) as benchmarks for their own frequency-support market design and to assess whether similar inertia-scarcity pressures apply to their fleets.
documents.ai_summary: ERCOT's June 2026 frequency control report shows CPS1 performance at 184.12% (12-month rolling average 181.97%), zero BAAL exceedances, and continued decline in synchronous inertia: minimum synchronous inertia hit 114.7 GW·s in March 2026 (down from 143 GW·s in 2016) at a system load of 48,013 MW, with non-synchronous generation comprising 81% of system load. ERCOT has awarded 430 MW of fast-frequency-response (FFR) capacity in 2026, up from 298 MW in 2025, indicating accelerating reliance on synthetic inertia products to manage declining synchronous capacity. For hydro operators in other RTOs, this illustrates the trajectory of inertia scarcity and the market mechanisms (FFR procurement curves, critical-inertia thresholds being lowered from 100 GW·s to 87 GW·s) now appearing in frequency-response design — a harbinger of similar pressures in hydro-dominant systems as wind and solar penetration rises.

documents.title: Regulation Analysis PDCWG Jul-26

documents.ai_summary: ERCOT Operations Planning presented a detailed analysis of regulation-service bias, wind and solar ramp-rate mean absolute errors (MAE), and time-error accumulation across three June periods (2024–2026). The analysis examines regulation deployment trends, regulation bias across consecutive 5-minute SCED intervals, zero-crossing patterns, and factors contributing to time-error accumulation (load, wind/solar ramps, unit start-up/shut-down, short-term load forecast error, and non-SCED large-load ramping). No regulatory proposal or vote is noted; this is a performance report to the PDCWG. Relevance to hydro: the document demonstrates how ERCOT—a non-hydro grid—addresses intra-hour flexibility, regulation bias mitigation, and ramp-management without access to hydro's inherent flexibility, informing comparative analysis of how hydro-rich markets (PJM, NYISO, CAISO, WEIM) design and deploy regulation and frequency-response products differently. documents.title: Revised Straw Proposal - Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design - Track-2 - Jul 17, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO's revised RAAIM design directly affects how hydropower and pumped-storage resources are assessed for availability during reliability events, changing the financial incentives and operational obligations tied to RA accreditation and performance metrics.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO proposes replacing its static, monthly Resource Adequacy Availability Incentive Mechanism (RAAIM) with an event-based framework that ties penalties to periods of elevated reliability risk, moving away from fixed Availability Assessment Hours and monthly averaging to more targeted assessments. The proposal integrates with UCAP-based accreditation: UCAP reflects historical availability in forward RA counting, while revised RAAIM assesses whether shown RA capacity is operationally available during identified reliability events. Hydro and pumped-storage operators face revised non-availability charges, modified must-offer obligations, and enhanced outage-substitution processes; the design recognizes different operating characteristics of resource types. This is a revised straw proposal with stakeholder working group feedback incorporated; next steps and comment deadlines are not stated in this excerpt.

documents.title: Presentation - Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design - Track 2 - Jul 22, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO's revised RAAIM (Resource Availability and Accuracy Incentive Mechanism) directly reshapes penalty exposure and revenue-recovery allocation for hydropower and storage resources during stress events, moving from a monthly netted assessment to per-event tiered triggers that substantially increase payoff volatility and compliance burden for use-limited resources.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO proposes overhauling its RAAIM availability-penalty mechanism, replacing a $4.40/kW-month fixed charge assessed over monthly AAH windows with event-based tiered pricing: Tier 1 (Elevated Reliability Risk) at day-ahead LMP, and Tier 2 (Critical Capacity Insufficiency, keyed to EDAM RSE failures) at $2,000/MWh. Hydro, storage, VERs, thermal, and DR would receive technology-specific treatment: hydro and thermal face shown-RA-based availability assessment against bids and outage status; storage's obligation is tied to SDM-modeled feasibility limits and SOC nonlinearity (not automatic outage exposure); VERs are exempted from low-wind/solar/ambient variability but remain exposed for forced equipment outages. Co-located and hybrid resources receive configuration-specific rules. The proposal eliminates the <1 MW exemption and tightens exemptions overall. Stakeholder feedback flagged that storage and hydro need duration, state-of-charge, and hydrologic limits recognized; that Tier 2 exposure should reflect cost causation not any EDAM failure; and that penalty exposure must not exceed shown RA. No vote or comment deadline is stated in this presentation; next steps are listed as pending.

documents.title: Straw Proposal - Storage Design and Modeling - Uplift, Default Energy Bids, and State-of-Charge Management - July 15, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO is fundamentally restructuring how storage resources bid, recover costs, and manage state-of-charge — directly affecting pumped-storage revenue recognition, mitigation treatment, and bidding complexity; default energy bids and uplift are core mechanisms for use-limited resource cost recovery.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO proposes a sequenced reform of storage market rules, starting with near-term enhancements to default energy bids and bidding structures, culminating in a draft final proposal by end of 2026 that integrates these changes with broader uplift redesign. The straw proposal recommends two approaches to replace the current static storage default energy bid: a time-of-day approach (ISO's preferred option, using scaled inputs from prior market processes and limited temporal differentiation) and a static approach; CAISO also proposes a 'greater-of' method for hybrid resource default bids based on the highest-cost component. The reframing section introduces a potential alternative bidding model where storage would submit a single bid reflecting the value of ending a period with more or less stored energy, replacing hourly bid-and-forecast submissions, intended to improve charging/discharging alignment and reduce operator complexity. Most exposed are pumped-storage operators currently relying on static default bids and hourly state-of-charge forecasting; the shift to time-of-day or reframed bidding will alter cost-recovery timing and mitigation exposure. Next steps include stakeholder feedback on this straw proposal, leading to draft final proposal by end of 2026.

documents.title: Presentation - Storage Design and Modeling - Jul 22, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO is redesigning default energy bids for storage and hybrids, which directly affects the opportunity-cost offer framework for pumped storage and creates a precedent being leveraged across EDAM/WEIM; storage DEB is the primary mitigation-compliant bidding pathway for PSH and energy-limited resources.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO is evaluating two methodologies to reform storage default energy bids (DEBs): a time-of-day approach that incorporates hydro DEB elements with hourly multipliers (1.4 pre-opportunity-cost hour, 1.0 after) and a static hydro-based approach. The time-of-day approach, currently preferred by CAISO, applies upward-only scaling of price proxies and addresses a core PSH challenge—that current static DEBs using day-ahead LMPs become 'stale' in real-time and prevent WEIM-only storage from accessing the DEB option at all. The time-of-day approach enables WEIM-only resources to use real-time DGAP and LMP scaling, and extends this framework consistently across EDAM and WEIM. A revised straw proposal is due September 2, 2026, with comments due September 30, 2026; final proposal is targeted for October 28, 2026. Pumped storage operators reliant on negotiated DEBs or using stale price proxies gain material upside if the time-of-day approach adopts the 1.4 multiplier on opportunity cost; conversely, stakeholders opposing time-of-day multipliers below 1.0 or favoring simpler hydro-based static methods will shape whether the structure is simplified or retained.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Interconnection Process Working Group met June 9, 2026, to review generator-queue procedures under FERC Order 2023 compliance. Key developments: (1) DPP 2026 cycle application deadline is September 10, 2026, with study cycle kick-off December 9, 2026; application fee (D1) is $7,600, with all projects in the cycle required to recalculate and 'true-up' fees every three years per GIP Section 3.6. (2) East (ITC) Regional Queue Cap has been met; the Queue Cap Tracker includes all submitted projects. (3) Expedited Resource Addition Study (ERAS) Cycle 4 is underway for six LSE projects (launched June 1, 2026); IPP requests are pending but proceeding as designed. (4) MISO reorganized its Resource Planning Team and is aligning DPP schedule with annual MTEP cycle, with Order 2023 requiring annual cluster studies. These procedural and fee changes affect cost, timing, and queue position for hydro and PSH projects seeking interconnection or uprates in MISO, especially those filing in DPP 2026 or competing within the regional cap; no comment deadline is stated in the minutes.

documents.ai_summary: The MISO-SPP JOA redline document updates interconnection procedures for requests spanning or impacting both RTOs' transmission systems, including cluster definitions, decision-point sequencing, queue-priority rules, and tie-line upgrade requirements. Key changes include: (1) cluster-definition language split by request date (pre/post April 1, 2026) to align with SPP's ICS terminology; (2) queue-priority rules shifted from Decision Point One/Two closure dates to anticipated start dates for Decision Point Two/subsequent points; (3) new provisions for Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue (JTIQ) portfolio screening and cost allocation; and (4) tie-line upgrade rules requiring the impacted party's result if the direct-connect party's upgrade is insufficient. Study-delay penalties begin with MISO DPP-2026 and SPP ICS-2030 clusters. The document is a redline in active working-group review; no vote date or next steps are stated in the excerpt. Hydro and PSH interconnection requests in either footprint or crossing the seam will face revised queue positioning and cost-allocation rules; generators and storage operators should monitor for final JOA adoption and board approval timelines.

documents.ai_summary: MISO and SPP are revising Section 9.4 of their Joint Operating Agreement to codify coordination procedures for SPP's new Interconnection Cluster Study (ICS) process, clarify affected-system study timelines and cost allocation on shared tie lines, and add a requirement that interconnection customers comply with Facilities Construction Agreements (FCAs) in the impacted party's tariff. Comments are due August 4, 2026; MISO expects to file with FERC by end of 2026 to early 2027, with an effective date 60 days after filing. Hydro generators seeking interconnection at the MISO-SPP seam will face new mandatory FCA execution timelines and clarified cost allocation for tie-line upgrades when both parties identify violations; projects in SPP's ICS clusters (2030 forward) will experience revised study schedules and delay-penalty provisions.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE's Capacity Auction Reforms–Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) proposal, with Q2 2027 effective date, introduces seasonal capacity procurement tied to accreditation reforms and a winter gas constraint. The document clarifies offer-formulation principles for resources whose accreditation (MRIC) differs from installed capacity, showing that resources exiting energy markets without a capacity sales obligation would face higher per-MW offer prices under MRIC-based accreditation than under prior QC methods. For imports and energy-limited resources, CAR-SA requires demonstration of 16-hour fuel availability for accreditation; external resources using stored fuel must show historical usable-inventory measures over past three like-seasons. Capacity Offers may include risk premia for pay-for-performance (PFP) costs, and the ISO is publishing offer-formulation guidance (contact: Jasleen Singh, jsingh@iso-ne.com) with questions due by the August Markets Committee. Most exposed are operators of energy-limited hydro and storage whose accreditation drops relative to summer nameplate, forcing higher per-MW asks in seasonal auctions to recover fixed obligations.

documents.title: 2026-07-21 MC A03b - CAR-SA: Offer Formulation Memo
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: This memo directly addresses offer formulation rules for ISO-NE's Capacity Auction and Resource (CAR) market, which determines how resources—including hydropower and pumped-storage facilities—calculate and submit capacity bids; the rules govern the cost basis (incremental costs, opportunity costs from Pay for Performance, annual-cost allocation) that hydro operators must use to stay competitive and avoid mitigation challenges, and it explicitly addresses the interaction between offer formulation and market-power mitigation thresholds.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE has issued a detailed guidance memo on how Capacity Resources should formulate competitive offers under the CAR-SA (Seasonal Accreditation) framework. The memo teaches that a competitive offer must equal the resource's expected incremental cost of accepting a Capacity Supply Obligation, including the opportunity cost of the PfP (Pay for Performance) scarcity-condition obligation and the cost of any annual-basis expenses allocated across seasonal offerings. The guidance explicitly advises market participants to consult the Internal Market Monitor (IMM) before submitting offers that may exceed the Capacity Offer Price Threshold or involve resource-specific concerns such as risk modeling or annual-cost treatment; the IMM cannot direct offer prices but can validate cost assumptions and whether expectations are reasonably justified. This creates a new compliance pathway for hydro and PSH owners in ISO-NE: operators allocating multi-year capex or seasonal energy availability into capacity-offer costs will need to pre-clear their methodology with the IMM to avoid triggering mitigation and price caps. The memo is comprehensive reference material (no vote or deadline stated) suitable for long-term corpus use by NHA members evaluating ISO-NE's cost-substantiation regime.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE's Internal Market Monitor reports that Winter 2026 (Dec 2025–Feb 2026) saw record $6.5 billion wholesale costs, with energy prices reaching $147.99/MWh day-ahead and $137.66/MWh real-time, driven by a 19-day cold snap in late January and 31% year-over-year rise in natural gas prices to $17.79/MMBtu. Opportunity-cost adders (EMOC) preserved 433 GWh of oil generation by allowing offers over the soft cap to $460/MWh day-ahead during scarcity. The NECEC transmission line (in service Jan. 16) initially improved day-ahead prices but caused poor day-ahead-to-real-time convergence during the cold snap; Quebec imports reversed during peak cold, forcing New England to export briefly. For hydro operators, the data illustrates how scarcity pricing and opportunity-cost mechanisms reward withholding of use-limited resources, how transmission reconfigurations (NECEC, LNG injection swings) reshape import/export flows and local clearing patterns, and how interregional cold events can reverse import directions — all material to hydro's revenue and positioning in regional exchange markets. documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ proposes adding an optional MUI/API parameter called 'Ambient Capacity Adjustment' to allow market participants to submit hourly ambient derates (such as temperature-dependent derate for thermal generators, but applicable to any resource with ambient sensitivity) rather than forcing them through the CROW system, which has technical volume limits. Currently, derates affecting must-offer calculations must be submitted in CROW at high frequency, risking dataflow congestion; the MUI already handles hourly resource data for Markets+, so SPP recommends shifting hourly/frequent ambient derates there while keeping longer-term forced outages in CROW. The proposal was presented to MORWG on May 27, 2026, and will be presented to MRATF on July 20, 2026, with protocol updates and an MIR (Markets+ Issue Resolution) to follow. For hydropower operators, this changes the technical pathway for submitting capacity adjustments driven by water temperature or other ambient factors that reduce available capacity within the same day or operating horizon — shifting to a more frequent submission path may reduce compliance friction but also clarifies the must-offer framework's application to use-limited resources.

documents.title: 05_WRAP Program Split _ Market impacts.pptx  [in MRAFT Meeting Materials 20260720.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: SPP Markets+ is restructuring its Operations Program and Forward Showing Program (WRAP), which directly affects how use-limited resources including hydro and pumped storage participate in resource-adequacy calculations, must-offer submissions, and market dispatch — a core revenue and obligation mechanism for Western hydro owners in the WRAP/Markets+ footprint.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ and WPP propose to split responsibilities for WRAP (Western Resource Adequacy Program): Markets+ will assume the Operations Program (real-time sharing and holdback optimization) starting October 2028 (Wave 2 go-live), while WPP retains the Forward Showing Program. The split requires governance changes to both programs and new tariff provisions; Markets+ will move holdback calculations and sharing-zone optimization into its market clearing engine, potentially expanding the resource pool to meet operational requirements and refining the fixed uncertainty calculation. WRAP binding-season participants not in Markets+ (including BPA, Idaho Power, Puget Sound Energy, Salt River Project, Seattle City Light, and others—many of them major hydro or hydro-hybrid operators) will participate under a limited-participation tariff model and must sign a Participation Agreement; governance will shift from the sunsetted MRATF to a new Markets+ Resource Access Working Group (MRAWG) effective Q3 2026. MPEC is expected to provide feedback or decision in August 2026, with MRAWG standing up in Q3 2026 and MRATF sunsetting Q1 2027.

documents.ai_summary: Markets+ is revising its Settlement Calculation Guide to allocate must-offer charges and credits from the Market Participant (MP) level down to Asset Owner (AO) level using load-ratio-share methodology. Currently, must-offer is assessed only at the MP level, leaving no AO-level settlement detail for invoicing, shadow-settlement audits, or determinant reporting. The proposed fix assigns MP-level must-offer amounts proportionally to each AO modeled under the MP for reporting and reconciliation purposes, while keeping financial responsibility at the MP. These changes (sections 2.6.17, 2.6.18, 2.7.26, 2.7.27 of the Calculation Guide) were reviewed at the June 2026 MSUF meeting and incorporated into the posted Guide without formal approval (no Tariff/Protocols changes required). Hydro and pumped-storage operators modeled as separate AOs under a single MP will now see their must-offer obligations and charges/credits broken out in settlement reports and invoices, improving visibility into compliance assessments and amounts due—critical for owners auditing weekly invoices and managing capacity-contribution risk.

MECHANISM: Non-firm load participation raises two direct concerns for hydro owners. First, if non-firm large loads are NOT counted toward resource-adequacy requirements (or counted with heavy discounts), the RA bar for other resources including hydro rises, while loads receiving scarcity benefit bear no capacity obligation — this inverts normal cost-allocation. Second, if non-firm loads ARE curtailed preferentially during scarcity events, hydro operators face reduced dispatch value in real-time scarcity periods, since the non-firm load absorbs the curtailment instead of pushing higher locational prices. MISO's design choices on RA treatment and curtailment-dispatch rules will determine whether non-firm loads are free-riders on hydro's scarcity value or are appropriately penalized. This affects all hydro in MISO, particularly reservoir and run-of-river operators in tight seasonal periods.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group (LLWG) is advancing four issues in H2 2026 that reshape how large loads integrate into the market: (1) Large Load Firm Service Step Up tariff revisions, with final redlines due August 27; (2) Large Load Reserve Product Enhancements (LLWG-2026-2), undergoing cost-allocation review with recommendations expected in Q4 2026; (3) Creation of Large Load BPM 032 governing conditional/nonfirm transmission service; and (4) newly launched 'Generation and Large Load Alignment' (LLWG-2026-6) and 'Non-Firm Large Load' (LLWG-2026-5) issues debuting July 16. These initiatives directly affect hydro owners' ability to serve large co-located loads, secure firm transmission for dispatchable assets, and coordinate generation dispatch with large-load operational requirements. Hydro operators in MISO should monitor the Generation and Large Load Alignment issue (LLWG-2026-6) and the firm service tariff redlines; the alignment framework may establish precedent for how synchronous, dispatchable resources (including run-of-river and reservoir hydro) must adapt real-time operations to synchronize with large-load demand profiles.

documents.title: 20260716 LLWG Item 07c BITS Proposal Alliant Energy
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: BITS enables large loads to interconnect and ramp into service on an interim basis while transmission upgrades are constructed, directly affecting hydro's strategic options for co-located load service, behind-the-meter arrangements, and the economics of load growth as a driver of scarcity value.
documents.ai_summary: Alliant Energy proposes Bridge Interim Transmission Service (BITS), a non-firm interim transmission product for large loads in MISO that allows service to begin once load interconnection studies are complete and local facilities are built, while required network upgrades are under construction—automatically converting to firm Network Integration Transmission Service (NITS) when upgrades finish. BITS requires load to have metering and telemetry in place, 24/7 contact availability, and ability to reduce load in 30 minutes if curtailed; loads are backed by accredited capacity resources and included in Module E forecasts. This removes a timing mismatch that has deterred large-load interconnection: hydro owners co-locating loads or offering behind-the-meter service can now ramp customers into service faster, capturing scarcity premiums from load growth without waiting years for transmission buildout. The proposal aligns with FERC's Large Load Show Cause Order (EL26-70) for MISO; Alliant seeks stakeholder feedback by August 7, 2026, and proposes FERC filing in Q4 2026 with implementation March 2027.

documents.ai_summary: MISO is developing a three-part framework to integrate large loads with accelerated interconnection timelines (120 days to GIA) and flexible transmission service options, including a novel Firm Service Step-Up mechanism and co-located generation-load arrangements (ZGIA). The framework addresses a FERC show-cause order and includes alignment of large-load and generation interconnection studies, new reserve product enhancements for large-load support, and real-time market pricing signals and demand-response products to coordinate large-load variability. Stakeholder feedback on tariff language and process details is due July 30, 2026, with filings on interconnection reliability requirements and ZGIA registration expected July 31, 2026. The Firm Service Step-Up and non-firm service options, combined with co-location rules, could enable pumped-storage and conventional hydro operators to participate as flexible resources backing large-load commitments or to co-locate generation with load behind a single point of interconnection—expanding the strategic toolkit for hydro assets in MISO, particularly those seeking firm transmission service without full generation-only interconnection costs.

documents.ai_summary: FERC issued a Show Cause Order to MISO on June 18, 2026 (195 FERC ¶ 61,212) directing tariff improvements to accommodate large load integration and resource adequacy. MISO is filing an informational report by July 20, 2026 addressing resource-adequacy tools, state roles, and current/under-development initiatives (Seasonal Planning Resource Auction, Reliability Based Demand Curve, Direct Loss Of Load accreditation, and a proposed Generation and Large Load Alignment coordinated study process). For hydro owners in MISO's footprint, this opens the door to rule changes in how resource adequacy is calculated and how large load growth affects accreditation requirements—particularly relevant to pumped storage and conventional hydro seeking to establish or maintain RA capacity value. The July 20 filing date triggers a FERC compliance timeline that will likely spawn tariff proposals through 2027.

documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes aligning large load studies with generation interconnection timelines to reduce delays, optimize network upgrades, and improve reliability assumptions. The proposal addresses a procedural bottleneck where signed Generator Interconnection Agreements (GIAs) are currently required before generation can be included in load studies, creating timing mismatches. MISO reports 27 GW of large load complete or under study in MTEP26, with 34 GW of newly-signed GIAs added in the past year, indicating rapid co-arrival of load and generation. For hydro owners, accelerated load-aligned transmission planning will expose more clearly which regions face generation scarcity (raising scarcity-pricing upside) and where existing hydro capacity becomes strategically constrained or critical to reliability — improving the business case for uprates, resource adequacy accreditation, and interregional export capability. The issue is under Large Load Working Group adoption; no deadline is stated in this excerpt.
