documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes a new streamlined process for studying large loads (250+ MW+) paired with associated generation in parallel, rather than sequentially, aiming to achieve MTEP approval and full study completion within 120 days (vs. 180+ days in current serial process). Outcomes include allocation of generation injection rights, transmission service for reliable load withdrawal, and optimized network upgrades; the proposal harmonizes with FERC's show-cause order (Paragraphs 114–118) on efficient infrastructure build to support large loads. The process imposes a $250,000 nonrefundable application fee per party, requires generation ≤150% of identified load need with firm offtake agreement, full site control through point of interconnection, and ability to reach commercial operation within 3 years; generation must transition to normal interconnection queue if load goes away. This is particularly relevant to pumped-storage and large hydro operators evaluating co-location with industrial or data-center loads—the faster study and clearer transmission-cost allocation could unlock new partnership models—and to all hydro owners tracking transmission-planning acceleration and the precedent it sets for generation-load nexus outside traditional firm-injection assumptions. Stakeholder feedback due July 30, 2026; tariff filing expected September 2026.

The option addresses load desire for expedited interconnection despite insufficient firm transmission service. This changes the operational and economic context for conventional hydro and pumped storage in MISO: faster load growth increases scarcity-pricing opportunities and frequency-response demand during tight conditions, but curtailable load rules may also reduce peak scarcity duration and shift dispatch incentives away from high-margin run-of-river generation toward storage/peaking units. Assignment to the Large Load Working Group indicates continued development; no deadline or vote date is stated in this issue-acceptance document.

Hydro owners (especially those in MISO footprint or considering it) should monitor MISO resource-adequacy and seasonal energy studies to assess whether accelerated load stepping raises scarcity rents during high-load, low-hydro periods, and whether co-location tariffs allow existing hydro to contract with stepping loads at intermediate thresholds.

documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes a Large Load Participation with non-firm Transmission option allowing data centers and other large loads to interconnect expeditiously without procuring firm transmission service, subject to curtailment under grid stress. The proposal touches resource adequacy (whether non-firm loads have capacity obligations), day-ahead/real-time energy and ancillary-service market participation, curtailment prioritization, and settlement—all of which reshape dispatch incentives and scarcity pricing that hydro relies on. MISO seeks stakeholder feedback by August 7, 2026, and intends to file a tariff no later than Q4 2026. Most exposed are hydro owners in MISO whose revenue from scarcity-driven energy prices and reserve products may compress if large non-firm loads reduce system tightness, and whose must-offer/dispatch obligations may shift if non-firm load is modeled separately in market clearing.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group is drafting tariff language (Attachment FF) governing transmission expansion planning and the participation of co-located generation and load under the ZGIA framework. This redline excerpt focuses on the MTEP (MISO Transmission Expansion Plan) process, which integrates interconnection planning, load interconnections, and transmission-to-transmission projects. The document includes restrictions on storage-as-transmission-only assets (SATOA): SATOA may only inject/withdraw energy to receive/provide the services for which it was included in the MTEP, and may NOT participate in energy, operating reserve, or PRA markets unless the tariff is later amended to allow cost-based revenue recovery for storage assets in those markets. For pumped-storage operators, this language constrains how PSH co-located with load or generation can use the ZGIA framework to monetize ancillary services, energy arbitrage, or capacity unless MISO later changes the tariff to permit broader market participation for storage cost-recovery assets. The restriction effectively quarantines SATOA participation pending future tariff reform. Most exposed are PSH owners considering ZGIA enrollment to serve co-located load or to participate in MISO markets; redlines are in draft and subject to LLWG review, with final tariff language still developing.

This framework enables co-located hydro and pumped-storage operations under state law, directly expanding the strategic options for hydro owners to serve large on-site loads (e.g., data centers) and avoid transmission congestion and market-power mitigation. Hydro owners evaluating small-hydro or hybrid co-location, or PSH with adjacent loads, must track how ZG interconnection eligibility, transmission-loss rules, and capacity-accreditation linkage to load forecasting affect economics; the tariff language also clarifies deliverability accreditation for energy-storage resources coupled with firm transmission. Large loads must establish separate CPNodes (pricing/settlement nodes) to prevent load-distribution skew between day-ahead and real-time models. This directly affects hydro owners with co-located generation or storage at large industrial facilities—they face clearer rules on whether plant-level generation participates in MISO markets or remains behind-the-meter, and how storage (BESS) and ramp-support devices are metered and dispatched. Feedback is due Monday, July 31, 2026.

documents.ai_summary: MISO has launched its 2026 Long-Range Transmission Planning (LRTP) process for the Midwest and South regions, with issue identification and solutions development following a seven-step process; solutions proposals are anticipated in 2027. The LRTP will assess reliability and load-serving needs across a 20-year horizon (CAGR ~1.5% annually) using Future 2 and 3+ scenarios that show resource and energy adequacy under MISO's 1-in-10-years Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) criterion. Hydro owners' revenue and dispatch flexibility are affected because transmission bottlenecks identified in LRTP feed into the solutions phase — constraints on interregional transfers or load pockets in the South region (Louisiana/Texas) directly impact where MISO can call on existing hydro for scarcity pricing and ramping services, and load growth shapes the baseline scarcity against which hydro's flexibility premium is valued. Feedback on Future scenarios is due June 17, 2026; solutions will be developed in 2027, making this the foundational study for MISO transmission expansion over the next decade.

documents.title: Item 04b – Michael Kurtz Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: PJM's proposed bifurcated capacity market directly affects how existing hydro and PSH generators are paid for capacity — the proposal would maintain short-term pricing with caps/floors for existing resources (including hydro) while creating uncapped long-term auctions for new entry, fundamentally altering existing-resource revenue certainty and scarcity pricing signals in a resource-constrained era.
documents.ai_summary: Michael Kurtz (Boehm, Kurtz & Lowry) presents a proposal to modify PJM's Path A, Option 2 capacity-market reform by creating a bifurcated market: a 'Legacy Auction' with one-year auctions and maintained price caps/floors for existing generation (projected 95.4% of capacity), and a 'Reliability Auction' with no price caps/floors for new generation (projected 4.6%), with blended pricing passed to non-Reliability-Backstop consumers. The proposal is framed as a middle path between PJM's conclusion that even $625/MW-day may be insufficient to attract new entry (versus real-world CC financing needing $633–$2,070/MW-day) and the risk of paying existing generators the premium needed for new construction, which Kurtz argues would constitute a windfall and violate the just-and-reasonable standard under the Federal Power Act. Existing hydro and pumped-storage generators would remain under the capped short-term regime, preserving their current rate treatment but constraining their upside if scarcity pricing rises; the proposal is presented to PJM's PRTMDW (Pricing, Risk and Transmission Market Design Working Group) on July 15, 2026, and reflects ongoing PJM resource-adequacy tensions triggered by supply-demand gaps and data-center load growth.

documents.title: Item 01a – Ron Mcnamara Phd Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Addresses PJM capacity adequacy and investment dynamics in a scarcity-driven environment shaped by data-center load growth and accelerated retirements — directly affecting hydro revenue through capacity-market pricing, resource-adequacy constructs, and the strategic value of dispatchable generation.
documents.ai_summary: Ron McNamara (First Principles Economics) presents a conceptual framework for PJM's capacity adequacy problem to the PRTMDW, arguing the root issue is inadequate investment, not market design per se. He emphasizes that restructured markets eliminated the guaranteed cost-recovery and stable counterparty that regulation provided, forcing capacity investment to compete as economic/commercial ventures bearing price, policy, and rule-change risks — a fundamentally different risk profile than pre-restructuring. McNamara recommends PJM adopt an agreed end-state vision (5–20 year horizon) against which all capacity proposals should be evaluated, with preferences for decentralized solutions and accelerated permitting/build timelines. The presentation does not propose specific rule changes but frames the investment-scarcity nexus as central to hydro's strategic positioning: in a market now "managing scarcity," the value of reliable, dispatchable generation (hydro's signature) rises, but only if the market and regulatory framework create stable revenue streams and counterparties for that capacity.

documents.title: Item 01b – Revisiting Root Causes And Their Implications In Pjms Powering Reliability Through Market Design – Pa Oca Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Addresses PJM's resource-adequacy crisis driven by data-center load growth and proposes alternatives to price-based solutions, directly affecting hydro's role in meeting reliability via capacity accreditation, pricing mechanisms, and interconnection/transmission planning for new resources.
documents.ai_summary: PA OCA argues that PJM's May 6th 'Powering Reliability Through Market Design' paper misdiagnoses the root cause of resource adequacy as price signals, when the real problem is the speed and scale of data-center interconnection outpacing infrastructure capacity. PA OCA rejects higher energy, capacity, and ancillary-service prices as the solution and recommends instead administrative approaches: mandatory data-center cost-sharing for new capacity, bilateral contracts, interconnection and transmission queue management, and ELCC reforms. The recommendation is preliminary; PA OCA requests PJM release bilateral-contracting feedback from suppliers and large loads to inform next steps. This reframing bypasses the price-centric architecture that would normally raise revenue for all dispatchable resources, including hydro, and instead emphasizes infrastructure buildout and queue/transmission reform—directly affecting which resources get built, when, and how their capacity is valued in RA frameworks.

documents.title: Item 04b – Bifurcated Capacity Market Under PJM Path A Option 2 – Michael Kurtz Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Proposal to bifurcate PJM's capacity market into separate auctions for existing and new generation directly affects revenue certainty, accreditation mechanics, and pricing for dispatchable resources including hydropower in a scarcity environment.
documents.ai_summary: Michael Kurtz (Ohio Energy Group) presents a proposal to modify PJM Path A, Option 2 by creating a bifurcated capacity market: a "Legacy Auction" continuing short-term (one-year) Base Residual Auction pricing with caps and floors for existing generation, and a separate "Reliability Auction" with uncapped, long-term pricing for new generation. The proposal addresses PJM's transition from surplus to scarcity management—the December 2025 BRA cleared at the $333/MW-day cap with 6,516 MW UCAP below reliability requirement—but avoids paying existing generators the premium long-term rates needed to attract new merchant capacity, instead using RMR authority and flexible pricing floors to retain older dispatchable units. Existing hydro and dispatchable resources would remain on short-term capacity pricing with caps, avoiding windfall effects, while new merchant capacity would access long-term revenue certainty in a separate clearing; a blended wholesale price across both auctions would flow to retail markets. The proposal implicitly treats all dispatchable generation (including existing hydro) as reliability units warranting cost-of-service or floor protection during scarcity, and no vote or comment deadline is stated in the presentation.

documents.title: Item 04c – Initial Considerations And Recommendations – Maryland Opc Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Directly addresses resource adequacy design and capacity market constructs affecting how PJM procures capacity, with implications for how hydro and storage resources are valued in reliability frameworks and compete against large-load-driven procurement signals.
documents.ai_summary: Maryland OPC (Offices of People's Counsel) presents initial recommendations for redesigning PJM's resource adequacy construct, arguing that uncertain large-load growth is artificially inflating capacity procurement requirements and cost allocation. The presentation proposes three design paths—(A) risk allocation, (B) reliability consequences, (C) E&AS reform incentives—and an alternative "Commit-to-be-counted" model requiring large loads to make verifiable capacity commitments, fund/bring new capacity, or accept priority curtailment before being added to shared RA obligations. This reframes the capacity market's demand side from forecasts to binding commitments, directly affecting which resources (dispatchable hydro, PSH, and storage) compete for RA accreditation and what price signals they face when loads have uncertain, non-binding demand profiles. The recommendation prioritizes cost-causation allocation—meaning new large loads, not ordinary customers, absorb reliability and cost risk—which can shift the investment incentive landscape for existing hydro and storage resources competing in capacity auctions.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Revised Straw Proposal on scarcity pricing (Day 2 of Phase 2 Price Formation Enhancements, July 14, 2026) modifies two mechanisms: (1) load-shed pricing extends the scarcity signal into both real-time dispatch (RTD) and 15-minute forecasting markets (FMM) when a BAA enters EEA Level 3 emergency and operators shed firm load, treating curtailed load as unserved demand to prevent market prices from collapsing; and (2) armed-reserve pricing adds an opportunity-cost adder in RTD to reflect when reserve capacity is released into energy markets, capturing the scarcity value that the 15-minute ancillary-service procurement (RTPD) process already recognizes. Both mechanisms include operational safeguards: operators can pause either mechanism, and the load-shed signal turns off after four cumulative hours of load shedding in a 24-hour window. The proposal defers comprehensive scarcity redesign to a future phase. Feedback on grouping, CAISO BAA treatment, load-shedding implementation options (verified MW vs. forecast approach), and whether the mechanisms adequately preserve scarcity signals without over-mitigation is requested before the draft final proposal.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Revised Straw Proposal reforms BAA-level MPM by grouping BAAs via Marginal Export Capacity and export-transfer connectivity (instead of testing each in isolation), subtracting interval-specific load-serving obligations from withholdable capacity, and mitigating only pivotal suppliers after a grouped BAA fails the 3PS test. CAISO BAA retains default-competitive status and will not be subject to the BAA-level test as a group — a deferent to concerns that economic intertie imports are undervalued by the current framework. The proposal advances grouping and LSO changes near-term but defers comprehensive scarcity pricing and CAISO BAA mitigation to a broader future phase, with Day 2 stakeholder feedback to focus on scarcity-pricing mechanics, implementation choices, and safeguards. For hydro operators, especially those with multi-BAA footprints or export capability (e.g., Northwest PSH and reservoir operators), the grouping and LSO logic could narrow the suppliers subject to mitigation during tight intervals, raising energy prices and ancillary-service value when genuinely pivotal capacity is constrained — but the deferral of scarcity pricing means no new scarcity-pricing adders are being adopted yet. Most exposed: large dispatchable generators and PSH with withholdable capacity in grouped BAAs; comment deadline not stated in document.

documents.ai_summary: PJM is implementing Regulation Redesign Phase 2 on December 1, 2026, replacing its one-signal bidirectional regulation product with two separate products: RegUp (operates above zero crossing) and RegDn (operates below zero crossing). Each product has its own market requirement MW (seasonal and hourly, possibly asymmetric), clearing price, performance metrics (score, mileage, bias factor), and settlement billing; resources will bid separately for each and receive independent awards, though only one product deploys in any given interval. Regulation market participants (including hydro operators) must submit RegUp/RegDn offers and parameters to the Markets Gateway sandbox immediately (deadline overdue), complete signal conversion testing (overdue), and prepare for cutover by December 1, 2026; a virtual open house is scheduled July 30, 2026, and special education sessions occur October–November 2026. For hydro and pumped-storage owners, this restructuring requires new offer engineering for each product and affects how flexibility revenue is recognized — operators will need to optimize bids separately for up and down regulation rather than offering a single bidirectional capability, potentially exposing separate value in each direction depending on system conditions and seasonal asymmetries.

Statistical analysis of participants in the ReliabilityFirst region between November 2023 and March 2025 shows significant improvements in Equivalent Forced Outage Rate (EFOR), Weighted EFOR, and Unavailability Factor (UF) among visited units compared to non-participating generators. Best practices shared include heat tracing, insulation, windbreaks, temperature monitoring, pre-staged supplies, and dual-fuel testing. Hydro operators selected for visits are identified by NERC GADS data, PJM eDART data, recent ownership changes, units deemed critical by the ISO, and black-start-capable units; visits are non-binding and not part of compliance enforcement, but recommendations and findings are documented in confidential reports. The expansion and formalization of this program signal PJM's prioritization of winter preparedness as a reliability obligation touching all generator types, and the demonstrated performance improvements may raise expected standards for forced-outage and unavailability metrics across the fleet.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's 2026 biennial review recommends keeping nine market-design issues inactive, including three with direct hydro impact: MSC-2020-1 (Using Storage as a Transmission Asset to Provide Market Services), MSC-2020-3 (Enhanced Hybrid Resource Participation Model), and MSC-2021-9 (Uncertainty Product in DA, RT, AS). MSC-2020-1 has been inactive since December 2022; MSC-2021-9 was reactivated in February 2024 but returned to inactive status in November 2024. These issues, once active, would expand PSH's ability to offer grid services beyond energy and ancillary services, unlock hybrid participation in MISO's markets, and introduce flexibility products that could shift PSH's revenue sources—but no work is scheduled before the next biennial review in 2028.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO's Independent Market Monitor proposes revisions to market-monitoring and mitigation rules (Module D) that directly touch offer validation, commitment-cost caps during tight conditions, and reference-level development for demand-response resources — mechanisms that affect how dispatchable and use-limited resources (including hydropower and PSH) are mitigated and priced in real-time and emergency conditions.
documents.ai_summary: The MISO Independent Market Monitor (Potomac Economics) presented stakeholder feedback on proposed Module D revisions to market-monitoring authority, duty-of-candor requirements, transmission withholding surveillance, and cost caps on startup/no-load offers during emergency-energy events and tight conditions. Key findings: Entergy and OMS MWG support IMM verification and capping of startup and no-load costs during emergencies (addressing very high offers submitted during winter storms not otherwise validated under tariff); the IMM is developing clarified authority to assess reference levels for demand-response and validate opportunity-cost components of startup offers (including costs from regulatory or emissions-based start restrictions). Redlined tariff language addressing stakeholder concerns on duty of candor scope, transmission "full capability" definition, and rule clarity is expected. Most affected are generators offering into tight/emergency conditions and demand-response resources used to validate reference levels; no vote date is stated.

documents.title: 20260709 MSC Item 06 IMM 2025 State of the Market Recommendations.pdf
documents.filename: 20260709 MSC Item 06 IMM 2025 State of the Market Recommendations.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Independent Market Monitor recommendations on capacity accreditation, emergency-range penalties, storage dispatch optimization, real-time capacity products, and interchange optimization directly affect hydro and PSH revenue through RA/accreditation rules, ancillary-service and reserve payments, and real-time energy pricing mechanisms.
documents.ai_summary: MISO's IMM presented 2025 State of the Market findings and six new recommendations to the Market Subcommittee on July 9, 2026. Key proposals affecting hydro and PSH include: (1) improved capacity accreditation with corrections to maintenance-margin calculations and modified off-control unit treatment (2025-5); (2) penalties on units failing to provide emergency output, with estimated impact of $5.6M on coal and $12M on gas/oil emergency-range capacity payments (2025-6); (3) reduced make-whole and reserve payments for deviating resources to strengthen dispatch-following incentives (2025-2); and (4) revival of existing recommendations for a real-time capacity product for 2–4 hour start resources (2020-1) and look-ahead dispatch optimization for storage management (2021-4). The report also flags 26.6 GW of projected load additions by 2030 and evening ramp demands up 50% year-over-year, driven by solar growth. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this summary document, but the recommendations are now before the Market Subcommittee for consideration of tariff filing. Hydro and PSH owners benefit from tighter accreditation rules that reduce overstated capacity claims by competitors, from enhanced real-time products that play to their flexibility, and from optimization of storage dispatch timing; they face potential penalties if emergency-range claims are overstated.

documents.title: 20260709 MSC Item 07 IMM Quarterly Report.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: IMM quarterly market-monitor report documents energy price formation volatility, storage resource participation and dispatch efficiency, contingency reserve shortages, capacity accreditation methodology, and interchange optimization affecting real-time pricing—all directly material to hydro revenue and PSH dispatch strategy.
documents.ai_summary: Potomac Economics' Spring 2026 IMM quarterly report to MISO Market Subcommittee (July 9, 2026) identifies rising evening net-load ramp demand (averaging 15 GW between 3–7 pm, up 45% year-over-year), 20 shortage-pricing intervals (nearly double prior year), and 187 intervals with negative system-wide prices as solar penetration increases. Energy Storage Resources (ESRs) now comprise 1.3 GW capacity, setting system and local prices in 5% and 16% of intervals respectively and providing 28% of regulation; a software flaw caused 7% ESR unavailability when outside state-of-charge limits, dispatching units inefficiently (e.g., above-max ESRs discharging into negative-price hours, below-min ESRs charging at >$200/MWh), now addressed with a July software fix. The report recommends optimizing MISO–SPP/PJM interchange through alternate real-time dispatch cases to lower volatility and average energy prices by ≥$2/MWh (saving >$40 million/year), and shifting existing-solar accreditation from 2–5 pm (68% summer) to 4–7 pm (∼50%) to correct over-crediting that artificially suppressed 2026 PRA clearing prices and reduced summer bids by $240/MW-day. Hydro and PSH owners should track storage accreditation methodology changes and price-volatility patterns as ESR fleet grows; the interchange optimization recommendation indicates MISO may adopt real-time co-optimization mechanics that would affect locational value and ramping-product revenue.

documents.title: 20260709 MSC Item 12 Enhance Reserve Deliverability for DA and RT Market (MSC-2026-2).pdf
documents.filename: 20260709 MSC Item 12 Enhance Reserve Deliverability for DA and RT Market (MSC-2026-2).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO's Regulation reserve market performance and clearing mechanism directly affects hydro and pumped-storage revenue from ancillary services (the largest and most volatile reserve product in MISO), the treatment of battery entry into Regulation markets, and potential automation of performance-based disqualification rules that could reshape how dispatchable and storage resources compete for reserve procurement.
documents.ai_summary: MISO staff presents an analysis of Regulation reserve clearing and performance deterioration: Regulation requirements roughly doubled on July 1, 2024 (to ~800 MW base), Regulation reserve prices rose 53% and mileage prices 71% year-over-year in 2025, yet non-performance penalties reached 31% of total Regulation revenue by 2025, with gas resource penalties rising more than 2x year-over-year. The document identifies that (1) Regulation performance is assessed only in settlement, after-the-fact, with no automated real-time feedback loop to disqualify poor performers (unlike offline Supplemental and STR); and (2) coal and gas performance has deteriorated while batteries have entered as significant Regulation suppliers. MISO staff indicate they are evaluating options to improve real-time clearing and performance monitoring, with next steps to follow. Pumped-storage operators should monitor this closely because: (i) rising Regulation prices increase PSH revenue exposure to that product, but (ii) potential automation of performance testing and real-time disqualification could advantage faster-ramping technologies (batteries) and penalize PSH and conventional hydro more heavily if response-time or consistency standards are tightened without accounting for hydro's multi-hour operational flexibility constraints.

documents.title: 20260709 MSC Item 11 FTR-ARR Market Enhancements (MSC-2025-5).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO is evaluating the Auction Revenue Right (ARR) nomination and Financial Transmission Rights (FTR) allocation process, which directly affects how transmission-hedging revenue flows to generation owners, including hydropower and pumped-storage facilities that rely on point-to-point FTR positions for congestion hedging and revenue certainty.
documents.ai_summary: MISO is conducting a holistic review of its ARR/FTR market under FERC Order 681/681-A compliance constraints, with focus on the ARR nomination process (Reference Year, definition of baseload supply resources), changes to the allocation of ARRs into monthly MPMA auctions, and improvements to transmission-outage reporting incentives. The current ARR allocation uses a fixed Reference Year tied to historical transmission usage to balance stability against gaming and accords long-term (10-year rollover) financial rights to Load Serving Entities for power supply hedging; MISO is evaluating whether the Reference Year, RSP definition, or tariff execution rules should be modified, while ensuring full funding of existing LTTRs and no introduction of new gaming opportunities. MISO requests stakeholder feedback by July 23, 2026, and will present next steps and proposed outage-reporting mechanisms at the August MSC meeting. Most exposed are generation owners (particularly hydropower and storage) whose ARR holdings and FTR self-scheduling optionality depend on stable path valuations; changes to Reference Year or baseload definitions could shift which generation types retain long-term transmission-hedge access.

documents.ai_summary: MISO filed tariff revisions (ER26-2705-000, effective date August 4, 2026) to update demand curves for Regulation, Spinning Reserves, and Up Ramp Capability (URC) in response to rapid solar penetration and net-load ramping stress. Regulation and Spinning curves are being simplified to a single $98/MWh value, and the URC cap rises to $96/MWh to strengthen market signals during tight conditions. Separately, MISO is advancing 'Enhance Reserve Deliverability for DA and RT Markets' (MSC-2026-2) with most stakeholder feedback supportive, and pursuing updates to the Freeze Date congestion-management construct along MISO seams (jointly with PJM, SPP) to improve interregional coordination. These changes directly affect the price and procurement of flexibility and ramping products hydro supplies; URC and Regulation are primary revenue streams for dispatchable hydro and pumped storage. No comment deadline is stated for the demand-curve filing beyond FERC's statutory review.

documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes revised rules for allocating Real-Time Revenue Sufficiency Guarantee (RRSG) Constraint Management Charges to electric storage resources, distinguishing treatment by day-ahead and real-time commitment status (Charge, Discharge, Available, Continuous). The rules separately govern deviations prior to and after the Notification Deadline, using Economic Minimum/Maximum Limits and Hourly Integrated Forecast constraints to determine which storage deviations trigger charges. PSH operators face altered settlement exposure depending on whether they are committed to charge, discharge, or remain available — with charges assessed when real-time dispatch deviates from day-ahead schedules in ways that increase active transmission-constraint flow. Most exposed are pumped-storage facilities with multi-hour round-trip commitments, where transitions between commitment states and forecast adjustments near the Notification Deadline will materially affect hourly net revenue. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this excerpt; this appears to be a working redline under MSC review.

documents.title: 20260709 MSC Item 13 Evaluation of Updates to Congestion Management and TCDCs (MSC-2026-6).pdf
documents.filename: 20260709 MSC Item 13 Evaluation of Updates to Congestion Management and TCDCs (MSC-2026-6).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO is evaluating transmission constraint demand curves (TCDCs) and congestion management during reserve shortages, which directly affects how dispatch and pricing decisions treat dispatchable generation—a core revenue mechanism for hydro—and how make-whole payments (DAMAP) are triggered when congestion and reserve scarcity interact.
documents.ai_summary: MISO is evaluating updates to transmission constraint demand curves (TCDCs), which cap the shadow prices the market will pay to enforce network constraints, with particular focus on how undersized TCDCs interact with operating-reserve shortages to cause manual redispatches and Day-Ahead Marginal Assurance Payment (DAMAP) uplift. The document illustrates how reserve scarcity can overwhelm congestion signals, forcing resources down post-facto and triggering make-whole payments (e.g., Winter Storm Elliott example). MISO is considering expanding TCDC breakpoints, adding steps that increase during reserve shortages, and adjusting weighting between base and contingent constraints; a feedback request and implementation plan will be shared later in 2026. Dispatchable generators (including reservoir hydro) are most exposed: when reserves are scarce, high MEC penalties can force dispatch back to EcoMax despite binding constraints, then manual redispatch down creates the DAMAP liability. Hydro owners should track this work because enhanced TCDCs or dynamic reserve-shortage scaling could improve real-time economic dispatch and reduce the frequency of out-of-market corrections.

documents.ai_summary: ERCOT's May 2026 operations report documents system conditions during a month with record-high renewable penetration (86.77% at peak) and extreme net-load ramps (16,825 MW over 60 minutes on 5/2/2026), managed through 76 reliability unit commitments for capacity and two frequency events met by synchronous unit trips. The report shows how a low-hydro, predominantly thermal/renewable system accommodates multi-GW ramp rates and high wind/solar variability—a contrast to hydro-rich RTOs where flexible ramping and frequency response from conventional hydro avoid equivalent RUC commitments. documents.ai_summary: ERCOT is reviewing its 2027 ancillary-services (AS) methodology for Regulation, Responsive Reserve Service (RRS), and reserve procurement (ECRS/Non-Spin), with votes scheduled August 5–6, 2026, and PUCT approval targeted November–December 2026. The 2026 methodology introduced a probabilistic framework for reserve procurement; 2027 will refine that engine by testing sensitivities in risk inputs (forecast error, forced outages), risk credits (headroom discounts for already-committed capacity), and convergence criteria, while separately monitoring whether large-load ramping (up to 400+ MW spikes) requires a new Regulation adjustment factor. ERCOT noted that inertia trends have shifted lowest-inertia hours from night to midday since 2025, affecting RRS requirements keyed to inertia and frequency-response obligations (NERC BAL-003 IFRO); 2027 RRS quantities remain pending NERC's 2027 IFRO assessment. The sensitivity analysis will compare risk levels (Watch, EEA1, EEA2 vs. Load Shed Probability targets of 1-in-10/5/1-year), look-ahead windows (1–6 hours), risk credits (current 60% night / 25% day vs. higher levels), and solar forecast-error logic. This is a reference point for how non-hydro-dominant RTOs structure flexibility and reserve procurement under high renewable penetration and intra-hour load volatility.

documents.ai_summary: ERCOT DWG proposes PGRR 122, setting a 3,200 MW stability threshold for total load loss across P1/P2/P4/P5/P7 single contingencies and certain multi-event scenarios. When this threshold is exceeded, ERCOT will first evaluate transmission solutions (capital cost cap: $200M), then may limit Large Load interconnection allocation, and finally apply operational mitigation (IROLs, real-time curtailment) as backstop. This creates a new transmission constraint and potential dispatch curtailment mechanism that could affect hydro owners with co-located large loads or those operating in constrained areas where operational mitigation is invoked; the proposal is advancing to ROS (Reliability and Operations Subcommittee) for action, with implementation language refinement ongoing as of the July 9, 2026 meeting.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO's DDEMI Track 1 proposal would allow demand response aggregations to include behind-the-meter exports from utility-authorized end-use customers (e.g., rooftop solar + battery, behind-the-meter pumped storage), while capping the aggregation's net export at the resource level rather than the individual-customer level. Currently, customers exporting more than they consume are 'zeroed out' individually, preventing aggregators from accessing the full export capability of behind-the-meter storage; the proposal shifts the floor from customer to aggregation level to reflect market topology. This affects how pumped-storage and battery-backed demand response resources are metered, settled, and compensated for their dual load-curtailment and export capability. Stakeholders have until July 16, 2026 to submit written comments; the proposal applies to both Proxy Demand Resource (PDR) and Reliability Demand Response Resource (RDRR) models across all BAAs.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ Design Working Group is adopting a new registration and modeling framework for 'dynamically scheduled quasi-pseudo-ties'—external resources that are modeled as pseudo-tied into a participating BAA for Markets+ purposes while remaining dynamically scheduled (not formally tied) between Native BA and Attaining BA per NAESB standards. The framework adds a new resource designation to Section 9.1.1 and creates two pathways: formal electronic pseudo-ties (Section 9.1.9.1) and dynamically scheduled quasi-pseudo-ties (9.1.9.2–9.1.9.3). This clarification benefits external hydro plants and other resources in adjacent balancing authorities that wish to participate in Markets+ while preserving existing dynamic-schedule operations, reducing administrative ambiguity and enabling more consistent participation pathways. The framework is documented in Markets+ Protocols version 12.0a; this is SPP's comment form on the MIR with proposed edits, indicating the proposal is in design and comment phase.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: This document establishes the Markets+ Revision Initiative Request (MIR) process — the governance procedure by which hydro and storage owners can submit proposals affecting Markets+ Tariff, Protocols, and systems. Understanding who can submit MIRs, what qualifies as a complete submission, routing to working groups, and approval pathways directly determines hydro's strategic option to initiate rule changes affecting revenue, obligations, and operational flexibility in the SPP Markets+ footprint.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ has adopted and clarified a Revision Initiative Request (MIR) Process (effective November 13, 2025; current version 2.0 as of May 12, 2026) governing how stakeholders submit and advance proposals to change the Markets+ Tariff, Protocols, and related documents. Qualified Entities—including any Markets+ Participant, SPP Staff, the Market Monitoring Unit, governmental authorities, and SPP Members—may submit MIRs via the RMS using a standardized Submission Form; incomplete submissions are rejected and resubmitted by deadline. Submissions are routed by Primary Policy Coordination staff to the appropriate Primary Working Group (MDWG for Tariff/Protocols/MIR Process itself) and Secondary Working Groups; comments must be filed within five business days of Primary WG scheduling and are posted within three days. The Primary Working Group (e.g., MDWG) approves or rejects changes, which then route through Secondary WGs, the Markets+ Participant Executive Committee (MPEC), and the Markets+ Independent Panel (MIP) for final approval; system-change MIRs receive impact analysis (scope, budget, timeline, staffing implications, alternatives) within 30 calendar days of Primary WG approval. This process is the formal gateway by which hydro and PSH owners can propose market-design changes—faster than new tariff proceedings but still multi-stage—and affects what rule changes are feasible to pursue in Markets+.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Interconnection queue management and transmission service request processing timelines directly affect hydro's ability to submit and advance generation or storage interconnection requests, and alter the practical timing constraints on transmission-service applications.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ proposes revising its OASIS Queue Pause rules (MIR82-R) to allow individual Transmission Service Providers (MTSPs) flexibility in managing transmission service requests during the Day-Ahead Market window, rather than imposing a uniform mandatory pause. The revision shifts from a hard pause to a managed-pause model, requiring each MTSP to document its own queue-management procedures and coordinate with Market Operator timelines while preserving request prioritization. The change addresses NAESB WEQ 001-4.13 timing-compliance concerns SPP Legal identified as preventing a global waiver; it moves the choice of queue-management approach to individual MTSPs. The MDWG is scheduled to approve MIR82-R on July 8, 2026, with MPEC approval targeted for August 25, 2026. Hydro and storage interconnection applicants relying on queue advancement in the day-ahead timeframe should monitor which MTSP service territories are affected and what queue-pause conditions each MTSP implements under the new flexibility provision.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: INTERCONNECTION/TRANSMISSION: PSE's comments on Markets+ MTSP queue-pause rules affect transmission service request (TSR) processing timing and how interconnection queues coordinate with day-ahead market timelines — a core strategic issue for hydro and storage seeking new capacity or deliverability upgrades in the Markets+ footprint.
documents.ai_summary: Puget Sound Energy proposes revising Markets+ tariff and protocol language governing when Transmission Service Providers must pause or manage processing of transmission service requests relative to Day-Ahead Market operations. PSE seeks clarification on queue-processing definitions, pause triggers, and the duration of TSRs subject to pause, proposing language that allows each MTSP to determine queue-management conditions based on its own operational requirements rather than adhering to a universal pause obligation. The revision aims to reduce administrative burden, enhance market–transmission coordination, and improve transparency by requiring MTSPs to document and publish their queue procedures. This affects hydro and storage developers' ability to move TSRs through interconnection queues smoothly and predictably; interconnection queue timing and coordination with market operations directly shape the cost and speed of new capacity coming online and existing-plant uprates, both strategic levers for fleet adequacy decisions.

documents.title: 11-WRAP Program Split _ Market impacts.pptx  [in MDWG Meeting Materials 20260708.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document addresses governance and market-system integration affecting how WRAP binding-season participants (including hydropower owners) interact with Markets+ operations, which directly impacts must-offer rules, holding requirements, resource-sharing calculations, and operational-program settlements affecting hydro revenue and compliance obligations.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ and the Western Renewable Power Pool (WPP) are proposing to split operational responsibilities: starting October 2028 (Wave Two go-live), Markets+ will assume WRAP's operations-program functions (including sharing calculations, holdback optimization, and reserve-zone coordination), while WPP retains the forward-showing program. WRAP binding-season participants (including Bonneville Power Administration, Avista, Idaho Power, Puget Sound Energy, and others) who are not full Markets+ members would participate under a limited-tariff model and must sign participation agreements; governance changes and a new Markets+ WRAP-focused working group (MRAWG, standing up Q3 2026) will address tariff bifurcation, settlements, and coordination between the two programs. For non-Markets+ WRAP participants and full Markets+ members alike, the move integrates holdback inputs, must-offer ceilings, and sharing calculations into the M+ market-clearing engine, potentially refining uncertainty inputs and expanding the resource pool eligible to meet load via reserve zones. MPEC feedback/decision is scheduled for August 2026.

documents.title: 12-MIR8.1-R MSR SOC Management draft language.docx  [in MDWG Meeting Materials 20260708.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Modifies state-of-charge management rules for Market Storage Resources (MSRs)—pumped storage's core participation model in Markets+. Shifts from participant-forecast to market-operator calculation of SOC within Day-Ahead and RUC studies, directly affecting PSH dispatch feasibility, financial penalties for forecast mismatches, and capacity commitment reliability—a use-limited-resource obligation that hydro owners must track.
documents.ai_summary: SPP and the MSR Subgroup propose enhanced MSR state-of-charge management by introducing time-coupled intervals in Day-Ahead Market and RUC studies, allowing the market operator to calculate SOC rather than relying solely on participant forecasts. Currently, market participants bear full responsibility for SOC prediction in their Resource Offers, creating risk that Day-Ahead commitments become infeasible in real-time and expose operators to financial penalties and capacity shortfalls. The proposal—submitted as draft tariff and protocol language—reduces the burden on MSR participants by enabling more accurate SOC tracking across study horizons. Pumped-storage operators in Markets+ should review whether this shifts SOC management burden away from them and how it interacts with their obligation to register loss-factor parameters and directional commitment limitations.

documents.title: 13-MIR8.2-R Co-Located Resource Constraints draft language.docx  [in MDWG Meeting Materials 20260708.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Co-located resource constraint mechanism directly affects how pumped-storage hydro and paired-resource portfolios are dispatched, offered into must-offer obligations, and accounted for at injection-constrained points — a novel market design rule that creates or removes revenue optionality for PSH and hybrid hydro installations.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ proposes a new Co-Located Resources Constraint mechanism (MIR8.2-R) that formalizes 'clipping' — transferring MWs between co-located resources behind a single interconnection point when their combined capacity exceeds the injection limit. The rule applies to Day-Ahead Market, RUC, and Real-Time Balancing Market, with the market-clearing engine respecting whichever is lower: the sum of individual resource capacities or the declared co-located constraint. Critically, must-offer obligations for co-located resources use the same lesser-of logic, meaning a PSH facility paired with solar (for example) could see its must-offer requirement capped by the injection limit rather than its full capacity. This changes the dispatch flexibility and revenue recognition for PSH in portfolios with injection constraints, and improves market visibility into actual MW availability at the point of interconnection. The draft language touches tariff definitions, participation rules, must-offer requirements, and settlement guidance; status and comment deadline not stated in this excerpt.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: SHOC (Seasonal Hydroelectric Offer Curve) is a hydro-specific offer-formation mechanism in Markets+; the choice of default pricing hubs directly affects the short-term energy component of hydro revenue and bid development.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ is proposing to define default electric pricing hubs for the Seasonal Hydroelectric Offer Curve (SHOC), which currently contains a 'TBD' placeholder in Appendix D, Section D.7.f of the Markets+ Protocols. SHOC's short-term component is indexed to peak day-ahead prices and on-peak monthly futures at a default hub; the hub choice determines the price signal hydro generators see when structuring seasonal offers. Candidate hubs include Mid-Columbia (Northwest) and Palo Verde (Arizona), selected by liquidity (≥2,000 MWh average daily volume or ≥5 transactions/counterparties) and location (footprint representation, regional fit). The MMU will submit an MIR for MDWG approval in August 2026, with MPEC approval targeted for August or November; hydro operators in Northwest and Southwest regions should monitor hub selection, as basis between their resource location and the default hub will shape the financial foundation of SHOC bids.

documents.ai_summary: SPP staff (Dan Kheloussi) submitted MIR 36.1-R to clarify Markets+ Protocol sections 4.2.3.3 and 9.1.14, refining the validation criteria and operational mechanics for High Priority Export System Sales tied to LRE slice-of-system resources during WRAP Binding Seasons. The proposal designates exports as "High Priority" when they originate from an LRE's WRAP-reserved seasonal surplus (monthly positive difference between QCC capacity, contract adjustments, and forward-showing obligation) or are backed by WRAP forward showings or holdbacks; pro-rata reduction rules apply when aggregate High Priority e-tags exceed available seasonal surplus. This streamlines administrative handling of export bids and aligns LRE seasonal-surplus accounting with export authorization, reducing financial risk for market participants maximizing seasonal flexibility sales. Implementation is targeted for Q1 2027, with MPEC approval sought in Q3 2026.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ proposes MIR90-R, which codifies the first-ever dispute resolution process between Market Participants and the MMU, covering three categories: reconsideration of market-monitor decisions, verification of actual costs over $1,000, and validation of mitigated offers. documents.title: Item 04 1 – Offer Verification Exception Request Timeline Definition – Problem Statement
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Defines submission timelines for offer-verification exception requests supporting high-cost offers in PJM, directly affecting how dispatchable resources including hydropower can justify offers above $1,000/MWh and recover make-whole payments when offers are rejected.
documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes to clarify and revise the deadline for submitting exception requests and supporting documentation when offers exceeding $1,000/MWh fail Markets Gateway validation. Currently, Manual 11 Attachment D requires submission by 11:00 AM EPT the next business day—a deadline from 2017 that PJM considers burdensome during extended winter Offer Verification events and outdated given enhanced Markets Gateway functionality. PJM seeks input on a revised timeline that would reduce the administrative load on Market Sellers while maintaining the integrity of the exception process. This directly affects any generator (including hydro and PSH) that must justify high-cost operating or opportunity-cost offers to recover make-whole uplift; a more relaxed timeline lowers operational burden during winter resource-scarcity events when such offers are most likely.

documents.title: Item 04 2 – Offer Verification Exception Request Timeline Definition – Issue Charge

documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising the deadline timeline in Manual 11, Attachment D for Market Sellers to request after-the-fact make-whole payments following Offer Verification events—a procedure triggered when equipment limitations or extraordinary market conditions prevent full energy output. The timeline, written in 2017, is being modernized to align with PJM's enhanced Markets Gateway functionality, which now allows faster upload and documentation of offer data and supporting materials. Work is assigned to the Market Implementation Committee under Quick Fix (Tier 1) process with a two-month duration and solution target before winter 2026 operations; no tariff changes are in scope. Hydro operators relying on make-whole recovery after unplanned or operational constraints during tight conditions should monitor the revised deadline to ensure timely claims.

documents.ai_summary: PJM is documenting the offer-verification exception-request process timeline in Manual 11, Section 2.3.6.2: generation owners whose resource offers fail the offer screen have 60 calendar days following the operating day to submit an exception request with cost documentation via Markets Gateway, supported by the Market Monitoring Unit. If Markets Gateway is unavailable, owners must email EnergyOfferVerification@pjm.com and MMU_Energy_Offers_Review@monitoringanalytics.com with unit name, operating date/time, cost calculation per Manual 15 (Cost Development Guidelines), and PJM dispatch contact details. This deadline and procedural specification is foundational to how hydro and storage operators defend cost-based offers against failed screens and maintain eligibility for dispatch, LMP setting, and operating-reserve credits — particularly relevant for storage operators and pumped-hydro plants offering complex cost structures that may not fit automated validation logic.

documents.title: Item 04 4 – Offer Verification Exception Request Timeline Definition – PJM Proposal
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Offer verification and make-whole procedures directly affect the revenue compensation mechanism for generation resources (including hydropower) committed by PJM when cost-based offers exceed $1,000/MWh; changes to the submission timeline and process documentation alter compliance obligations and settlement deadlines.
documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes updating Manual 11, Section 2.3.6.2 and Attachment D to clarify and extend the deadline for submitting offer-verification exception requests in support of incremental offers exceeding $1,000/MWh from 11:00 EPT on the business day following the operating day to 60 calendar days following the operating day. The change aligns the exception-request deadline with other PJM settlement deadlines and reflects enhancements to the Markets Gateway fuel-price exceptions functionality, deferring to email backup if tool outages occur. Generation owners (including any committed hydroelectric or pumped-storage units) will gain substantially more time to review bills, gather supporting documentation, and submit requests before the 60-day window closes, reducing the risk of forfeiting make-whole credits; the 60-day deadline also provides PJM, the MMU, and markets with certainty on settlement closure. Most affected are owners of committed units with cost-based offers that fail the automated screening and require after-the-fact verification to set LMP or receive operating-reserve credits.

documents.ai_summary: PJM is implementing Regulation Redesign Phase 2, effective December 1, 2026, which bifurcates the single bidirectional regulation product into two separate products: RegUp (above zero crossing) and RegDn (below zero crossing), each with its own requirement MW, clearing price, offer parameters, performance metrics, and settlement. Hydropower and pumped-storage resources must submit RegUp and RegDn offers and parameters in the Markets Gateway sandbox by overdue deadline and complete signal-conversion testing to participate; PJM is holding a virtual open house on July 30, 2026, and market open is scheduled for November 25, 2026. This redesign increases the complexity and granularity (from hourly to 30-minute) of regulation participation, requiring hydro owners to develop separate bidding strategies for each directional product and validate system integrations before go-live.

documents.title: Item 07 1 – Periodic Review Of Default CONE And Acr Values
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CONE and ACR values directly determine the Minimum Offer Price Rule (MOPR) floor bids and Market Seller Offer Cap (MSOC) that apply to all capacity-market resources in PJM, including hydropower and pumped storage; changes to these values alter the competitiveness and profitability of hydro's participation in the capacity auction.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is updating its default Gross CONE (Cost of New Entry) and Gross ACR (Avoidable Cost Rate) values for delivery years 2030/2031, which feed directly into MOPR floors for new resources and MSOC offer caps for existing resources under Attachment DD §§ 5.14(h-2) and 6.4. Brattle Group and Sargent & Lundy are conducting the analysis; PJM will present draft values to the MIC in July 2026, with final values going to the MRC and MC for an advisory vote in August, and tariff filing at FERC by October 1, 2026. The update includes tax-law adjustments (100% bonus depreciation reinstatement) and revised overnight-capital and fixed-O&M assumptions from EIA 2026 and the 2025 Quadrennial Review. For hydropower and pumped storage operators, the revised Gross ACR directly impacts the offer cap applied to their existing units; a lower ACR narrows the band within which they can bid and may compress margins, while higher ACR provides headroom. The preliminary Gross CONE values span from $298–$4,403/MW-day depending on technology and delivery year, and Battery Energy Storage is preliminarily set at $502–$696/MW-day, which establishes a competitive benchmark for long-duration storage against which PSH will be evaluated for capacity qualification. Deadline for FERC filing is October 1, 2026.

documents.title: Item 10 1 – Energy Storage Resource Model Enhancements – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's ESR model design directly determines how pumped-storage hydro and battery storage compete for capacity accreditation, ancillary-services revenue, and energy-market dispatch—the core mechanisms by which storage owners recover fixed costs and optimize multi-hour operating decisions.
documents.ai_summary: PJM presented its current Energy Storage Resource (ESR) participation model, covering opt-in market participation, state-of-charge tracking, ancillary-services eligibility, cost-offer development, and capacity accreditation. The ESR model is a self-schedule framework (no PJM commitment); resources offer as one continuous resource with charge/discharge modes and optional SOC parameters, but PJM does not track SOC in dispatch and offers very limited opportunity-cost recovery for forward energy-limited constraints—a structural gap that disadvantages use-limited resources like pumped storage competing against batteries. Capacity accreditation uses class-based ELCC (4, 6, 8, 10-hour durations), and PSH with shorter physical duration can derate to match a longer ELCC class, but there is no explicit mechanism for PSH to reflect seasonal or hydrological variation in available energy. This presentation supports an active stakeholder issue charge on ESR model enhancements; no vote or comment deadline is stated in the slides, but the mention of a published position paper and ongoing stakeholder process signals that PJM is revisiting the model as the battery storage pipeline grows (8.4 GW under construction or in Cycle 2, 66.5 GW proposed).

This affects any hydro or storage operator whose cost-based energy offers rely on fuel-cost documentation; if PJM's policy shifts toward executable pricing or tightens affiliated-supplier treatment, it could change how operators substantiate offer reasonableness or hedge fuel-cost uncertainty in their bids. documents.ai_summary: PJM and Brattle Group have updated the 2026 Gross Avoidable Costs (GAC) for existing generation resources, a key input to PJM's Avoidable Cost Rate (ACR) mechanism used in capacity market accreditation and market-power mitigation. Hydro (3,275 MW) and pumped storage (5,232 MW) are classified separately as 'Unit Specific' resources, meaning no standardized cost range will be applied; instead, these resources will require individualized cost analysis. Other resources (natural gas, coal, nuclear, wind, solar, and new 4-hour battery storage) receive fleet-wide representative-plant cost ranges. The document represents initial analysis and solicits stakeholder feedback before finalizing the 2026 ranges. Most exposed are hydro and PSH owners seeking capacity accreditation or participating in must-offer/reference-level calculations—the 'Unit Specific' designation implies PJM views each facility's avoidable cost as too variable to fit fleet-wide formulas, which may shift negotiation burden from standardized rules to individual plant audits. Hydro and PSH operators benefit when this mechanism improves accuracy of LSE reserve obligations: precise allocation signals encourage load-serving entities to procure capacity-constrained products (like the ramping and storage flexibility hydro and pumped storage supply) at times of actual scarcity rather than all-hours forecasts. documents.title: 20260708 RASC Item 07 24 Hour Lead Time in Accreditation (RASC-2026-1).pdf
documents.filename: 20260708 RASC Item 07 24 Hour Lead Time in Accreditation (RASC-2026-1).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO proposes three alternative rules for how offline resources' capacity accreditation should be calculated based on lead time, which directly affects how thermal and hydro peaking units can be credited toward resource-adequacy showings during emergencies — the key revenue mechanism for dispatchable generation.
documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes three solutions to close a perceived gap in its 24-hour lead-time accreditation rule for offline resources. The problem: thermal generators increased their start-time lead times approaching Winter Storms Fern, Enzo, and Heather, rendering 3.1 GW unavailable for commitment in the Day-Ahead Market and Forward Reliability Assessment Commitment (FRAC) processes while still receiving full accreditation value, despite contributing to emergency deployment of LMRs. Solution 1 (12-hour max lead time) aligns offline-resource accreditation with the Operating Margin calculation but risks uneconomic commitments. Solution 2 (zero availability for lead-time increases within 48 hours of the operating day) would penalize changes near emergencies but allow longer-lead resources to participate in multi-day FRAC. Solution 3 (sliding scale: full availability at 4 hours, declining 5% per hour to zero at 24+ hours) offers graduated incentives. MISO will select a recommended solution in August 2026, file revised tariff at FERC in October 2026. Stakeholders should comment by July 22, 2026. Pumped-storage and conventional-hydro operators should monitor because the same accreditation rules govern their RA value; any tightening of lead-time rules that penalizes start-time flexibility, or that creates asymmetries between thermal and hydro accreditation, could compress the capacity credit PSH and peaking hydro claim during peak-scarcity periods.

documents.filename: 20260708 RASC Item 06 External Resources Accreditation (RASC-2024-5 and 2019-2).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO is reforming accreditation methodology for external resources (pseudo-tied and non-pseudo-tied), which directly affects how external hydropower (including pumped storage participating across seams) receives capacity-value accreditation and participates in the Planning Resource Auction—a core revenue and participation mechanism for hydro owners exporting into MISO or participating via external-resource schedules.
documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes to accredit pseudo-tied external resources using Schedule 53A (real-time offer data, 3-year lookback, 80/20 weighting between Tier 2 RA and Tier 1 non-RA hours) and non-pseudo-tied external resources using day-ahead e-Tag availability (same weighting, no outage exemptions, 3-year lookback). MISO is also eliminating the Use-Limited Resources category, redirecting accreditation of all use-limited assets (including run-of-river and storage hydro) into the Schedule 53A and Schedule 53B frameworks. The proposal shifts external hydro accreditation away from ad-hoc techniques toward seasonal-availability-aligned methods, but non-pseudo-tied resources (which may include many Northwest hydro exports) lose outage exemptions and rely on day-ahead e-Tag offers rather than real-time operational data—potentially reducing accreditation for resources whose actual availability exceeds their day-ahead self-commitments. Stakeholder comments are due July 26, 2026; MISO targets FERC filing in Q4 2026 or Q1 2027 with effective date Planning Year 2029/30 or beyond. Most exposed: pumped storage and run-of-river hydro exporting from adjacent balancing authorities via external-resource schedules; large reservoir hydro with seasonal energy constraints that may be miscaptured by day-ahead e-Tag methodology.

documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes revising Manual 14-H to transition the Interim Deliverability Study (IDS) from serial to cluster-based methodology, effective 2027/2028 Delivery Year. documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is revising its claimed capability audit rules (Section III.1.5–7 tariff redlines), with Claimed Capability Audits and Seasonal DR Audits ending August 31, 2027. The tariff specifies audit duration requirements for hydro by type: hydraulic turbine reversible (2 hours), conventional daily pondage (2 hours), conventional run-of-river (2 hours), and conventional weekly (2 hours); it exempts non-intermittent daily hydro from mandatory Establish Claimed Capability Audits and Seasonal Claimed Capability Audits. Seasonal audits must be conducted at least once per capability year (summer ≥80°F or during ISO-announced window; winter ≤32°F or window, once per three years), with failure to meet requirements resulting in zero seasonal values. This directly determines the claimed capabilities that underpin ISO-NE's capacity accreditation and RA obligations; hydro operators must ensure audits are scheduled and completed within deadlines to avoid penalty (zero seasonal value), making compliance on the August 31, 2027 sunset critical for any asset still accruing seasonal claims.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes to sunset existing Claimed Capability and Seasonal DR audits after August 31, 2027, replacing them with three new metrics: Global Maximum Capability (36-month rolling max hourly performance, updated weekly), Seasonal Maximum Capability (same but for seasonally-specific temperature conditions), and Seasonal Dependable Capability (median availability during the 100 highest load hours per season, with a performance factor applied to dispatchable resources). The framework treats dispatchable resources (those receiving electronic dispatch instructions) differently from non-dispatchable resources, applying a performance factor to dispatchable median offers. This is part of ISO-NE's broader Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA) initiative scheduled for Q2 2027 implementation. Most exposed are conventional hydropower operators, especially dispatchable hydro in ISO-NE's system, whose seasonal dependable credits will now hinge on demonstrated performance during peak-load hours rather than on-demand auditing — reducing discretion to claim seasonal uplifts and tying accreditation to actual dispatch compliance and offer discipline.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is implementing Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) with a three-year transition beginning in CCP 2028–29 (Q2 2027 proposed effective date). The reform shifts accreditation from a long-standing annual Qualified Capacity (QC) methodology to seasonal Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity (MRIC) values that reflect resource contributions to each season's adequacy. During transition, each resource's accredited capacity will be a weighted average: Year 1 (2/3 QC + 1/3 MRIC), Year 2 (1/3 QC + 2/3 MRIC), Year 3 (full MRIC). Hydro owners—particularly seasonal resources like winter-peaking or pumped-storage operators—will experience year-by-year accreditation shifts; some resources (e.g. passive demand response and winter solar) will see accreditation rise under CAR-SA, while others (especially summer-peaking hydro) will experience lower recognized capacity. The demand curve for procurement will also shift leftward across the three-year glide path, mirroring supply-side accreditation changes to maintain unit consistency and cost equivalence. Next steps include stakeholder review of transition mechanics and expected board/Markets Committee approval in coming meetings.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE's Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA) introduce a non-firm gas capacity demand curve effective Q2 2027 to reflect winter regional gas-supply constraints in capacity-market pricing. The proposal specifies: (1) gas-contract requirements (16-hour daily firmness for LNG; affidavit requirements dropped); (2) bilateral CSO (Capacity Supply Obligation) transaction limits tied to truncation points on the demand curve, preventing overtrading of constrained non-firm capacity across zones; and (3) restrictions on gas-only resource-backed imports, which cannot sell non-firm CSO in winter. The mechanism directly affects hydro's accreditation and capacity revenue: by capping non-firm gas capacity and pricing it separately, ISO-NE reduces the volume of low-cost gas capacity competing in winter auctions, tightening supply and raising clearing prices for all resources—especially valuable for pumped-storage hydro and reservoir hydro with winter peaking capability. The filing to stakeholders occurred in July 2026; the ISO notes it will "assess potential enhancements... in the months to come and after the CAR-SA filing." Most exposed are PSH and winter-peaking conventional hydro in zonal export-constrained areas, which benefit from reduced gas competition in winter RA auctions.

documents.title: 2026-07-07-09 MC A03g - CAR-SA: Flatiron Feedback, cont. - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAPACITY/RA accreditation methodology — proposal to reshape how ISO-NE models marginal resource adequacy contributions (rMRI) for all resources including hydro, affecting accreditation values, capacity-market clearing prices, and revenue recovery for dispatchable and storage units under ISO-NE's Competitive Auctions with Reserves (CAR) framework.
documents.ai_summary: Flatiron Energy presents a critique of ISO-NE's proposed Capacity Accreditation and Reserves (CAR-SA) modeling assumptions, arguing that the 'accreditation base case' (which adds 5 GW of load and uses historical 2002–03 extreme-weather years) creates artificially long marginal resource index (MRI) events that over-accredit resources designed for conditions that won't materialize. Flatiron proposes an 'Expected System Conditions' pathway: modeling expected supply and forecasted load without artificial load scaling, which would reduce or eliminate simulated MRI hours in a system with excess capacity. When MRI hours are minimal, Flatiron proposes accreditation shift to MRIC (marginal resource index credit) based on EFORd (equivalent forced outage rate) for most resource types, reflecting contingency-driven rather than energy-shortage-driven reliability events. ISO-NE's capacity demand curve and Net ICR would adjust accordingly, but the price-formation mechanism (reference-unit recovery at Net CONE × rMRI factor) would be preserved. This proposal, if adopted, would fundamentally change how all accredited resources including hydro, pumped storage, and thermal units recover capacity value, with most exposure to resource types whose value depends heavily on modeled energy availability in GE MARS software.

documents.title: 2026-07-07-09 MC A03f - CAR-SA: FirstLight Power - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE's CAR-SA capacity accreditation design—particularly seasonal payment-rate allocation, MRI-based CONE splits, and at-criteria accreditation—directly affects how pumped-storage hydro and seasonal hydro resources are compensated and incentivized to enter, especially when supply is tight in only one season.
documents.ai_summary: FirstLight Power presents technical analysis of interconnected design flaws in ISO-NE's Capacity Accreditation and Reserves-Seasonal Attributes (CAR-SA) proposal to the Markets Committee. The core issue: the current design allocates seasonal capacity payment rates proportional to Marginal Reliability Index (MRI) at Net ICR for each season, driven by an administrative 50/50 seasonal risk split, weather-year weighting that overstates winter event duration, and accreditation at 'at-criteria' conditions (demand-curve location inconsistent with actual clearing risk). FirstLight demonstrates that under this design, a reference resource may not recover Net CONE annually even when the system is tight in one season, suppressing entry signals for seasonal capacity. Potential solutions offered include dynamic seasonal risk splits aligned to actual system conditions, accreditation within a feasible clearing-point range, revised weather-year weighting, and payment-rate approaches that ensure annual Net CONE recovery. No deadline or vote date specified; this is positioned as urgent discussion to prevent compounding design errors before CAR-SA implementation. Pumped-storage operators—particularly those operating in winter-constrained regions or managing seasonal energy constraints—face material revenue exposure: if winter accreditation and payment rates are structurally overstated relative to summer, then summer-constrained capacity and flexibility are undervalued, and winter-heavy PSH assets may receive artificially elevated seasonal payments that don't reflect true entry incentives.

documents.ai_summary: Advanced Energy United presents three conceptual amendments to ISO-NE's Capacity Accreditation Reforms (CAR-SA): (1) replace peak-day weather-year weighting with multi-day event metrics to avoid overstating winter cold-snap frequency and undervaluing storage; (2) model intertie import profiles hourly rather than as flat capacity blocks to reflect overnight export availability when storage would charge; (3) reclassify storage resources as EL3 (energy-limited, fully rechargeable daily) rather than Type 3 to address systemic understatement of off-peak charging energy and state-of-charge modeling gaps. Under Amendment 3, a 4-hour battery would achieve rMRI of 0.253 instead of ISO's proposed 0.187. These amendments target the root cause that CAR-SA's accreditation model understates storage's realistic value and charging opportunities, thereby depressing investment signals for flexible resources that ISO-NE needs for seasonal adequacy and decarbonization. No vote date or comment deadline is stated in this presentation material; this represents the sponsor's position ahead of further committee consideration.

documents.ai_summary: MISO is establishing a Large Load Working Group (LLWG) reporting to its Advisory Committee to provide policy guidance on processes and market structures for integrating large loads in the MISO footprint, addressing issues spanning markets, operations, planning, and resource adequacy. For hydro owners, this signals formalization of large-load integration as a strategic market-design priority — policies emerging from the LLWG will directly shape how big loads (data centers, industrial, co-located generation) interact with hydro's locational dispatch value, ancillary-service opportunities, and potential hybrid/co-location participation pathways. documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group (LLWG) is developing several rule packages in 2026–27 that will shape how large loads and co-located generation participate in MISO markets. Key active issues include: (1) Market Participation and Registration of Co-Located Load and Generation with zero-injection GIA consideration (PAC-2024-4, feedback requested May 14 and June 10); (2) Large Load Firm Service Step Up (LLWG-2026-1, tariff redlines due August 27); (3) Large Load Reserve Product Enhancements (LLWG-2026-2, evaluation and cost-allocation recommendations due Q4 2026); and (4) Interconnection Reliability Requirements including stability assessments (LLWG-2026-3). The co-location rule package directly opens a pathway for hydropower and pumped-storage facilities to register and dispatch co-located load behind the meter, potentially unlocking new revenue streams from load service and reducing network-cost exposure. Reserve-product enhancements and firm-service mechanics will change the mix of flexibility and capacity products available to large, controllable loads—affecting how hydro-connected or hybrid-sited PSH competes for reserve and flexibility revenue. LLWG meetings are scheduled through Q4 2026, with tariff redlines and final recommendations due by December 2026.

No completion date is named in the action-items list, but the framework is post-go-live implementation. For hydro owners, the mechanism is two-fold: (1) GHG-based pricing will create new scarcity signals and marginal-cost adders that alter dispatch merit order, affecting when hydro generation is economically selected; (2) the tracking and reporting requirements (particularly for imports, exports, and storage state-of-charge) will impose operational and compliance obligations on hydro operators. Pumped-storage resources are explicitly targeted by the HSMR definition revisions and multi-configuration resource (MCR) merit-order stacking proposals (Action Item 180), which will reshape how PSH offers energy and frequency support. Most exposed are PSH operators and large run-of-river exports into SPP; smaller reservoir hydro in SPP territory will face reduced dispatch value in high-emissions periods.

documents.ai_summary: PJM is implementing automatic eDART (Outage Database) ticket creation in September 2026 to capture all unavailable MW from committed capacity resources in real time. The system will auto-generate forced-outage tickets when a unit shows unavailable in Markets Gateway but lacks an active outage ticket in eDART, closing a gap exposed by Winter Storm Elliott and reinforced by Winter Storm Fern where unplanned outages went unreported. This directly affects hydro and PSH operators' obligation to report unavailable capacity timely and accurately under Schedule 1 Section 1.10.1A(d) (must-offer rules); the auto-creation logic will flag operators whose availability data in Markets Gateway diverges from eDART submissions, and forced-outage rates derived from eDART feed into capacity accreditation, reserve calculations, and PJM's forecast accuracy to stakeholders. Hydro and PSH owners dependent on accurate outage reporting for capacity value and performance assessment should monitor the Tech Change and eDART forums as details are formalized before the September 2026 implementation.
