documents.title: 03b IPPNY Comments on NYISO Demand Curve Reset Methodology Improvement Project
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: IPPNY comments on NYISO's Demand Curve Reset (DCR) methodology directly touch capacity-market accreditation and proxy-unit design, which set the reference prices for NYISO capacity revenues — the 'missing money' mechanism on which dispatchable hydro and pumped storage depend for cost recovery and investment signals.
documents.ai_summary: IPPNY, representing 80% of New York generation, submits comments on NYISO's preliminary DCR improvements, urging four changes: (1) require proxy units to meet firm-fuel winter-availability requirements (minimum 8 hours daily operation December–February, or 56 hours on-site fuel storage); (2) adjust the Level of Excess to close the gap between market and planning assumptions; (3) shift the zero-crossing point (ZCP) of capacity demand curves rightward to reduce price volatility with small supply changes; and (4) improve annual escalation factors for financial parameters while retaining the quadrennial reset cycle, using New York-specific data for cost-of-debt and market-return indices. The core grievance is that NYISO's 2022 switch to a 2-hour battery as proxy unit excluded firm-fuel costs needed for winter reliability, causing capacity prices to fall below levels needed to retain or invest in generation — a signal deficiency that IPPNY argues has induced retirements and underinvests in reliability. Status: IPPNY feedback on preliminary recommendations; no vote or implementation date stated. Most exposed are any hydro/PSH operators relying on NYISO capacity-market revenues for cost recovery, particularly if they have winter firm-fuel capability that the battery-proxy ignores.

documents.title: 1 Agenda
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ICAP Demand Curve Reset (DCR) process directly affects capacity-market accreditation and RA pricing for all resources including hydro and pumped storage; NYISO's capacity market is a major revenue stream for NHA members.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Installed Capacity Working Group (ICAP/MIWG/PRLWG) is meeting July 1, 2026 to discuss improvements to the ICAP Demand Curve Reset (DCR) process and methodology — a core mechanism governing how NYISO's capacity accreditation and pricing are calibrated. The DCR controls the demand-curve parameters (cone, pivots, slopes) that determine what hydro and pumped-storage resources receive in RA revenue and how much capacity the market clears. No specific proposals or deadlines are stated in this agenda excerpt, but the working group is actively revisiting the methodology, which could reshape accreditation for all resources. This is an active process to monitor for substantive proposals in follow-up materials.

documents.title: 2 DADRP/DSASP Cleanup Tariff Revisions
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO tariff cleanup affecting market participation pathways for aggregations (including DER/small hydro) and energy storage resources; removes deprecated demand-reduction program language and integrates aggregations into cost-based reference-level framework, which bears on offer-development obligations and mitigation-offer rules for non-traditional participants.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO is cleaning up Market Services Tariff (MST) and Open Access Transmission Tariff (OATT) sections to remove obsolete language from the sunsunset Demand Aggregation/Demand Reduction Provider (DADRP) and Demand-Side Ancillary Service Provider (DSASP) programs. Key substantive change: aggregations (including small hydro and DER) are now folded into MST 23.7.3 cost-based reference-level framework, replacing a prior special exemption (MST 23.7.4) that had carved them out because NYISO previously did not calculate reference levels for demand-side resources. The removal of MST 23.7.4 means aggregations must now develop cost-based reference levels for mitigation-offer compliance, aligning them with generator standards. Other revisions correct grammatical errors, restore erroneously deleted BPCG recovery language in OATT 6.1.12, and clarify minimum-generation-bid and supplier definitions. Filing timeline: BIC discussion 7/15/2026; Market Committee vote 7/29/2026. Small hydro and distributed hydro resources participating via aggregation must monitor this closely, as it resets the compliance baseline for offer development.

documents.title: 3 ICAP Demand Curve Reset (DCR) Process and Methodology Improvements
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's ICAP demand curve reset methodology directly affects capacity accreditation and pricing for all resources including hydro and pumped storage, which depend on accurate CONE (Cost of New Entry) calculations and proxy-unit definitions to determine their capacity value and revenue.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO is redesigning its Installed Capacity (ICAP) demand curve reset (DCR) process and cost-to-build methodology, with initial recommendations evaluated against reliability-based valuation, transparency, investment efficiency, and ease of administration. Key proposals include: using EIA overnight capital cost data to streamline cost-to-build estimates (rather than consultant-driven bottom-up approaches), codifying proxy-unit screening criteria to increase predictability, implementing more frequent indexed updates to financial parameters, and adjusting demand curve structures (kinked curves, zero-crossing informed by Minimum Reliability Index). The document is an interim presentation (July 1, 2026) building to an initial concept proposal in August and a complete market design with tariff updates by year-end. For hydro and pumped-storage owners, changes to CONE inputs and proxy-unit definitions directly affect capacity accreditation values and the price signal that drives the DCR clearing price—hydro's primary revenue mechanism in NYISO; any shift toward faster reset cycles or non-consultant methodologies could increase or decrease the accuracy of cost-to-build estimates that anchor their capacity payments, and technology-prescriptive proxy choices (e.g., mandating a gas turbine) would exclude alternative dispatch profiles that might better reflect hydro's actual value.

documents.title: 09-10-MIR8.1 and MIR8.2 Update to MORWG June 2026.pptx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.filename: 09-10-MIR8.1 and MIR8.2 Update to MORWG June 2026.pptx
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MIR8.1 restructures how pumped-storage and battery resources manage state-of-charge forecasting across Markets+ unit-commitment studies, shifting from market-participant prediction to market-operator calculation of SOC trajectories — a material change to how storage revenue exposure and dispatch predictability are handled under Markets+ rules.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ MIR8.1 proposes to introduce time-coupled intervals in all unit-commitment studies (Day-Ahead Market, Day-Ahead RUC, Intra-Day RUC, and Short-Term RUC), allowing market operators to calculate state-of-charge for all intervals after the first, rather than requiring market participants to submit a SOC forecast for every interval. The change is optional: participants can elect either the current design (submitting SOC forecast for each interval) or the new coupled design (submitting SOC forecast only for the first interval, letting the market operator time-couple and calculate subsequent SOC values). The proposal targets a FERC filing timeline, with MPEC approval targeted for August 2026. For pumped-storage owners, this addresses a key exposure: misforecasting dispatch leads to infeasible SOC trajectories in real-time, triggering capacity shortfalls and financial penalties; time-coupling within studies mitigates that risk by ensuring the market solver respects physical charging/discharging constraints. The optionality preserves flexibility for hybrid resources and those charging/discharging outside the market (where the operator lacks full visibility). MORWG convened June 30, 2026; MPEC approval is scheduled August 25, 2026.

documents.title: 01 - June MORWG Agenda.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This agenda covers multiple Markets+ Market Design initiatives directly affecting hydro and storage revenue and operational rules: state-of-charge management for multi-hour storage (MIR8.1), co-located resource constraints (MIR8.2), dynamic scheduling and pseudo-ties for resource participation (MIR9.2-R, MIR9.3-R), and real-time market settlement mechanics (MIR81-R, MIR60-R).
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Markets and Operations working groups will discuss and vote on six Market Implementation Requests in June 2026, with August 2026 MPEC approval targets for most items. MIR8.1 (State of Charge Management) and MIR8.2 (Co-Located Resource Constraints) introduce new participation and operational frameworks for multi-hour storage resources—both drawn from MSR (multi-service resource) subgroup whitepapers and directly affecting how pumped storage and hybrid generators (including co-located hydro + solar) can operate and earn revenue. MIR9.2-R and MIR9.3-R expand dynamic-scheduling and pseudo-tie pathways, opening participation for neighboring resources and potentially enabling smaller or out-of-footprint hydro to access Markets+ balancing. MIR60-R and MIR81-R address real-time transaction settlement and dynamic multi-transaction-interchange pricing, altering how interchange flows (critical for Northwest-to-SPP hydro exports) settle and are valued. Comment deadlines range from June 18 to June 25, 2026; August MPEC vote is the approval milestone for most items.

documents.title: 02 - Antitrust Statement.pptx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This is a standard antitrust compliance statement with no substantive content on hydropower revenue streams, compliance obligations, or strategic options.

documents.title: 03a - May MORWG Meeting Minutes.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MIR9.1-R establishes rules for non-dispatchable physical resources (likely including run-of-river hydro and variable generation), and MIR78-R adjusts market-clearing rules for MCR transition states in Markets+—both touch hydro participation mechanics and obligations in SPP's evolving regional market.
documents.ai_summary: The Markets+ Operations and Reliability Working Group approved two market-initiative requests at its May 27, 2026 meeting. MIR9.1-R (Non-Dispatchable Physical Resources) creates a framework for resources whose owners are legally or contractually unable to submit financial offer information, allowing them to be modeled in the market without unavailable offer data—directly relevant to run-of-river hydro and other variable resources that cannot control output. MIR78-R (MCR Transition) removes a 30-minute transition-state eligibility constraint on reserve clearing that was ported from the Integrated Marketplace but does not apply in Markets+, simplifying multi-commitment-request behavior. Both motions passed unanimously; no comment deadlines or further action items were assigned in these minutes. The group also received education on MIR1 (Market System Outage BA Overrides) and MIR79-R (MIR Process terminology revision), with updates scheduled for June and July MORWG meetings.

documents.title: 04-MIR75-R SPP Comments-20260520.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: This MIR75-R proposal directly affects high-priority export scheduling and adjustment procedures for hydro and other dispatchable resources in SPP Markets+, touching revenue realization for exports and operational constraints on resource commitment and discharge.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ MIR75-R proposes clarified mechanics for adjusting high-priority export e-Tags when a resource's maximum economic limit or Variable Energy Resource forecast falls below committed export volumes. The proposal specifies that adjustments will be made pro-rata when multiple e-Tags share a single resource source, with a 1 MW minimum threshold and whole-MW rounding. Hydro and pumped-storage operators exporting power into or through SPP Markets+ will face automatic downward adjustment of export schedules when their available capacity (Max ECOL for conventional hydro, Maximum Discharge Limit for MSRs, VER forecast for wind/solar) cannot support the export commitment — a constraint that directly reduces realized export revenue and requires operators to manage export bids against real-time resource availability, especially during low-water or variable-generation conditions. The language resulted from an April 2026 MSWG/MDWG policy decision; this MIR specifies the operational algorithm. SRP supports the threshold addition.

documents.title: 05-MIR9.2-R Dynamic Schedule Resources June 2026.pptx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Markets+ Dynamic Schedule Resource rules establish how dispatchable hydro and other resources physically located in one balancing authority but serving load in another are accounted for in dispatch, power-balance settlement, and interbalancing-authority transfer accounting — directly affecting how hydro output is cleared, metered, and compensated across BA boundaries, particularly for multi-state/multi-BA hydro operators.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ proposes a new 'Dynamic Schedule Resource' participation type (MIR 9.2-R, June 2026) to solve a double-counting problem: when a dispatchable resource in one Balancing Authority (Native BA) is dynamically scheduled to serve load in another (Attaining BA), current rules treat its dispatch change in both the dynamic net scheduled interchange (NSI) and the market-to-interchange (MTI), forcing both BAs to regulate redundantly. The solution links a Dynamic Schedule Resource to a Dynamic Schedule Resource Interface; the resource remains dispatchable by Markets+ in real-time (RTBM), but only the interface value (not the resource's full output) is counted in the Attaining BA's power balance, preventing double-counting. The proposal defines five use cases: participating-to-participating BAs (resource-coupled or not), participating-to-non-participating (resource-coupled or not), and non-participating to participating. Most exposed are multi-BA hydro operators and pumped-storage facilities dynamically scheduled across BA lines; use-case 1a (participating-to-participating, resource-coupled) preserves dispatchability and shifts regulation responsibility via the interface, altering how dynamic hydro transfers compete in dispatch and how their locational and marginal-loss signals propagate across seams. Tariff and protocol sections are newly drafted; implementation timeline and stakeholder comment opportunity are not detailed in this presentation.

documents.title: 05-MIR9.2-R SPP Comments-20260602.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Dynamic Schedule Resources clarifies how Markets+ will treat dispatchability and real-time ICCP management of hydro and other resources subject to physical energy transfers across BA boundaries—a revenue and compliance issue for hydro sellers using dynamic dispatch to serve load or other BAs, and for multi-state resource compliance with e-Tag and regulation-burden rules.
documents.ai_summary: SPP staff proposes tariff and protocol revisions (April 2025/1.0a) to clarify registration, e-Tagging, and operational treatment of Dynamic Schedule Resources and Interfaces across Markets+ timeframes (DA, RUC, pre-RTBM, RTBM). The proposal distinguishes resource-coupled versus non-resource-coupled dynamic schedules and specifies when a resource may remain dispatchable under a dynamic schedule (internal transfers) versus when transactions must be non-dispatchable (certain exports). Key change: MSRs (multi-state resources, of which hydro is the canonical example) registered as Dynamic Schedule Resources can represent import or export depending on dispatch, but must coordinate separate e-Tags with the Native and Attaining BAs and accept ICCP-reported real-time quantities as fixed; Dynamic e-Tags referencing these resources are ignored by settlements, shifting compliance burden to the Market Participant. This reduces regulation burden on receiving BAs by eliminating pseudo-ties but locks the Dynamic Schedule Resource's output into the native BA's power balance and removes it from real-time economic dispatch in the attaining BA—a material constraint for hydro operators managing multi-BA export strategies. Status: tariff/protocol revisions have been proposed; next step and comment deadline are not stated in this excerpt.

documents.title: 06-MIR9.3-R Dynamic Schedule Resource Pseudo-Ties June 2026.pptx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Markets+ is refining pseudo-tie registration rules for external resources, which directly affects how hydropower and other dispatchable generation located outside the Markets+ footprint can participate, be dispatched, and settle — a strategic option for NHA members operating in non-participating balancing areas seeking access to SPP Markets+.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ (SPP's combined market and reliability coordinator) is adopting a new registration pathway (MIR 9.3-R) that allows external resources physically located in non-participating balancing authorities to be modeled as pseudo-tied within Markets+ using dynamic schedules instead of formal NAESB pseudo-tie agreements. External resources registered under this new option will be dispatchable by Markets+, settled at their physical-location LMP, and participate identically to formally pseudo-tied resources, but the underlying dynamic schedule between native and attaining balancing authorities will remain in place (and ignored by the market system and settlements). The change preserves all formal pseudo-tie requirements and adds two new attributes: the market participant must designate the resource as a "dynamically scheduled pseudo-tie" in the registration workbook, and the participating attaining BA must provide an attestation letter confirming its understanding that the resource will be modeled as pseudo-tied. This creates operational flexibility for BA arrangements that cannot or prefer not to establish formal pseudo-ties, potentially broadening external-resource participation. The document shows protocol language updates to sections 9.1.1, 9.1.9, 9.1.9.1, and 9.1.9.2 but states no vote date or comment deadline.

documents.title: 06-MIR9.3-R Dynamic Schedule Resource Pseudo-Ties submission.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: External resource pseudo-tie registration and modeling rules directly affect how hydropower resources outside the Markets+ footprint (including those in adjacent balancing authorities) can participate in the day-ahead and real-time energy market and settle, and clarifies the framework for pseudo-tied hydro to remain on dynamic schedules while competing in Markets+—a critical pathway for cross-BA hydro participation and revenue capture.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ (SPP's organized market launching 2027) is codifying registration and operational requirements for two forms of external resource pseudo-ties: formal pseudo-ties with binding BA agreements, and dynamically scheduled pseudo-ties where the resource is modeled as pseudo-tied into the attaining BAA in Markets+ commercial and network models while energy continues to flow as a dynamic schedule under NAESB/WECC standards between native and attaining BAs. The MIR (Markets+ Initiative Request 9.3-R) adds a new resource designation ('dynamically scheduled pseudo-tie') and defines meter-agent, attestation, and settlement responsibilities in Protocols Sections 9.1.1, 9.1.9, 9.1.9.1 (new), and 9.1.9.2 (new). SPP staff rates this as medium design, implementation, and operational complexity; MPEC approval is targeted Q3 2026 with Q1 2027 go-live. This standardizes a workaround already in Markets+ base design, reducing ad hoc handling and participation ambiguity for external hydro resources seeking to serve load within the footprint—directly relevant to northwest hydro exports and cross-border hydro from Mexican utilities or other external basins.

documents.title: 07-MIR60-R Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) submission.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.filename: 07-MIR60-R Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) submission.docx
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) establish a new framework for import/export transactions across the Markets+ boundary and internal transfers within the footprint, affecting how hydro and other resources can participate in interregional energy trading and settlement — a direct revenue vector for hydro owners seeking to export power or manage interchange scheduling within the expanding Markets+ footprint.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ is implementing the Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) framework, which creates generic system points (MPSP) within each Markets+ Balancing Authority Area to facilitate scheduling and tagging of import/export transactions across the Markets+ boundary and internal market transfers. The protocol revisions establish registration, operational, and settlement requirements for MPSPs as sources and sinks for interchange transactions, with optional hourly limits managed by each BA in the Day-Ahead and Real-Time Balancing Markets. For hydro owners exporting from or importing into Markets+ BAAs, MITSPS enables participation in interchange transactions that are not pre-scheduled bilateral trades but are cleared by the market — expanding the scheduling and revenue-participation pathways available to hydroelectric resources. The MIR seeks MPEC approval in Q3 2026 with implementation targeted for Q1 2027, affecting how existing hydro plants can access interregional markets and how new capacity (especially in growing Markets+ footprint) will schedule transactions.

documents.title: 08-MIR81-R Dynamic MTI-MOTI in RTBM submission.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: MTI/MOTI tagging and BAA Scheduling Constraints directly affect how SPP Markets+ dispatches interregional power flows in real-time; distinguishing Normal (DA-locked) from Dynamic (RTBM-only) transaction types changes the sequencing and flexibility of resource commitment and redispatch — a structural change to market dispatch that hydro operators use to optimize revenue from flexible ramping and interregional sales.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ (MIR 81-R) proposes to distinguish Normal and Dynamic MTI/MOTI transaction types, with Normal types locked after Pre-RTBM SCED and Dynamic types eligible only in RTBM. This allows BAAs to create separate BAA Scheduling Constraints on Dynamic paths without retroactively constraining the day-ahead and RUC commitment plan. The change is ranked High priority, with MPEC approval targeted Q4 2026 and implementation Q1 2027. Hydro operators in the SPP footprint benefit by avoiding artificial redispatch and binding constraints when BAs adjust transmission limits for reliability mid-day; it preserves the optimization value of DA and RUC schedules and lets BAs manage incremental transfer changes without forcing costly RTBM repricing and potential VRL violations. Most exposed are pumped-storage and flexible reservoir operators using MTI/MOTI paths for interregional arbitrage and capacity sales.

documents.title: 08-MIR81-R Dynamic MTI-MOTI in RTBM.pptx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Modifies balancing-area scheduling constraints and market-transfer-interface (MTI) rules that affect real-time dispatch flexibility and locational price signals — hydro's revenue from ramping/flexibility procurement and locational scarcity pricing depends on how transmission constraints are enforced across market intervals.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ proposes MIR81-R, which distinguishes Normal (day-ahead/RUC/pre-RTBM) and Dynamic (real-time only) MTI/MOTI transaction types to allow balancing authorities to set different scheduling constraints in RTBM than were used in DA commitment, preventing large NSI swings without undermining DA/RUC optimization. Normal MTIs become fixed quantities in real-time; Dynamic MTIs operate only in RTBM with nonbinding limits (defaulting to 99,999 MW unless constrained by BA-to-BA scheduling restrictions). The proposal updates tariff sections 4.2.7, 8.2, 8.2.1.1, 8.2.2.1, 8.2.6, and 9.4.1 to implement transaction-type registration and constraint-submission requirements via the MUI. This affects real-time dispatch optimization and price formation: by allowing separate constraints for incremental transfers, the scheme constrains BAA scheduling-constraint binding in RTBM while preserving DA-cleared transfers, potentially reducing real-time price separation and limiting the incremental scarcity premiums hydro can capture on flexible ramping in congested intervals. All market participants must submit Normal MTIs/MOTIs prior to DA market close and register at least one Dynamic MTI at resource registration.

documents.title: Presentation - 2025 Fourth Quarter Market Issues and Performance - Apr 02, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO market-monitoring report on Q4 2025 real-time pricing, regional generation mix by fuel (including hydro), transmission congestion, and interregional transfer flows — directly bearing on hydro revenue (price formation and regional scarcity signals) and strategic positioning in the West.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring reports Q4 2025 market outcomes: electricity prices in the West fell 7% year-over-year; less frequent high-price intervals occurred; Pacific Northwest shifted to net exporter across all hours; and California prices remain elevated by greenhouse-gas costs rather than congestion. The report shows generation-mix shifts by region (Slides 8–11) but does not propose tariff changes. For hydro owners, the data reveals that interregional transmission capacity and fuel-mix changes—especially lower prices and reduced Northwest scarcity—signal weakened export value from the PNW into California, while California's GHG-driven premium persists. Analysts using this as a reference point would identify market conditions affecting hydro's locational revenue; no comment deadline or action item is stated.

documents.title: Presentation - 2025 Third Quarter Market Issues and Performance - Jan 08, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO market-monitoring report analyzing Q3 2025 price formation, congestion patterns, WEIM transfers, and generation mix changes across multiple Western regions — directly informs hydro revenue via locational pricing signals, interregional trade dynamics, and operational conditions that shape dispatch and scarcity.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring presents Q3 2025 market performance: Western region prices down 4% year-over-year; California dominated by south-to-north congestion and GHG costs; Northwest saw higher solar-hour prices while California peaked in non-solar hours; WEIM transfers flowed from CAISO mid-day and from Intermountain/Desert Southwest in non-solar hours, with assistance-energy opt-ins increasing transfers for 8 of 10 entities. Real-time three-pivotal-supplier test found 4.2% of WEIM 15-minute intervals uncompetitive; RTD mitigation errors added ~37 MW incremental dispatch. Hydro owners should track the pronounced shift in congestion direction (north-to-south peak in Q3 2024 vs. current south-to-north pattern) and the interregional transfer behavior, which directly affects locational scarcity pricing and arbitrage opportunities for reservoir and pumped-storage resources positioned to move energy across the Western interconnect.

documents.title: Presentation - 2025 Second Quarter Market Issues and Performance - Oct 09, 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO market-monitoring report on Q2 2025 energy price formation, congestion, interregional transfers (WEIM), and resource dispatch patterns—directly informative for hydro owners assessing revenue drivers, transmission constraints affecting their exports, and strategic positioning across the West.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring reports Q2 2025 real-time market conditions: electricity prices in the West rose 12% versus Q2 2024, driven by south-to-north congestion and California greenhouse-gas costs; Northwest prices were higher during solar hours, California during non-solar hours—indicating hydro's value shifts with solar generation patterns. WEIM transfer congestion into or out of Pacific Northwest areas occurred over 20% of 5-minute intervals, and Mid-Columbia and Palo Verde bilateral prices converged with ISO market prices, suggesting arbitrage opportunities narrowed. Pacific Northwest coal output rose despite more outages, and transfers from the Intermountain West during non-solar hours declined Q-o-Q, signaling reduced availability or changed dispatch incentives. For hydro owners, these trends show tightening price signals in hydro-export corridors, persistent congestion reducing transmission access to California, and seasonal shifts in the regional generation stack that affect dispatch positioning and revenue timing.

documents.title: Presentation - 2024 Annual Report on Market Issues and Performance
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO's 2024 market-performance report provides comprehensive data on hydro generation patterns, regional price formation, congestion outcomes, and ancillary-services procurement mix — all drivers of hydro revenue and dispatch value — plus recommendations affecting storage bid-cost recovery, default energy bids, and local market-power mitigation that extend to hybrid resources including hydropower.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring presents 2024 annual performance data and forward recommendations. Pacific Northwest hydro generation increased in 2024 relative to 2023; Northwest prices rose mid-day during solar hours and followed net-load patterns, with transfer-congestion elevation noted (page 7, 11–12). Battery participation in ancillary services grew substantially (page 43), while overall flexible ramping product prices remained infrequent at system/BA level (page 42). Recommendations include extending local market-power mitigation to hybrid resources, enhancing default energy bids for batteries to reflect intraday opportunity costs (with standardized bids for WEIM batteries proposed), and revising bid-cost recovery rules — changes that would apply similarly to hydro and PSH if codified (pages 46–47). No specific vote or comment deadline stated in this presentation; this is a published annual report. Most exposure: pumped-storage operators subject to bid-cost recovery and default-energy-bid rules, and larger reservoir hydro in the Pacific Northwest tier where congestion pricing and seasonal price patterns drive revenue.

documents.title: Presentation - 2025 First Quarter Market Issues and Performance - Jun 26, 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO Q1 2025 market-monitoring report documents flexible ramping product procurement split by fuel type (hydro vs. solar/wind/batteries), WEIM interregional transfer patterns involving hydro-exporting regions (Pacific Northwest, Intermountain West), and price formation across WEIM footprint affecting hydro export value.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring Q1 2025 performance report shows hydro and batteries supplying the bulk of upward flexible ramping product (FRP) procurement, while solar and wind dominate downward FRP demand in the 15-minute market. Intermountain West and Pacific Northwest became dominant WEIM exporters during non-solar hours in Q1 2025, with PacEast and Idaho Power identified as main peak-hour exporters; transfer congestion into/out of those hydro-rich regions occurred in ~20% of 5-minute intervals, creating locational scarcity signals. Electricity prices in the West dropped 39% year-over-year but remain driven by south-to-north congestion and greenhouse-gas costs within California. The report is observational and carries no proposals or compliance deadlines, but provides a baseline on how hydro's FRP-market participation, export positioning, and regional pricing have shifted in the WEIM footprint — useful for understanding Q1 2025 hydro revenue dynamics and transmission-constrained export opportunity.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO is planning 2027 enterprise projects (internal technology and back-office improvements, no market rule changes) that include three items material to hydro/PSH: (1) Advanced Storage Tool—development of a software capability to model and manage storage operations, directly benefiting pumped-storage operators' dispatch and planning; (2) Black Start Automation Portal—automating black-start capability tracking and compliance for synchronous resources including hydro units; (3) Renewable Energy Forecast Integration and Reporting Enhancements (REFIRE)—improving NYISO's forecasting and reporting of variable renewable generation, which affects the reserve and ramping requirements hydro must meet and the scarcity signals hydro responds to. Additionally, System Resource Planning enhancements with AI capability are designed to improve the interconnection process, potentially reducing queue time for hydro uprates and new storage interconnections. documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Budget & Priorities Working Group is surveying stakeholders on 2027 project prioritization. Project 1 proposes five-minute transaction scheduling with Hydro-Québec to improve price convergence between RTC and RTD and increase real-time flexibility; market-design work is due in 2027. Project 3 (Aggregation System Integration) seeks API-driven automation of DER enrollment and safety review to streamline FERC 2222 compliance for Member System utilities and small DER operators. Project 4 (Demand Response Baseline Alignment) will investigate rules preventing DSRs from becoming net ICAP suppliers, addressing a MMU recommendation. Project 5 (Automatic ICAP Surplus Offers) implements tariff changes to auto-resell UCAP surplus and reduce clearing prices. Survey responses due July 15, 2026; all responses will be made public.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's 2027 Market Project Candidates document lists 62 proposed initiatives across four prioritization tiers (Prioritize, Mandatory, Continuing, Future). Hydro and PSH owners should track: (1) Balancing Intermittency Phase 2: Evaluating Needs for Duration in Reserves (ENDURE) — examining whether longer-duration reserve products are needed, directly relevant to PSH scheduling and RA accreditation; (2) Capacity zone redesign and locational capacity pricing enhancements — affecting where hydro gets recognized for RA; (3) Storage as Transmission — potentially enabling PSH to serve transmission functions and unlock new revenue; (4) Dynamic Reserves Phase 1 (Continuing) and Phase 2 (Prioritize) — redesigning how reserves are scheduled and cost-recovered, bearing on hydro's ancillary-service margins; (5) ICAP Demand Curve Reset methodology improvements and seasonal ICAP market improvements — updating capacity-auction parameters that determine bid acceptance and clearing prices for hydro's capacity offerings; (6) Outage scheduling enhancements, operating-reserve performance review, and fast-start pricing logic — touching dispatch and settlement rules affecting hydro's operational flexibility value. The document is a prioritization framework for budget and resource allocation; next steps and timelines are not specified within this excerpt, but member engagement through stakeholder survey is noted as ongoing.

documents.title: 2 2027 Proposed Market Projects Updates and Costs
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO is prioritizing 61 market projects for 2027 including capacity-zone redesign, DER enhancements, storage/intermittency-duration reserves, demand-response baselining, and large-load integration — all affecting hydro and storage revenue, accreditation, and participation frameworks; the document establishes the project pipeline and stakeholder-scoring process that will shape NYISO market design through 2027.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's 2027 budget and market-project prioritization process is now open for stakeholder input through a July 15, 2027 survey. The project slate includes 61 candidates (6 mandatory, 2 continuing, 42 prioritize, 11 future) spanning energy markets, capacity markets, new-resource participation, and reliability planning. Key projects directly touching hydro and storage include: Capacity Zone Redesign (SOM) [#7], Balancing Intermittency Phase 2: Evaluating Needs for Duration in Reserves (ENDURE) [#6], DER Market Enhancements [#8] (which will enable small hydro aggregation under Order 2222), and a newly mandatory FERC Order on Large Loads project that eliminates and absorbs three related projects (Reliability Planning & Large Load Integration [#32], DER Market Enhancements [#8], and Flexible Load Models—Large Loads [#16]). The FERC order's treatment of large-load interconnection, frequency support, and flexible supply will reshape the incentive for hydro participation. Weighted stakeholder scores (voting members only, governance-weighted by sector, with Generation Owner and Other Supplier each at 21.5%) will drive prioritization at the July 30 BPWG meeting, leading to Board approval in December 2026. Comments are due July 15, 2027.

documents.title: 20260716 LLWG Item 01c Minutes 20260610.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO's Zero-Injection GIA (ZGIA) proposal directly affects how co-located generation and load can participate in markets and be registered—a strategic option for hydro owners seeking to site generation with load, and a novel participation pathway that may extend to small hydro and hybrid resources under Order 2222 principles.
documents.ai_summary: MISO is developing a Zero-Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement (ZGIA) framework to enable market participation and registration of co-located load and generation. The proposal reflects six months of stakeholder input and is nearing a tariff filing at end of June 2026, with draft language and Planning Advisory Committee feedback still being incorporated. The framework adapts existing interconnection processes (surplus, replacement, ERAS) to zero-injection scenarios. For hydro owners, ZGIAs represent a new pathway to co-locate generation with large industrial load—potentially raising MW value by shifting pricing exposure, enabling behind-the-meter hydro dispatch, and avoiding transmission constraints; most relevant to pumped-storage operators and small hydro seeking high-load-density sites. Comment deadlines and detailed tariff language appear in related filings (PAC-2024-2B, LLWG-2026-3, LLWG-2026-2) due May 26–June 4, 2026.

documents.title: 20260629 LLWG Item 01b Agenda.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Large Load Working Group agenda addresses co-located load-and-generation registration, interconnection reliability, and operational requirements that directly affect hydro's strategic options for serving large loads and co-location arrangements, plus hydro's obligations for operational reliability and dispatch coordination.
documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group (LLWG) is meeting June 29, 2026, to address market participation rules for co-located load and generation (item 6: Zero-Injection GIA under PAC-2024-2B), interconnection reliability requirements (LLWG-2026-3), large-load telemetry/PMU requirements (LLWG-2026-4C), operational forecasting requirements (LLWG-2026-4A), and reserve product enhancements (LLWG-2026-2). The co-location and zero-injection items directly enable hydro owners to serve large loads behind the meter or as bundled resources, expanding revenue and strategic flexibility; the interconnection and operational requirements impose new compliance obligations on dispatchable generation (including hydropower) serving large loads. Next LLWG meeting is July 16, 2026. No voting or comment deadlines are stated in this agenda.

documents.title: 20260629 LLWG Item 01d Management Plan.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This MISO working group management plan addresses large-load integration, co-located generation/load, and operational reliability requirements that directly affect hydro and pumped-storage participation options, interconnection pathways, and reserve-product design.
documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group (LLWG) is tracking six active workstreams through Q4 2026 that reshape how large loads and co-located resources (including hydro-paired load) participate in MISO markets. Key items include: (1) Large Load Firm Service Step Up (LLWG-2026-1) and reserve-product enhancements (LLWG-2026-2), which will define capacity/reserve accreditation and service-level requirements for flexible resources attached to large loads; (2) Interconnection reliability requirements (LLWG-2026-3) and operational-reliability workstreams (LLWG-2026-4A/B/C covering forecasting, network models, and PMU/telemetry) that establish must-offer and real-time operational standards for co-located assets; and (3) Market participation rules for zero-injection GIAs (PAC-2024-4B), affecting how hydro or storage can register co-located load without serving the MISO grid. The June 29, 2026 meeting will surface a tentative FERC action and initial reserve-enhancement evaluation results; final tariff redlines and recommendations are scheduled for August and November 2026. Pumped-storage operators and conventional hydro owners considering co-location or large-load service opportunities need to monitor reserve-product design and the zero-injection GIA interpretation, as these will determine whether co-located capacity can stack ancillary-service revenues or will be constrained by MISO operational requirements.

documents.title: 20260629 LLWG Item 01c Action Items.pdf

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group issued feedback requests on June 10, 2026 (closed) for the Large Load Firm Service Step Up proposal (LLWG-2026-1), with comments originally due June 24. The proposal addresses how MISO accommodates large-load customers seeking firm service, a mechanism that intersects hydro's role in providing dispatchable energy and flexibility to serve new demand. Large-load firm-service design can shift the value of hydro by changing transmission constraints, scarcity pricing, and the premium for flexible supply — particularly for pumped-storage operators positioned to serve or compete with large loads. The document provides no detail on the proposal's substance, status, or next steps.

documents.title: 20260629 LLWG Item 07 Draft MISO Large Load Interconnection Requirement Technical Compendium
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Large load interconnection and operational requirements directly affect hydro's strategic options for co-location, load-following capability valuation, and transmission/grid-stability service revenue through emerging demand for ramp, ride-through, and dynamic-performance capabilities that hydro uniquely supplies.
documents.ai_summary: MISO has published a Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements technical compendium establishing interconnection standards for rapid-growth transmission-connected loads (data centers, AI computing, etc.), with four requirement categories: data/telemetry/forecasting; ramp management; voltage/frequency ride-through; and stability assessment. The framework defines minimum disturbance-performance expectations and dynamic-response capabilities that large loads must meet. This expands MISO's valuation of ramping, frequency support, and voltage stability — services hydro suppliers have historically dominated — and opens strategic pathways for hydro co-location with large loads and behind-the-meter service delivery. The document establishes technical requirements that may inform future MISO ancillary-services procurement and reserve-adequacy modeling as load volatility and grid-stability demands increase; hydro owners should monitor whether MISO translates these reliability needs into new product definitions or accreditation adjustments that reward fast-response, high-ramp-capability resources.

documents.filename: 20260629 LLWG Item 07 Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements (LLWG-2026-3).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Large load interconnection requirements and their operational reliability mandates (remote disconnect, ramp-rate controls, ride-through, telemetry/PMU) directly constrain how co-located loads (data centers, AI/HPC) can interact with the transmission system and may affect hydro's ability to serve or coordinate with these loads, plus set a precedent for how RTOs will require dispatchable resources to respond to fast-ramping demand.
documents.ai_summary: MISO is filing revised Tariff language by end of July 2026 to impose interconnection reliability requirements on large loads (≥50 MW new, ≥25 MW cumulative increase) and computational loads (≥1 MW of data-center-type digital demand), implementing FERC's show-cause order. Requirements include basic facility data, modeling, hourly forecasts, telemetry, and PMU data; computational loads face additional phasor measurement, ride-through (voltage/frequency), and ramp-rate controls; MISO will install and charge customers for remote disconnect equipment and control systems. A transitional provision exempts loads with service commencement before 11/1/2027 from ramp and ride-through requirements for their lifetime unless they upgrade by ≥25 MW after 10/1/2026. This affects hydro owners because (1) it establishes a co-location precedent — large loads are now defined as discrete withdrawal points, creating opportunities for hydro to site behind-the-meter generation and enter direct load-service arrangements; (2) the ramp-rate and ride-through enforcement on computational loads (AI, crypto, HPC) creates a demand-side flexibility requirement that could be partially satisfied by hybrid hydro-storage systems and (3) the remote-disconnect and PMU mandates on loads set operational-control expectations that may extend to dispatchable generation. Stakeholders expressed concerns about applicability, transition, and specific language; feedback has influenced the revised Tariff language.

documents.title: 20260629 LLWG Item 08b Large Load Operational Forecast Requirements (LLWG 2026 4A)
documents.filename: 20260629 LLWG Item 08b Large Load Operational Forecast Requirements (LLWG-2026-4A).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Large load forecasting requirements directly affect hydro's operational flexibility value and dispatch obligations, and the rule design (monitoring, incentives, settlement potential) may establish precedent for how variable/dispatchable resources' forecast accuracy is treated in MISO's commitment and real-time dispatch processes.
documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes to require large loads (data centers, industrial facilities, campuses) to submit short-term operational forecasts at hourly (next 1–168 hours) and 5-minute (next 6 hours) granularities, feeding into MISO's Multi-Day/Next-Day/Intraday reliability commitment and look-ahead commitment/real-time dispatch processes. Forecasts are submitted at the Commercial Pricing (CP) node level by the Tariff Customer; MISO will monitor timeliness and accuracy against telemetered actual load and is considering incentive mechanisms (ranging from escalation to settlement-based penalties). Status: requirements finalized for LLWG feedback by July 13, 2026; accuracy incentives and BPM implementation to follow. For hydro operators, the mechanism is load-side variability management: large loads add volatile demand that MISO's standard weather/calendar forecasts cannot capture; if these forecasts are inaccurate, MISO's commitment stack and reserve procurement tighten or loosen unpredictably, affecting the scarcity signals and ramping/flexibility value hydro receives in real-time and look-ahead markets. The settlement-based penalty option (SPP precedent cited) could create a parallel market-discipline framework applied to demand-side forecast accuracy, potentially informing future treatment of hydro forecast errors and opportunity-cost offers.

documents.title: 20260629 LLWG Item 09 Large Load Reserve Product Enhancements (LLWG 2026 2)
documents.filename: 20260629 LLWG Item 09 Large Load Reserve Product Enhancements (LLWG-2026-2).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO's revised methodology for quantifying reserve requirements (Regulation Reserve, Ramp Capability, Short-Term Reserve) directly affects how uncertainty and variability from large loads are valued in reserve-product pricing and procurement — a core revenue stream for hydro and pumped storage, which are traditional suppliers of all three products.
documents.ai_summary: MISO has established a dynamic reserve requirement methodology that quantifies net uncertainty and derives seasonal reserve requirements for Regulation Reserve (4 sec–5 min timeframe), Ramp Capability Product (10 min), and Short-Term Reserve (30 min–3 hr), with requirements varying by season, region, and time of day. Large loads exhibiting non-conforming behavior (volatile industrial or storage-adjacent profiles) were evaluated as a source of net-load and tie-line uncertainty; however, MISO's correlation analysis (sampling February–November 2025) found weak or negligible relationships between non-conforming load profiles and reserve-product uncertainty requirements across all three products, suggesting existing large loads have limited impact on reserve sizing to date. MISO will continue to monitor uncertainty patterns periodically and revise reserve methodologies if non-conforming load impact reaches criticality. Stakeholder feedback (six respondents, May 2026) was mostly supportive, and further engagement will occur at the Large Load Working Group.

documents.title: 20260629 LLWG Item 09 Reserve Product Enhancement (LLWG 2026 2) Feedback Response (20260514)

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO is evaluating reserve product enhancements and regulation requirements to manage load variability from large data-center and computational loads, which directly affects how much regulation and ramping reserve MISO procures and prices — the demand curve for these products that conventional hydro and pumped storage depend on for revenue.
documents.ai_summary: MISO is developing reserve product enhancements to accommodate fast ramp rates and variability from large loads (data centers, computational facilities), with focus on regulation (4-second dispatch cycle, 5-minute deployment) and contingency-reserve upward and downward directions. Stakeholder feedback from six participants—mostly supportive of MISO's approach—pushed MISO to evaluate whether existing initiatives (RSC-2024-1/2, MSC-2026-1) already suffice before adding new products, and to allocate reserve costs to the loads driving demand rather than socializing them. MISO commits to reserve-enhancement evaluation updates and cost-allocation recommendations at July or August 2026 and later in 2026 LLWG meetings. The mechanism: larger, more variable loads will increase MISO's procurement of regulation and ramping reserves; if MISO adds new reserve products or expands regulation requirements, traditional hydro and PSH owners will face higher competition for those product revenues and greater uncertainty in which resources are called upon to provide regulation—particularly affecting resources with ramp-rate and regulation-eligibility constraints.

documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes to require Zero-Injection GIAs (generation interconnection agreements where generation is co-located with large industrial loads) whose associated load exceeds the Large Load threshold to register as market resources. Market registration will ensure both load and generation volumes are reported separately for accurate ancillary-service charge allocation, affecting settlement and LMP exposure. This proposal responds to FERC's recent Show Cause Order. Stakeholder feedback is due July 15, 2026, with tariff filing expected July 2026. The mechanism matters most to pumped-storage operators and conventional hydro owners considering co-location with or service to large loads (data centers, manufacturing, etc.); the registration and metering rules will determine whether co-located generation can capture locational price signals or is treated as internal to the load node.

documents.ai_summary: ERCOT Operations Analysis reports May 2026 performance of its intra-hour ramp-rate forecasting (PWRR for wind, PSRR for solar) used in 5-minute SCED dispatch. documents.ai_summary: ERCOT's May 2026 RUC market review reports 386.9 effective resource-hours committed, with 78% addressing capacity needs and most commitments (71%) issued with lead-time margins of 2 hours or less. RUC triggered 181.2 Reliability Deployment Price Adder (RDPA) hours at a time-weighted average of $0.75/MWh for energy, plus ancillary-service RDPAs averaging $0.13–$0.18/MWh across regulation, responsive reserve, and contingency reserve. Make-whole payments totaled $1.14M in May; 77% of committed resource-hours came from generators at least 50 years old, predominantly non-opt-out resources. For hydro-centric markets, this illustrates ERCOT's reliance on must-offer thermal capacity and uplift cost-recovery rather than dynamic AS procurement or storage participation—a design that contrasts with how CAISO, NYISO, and PJM price flexibility and commitment from dispatchable and storage resources.

documents.ai_summary: ERCOT is considering methodology changes for 2027 ancillary-services procurement, with focus on Regulation Service (adding a potential Large Load adjustment factor for ramps exceeding 400 MW), Responsive Reserve Service (pending NERC's 2027 BAL-003 IFRO assessment), and refinement of the 2026 probabilistic framework for ECRS and Non-Spinning Reserve. The presentation notes that current Regulation methodology accounts for Large Load ramping only through the NLFE term but acknowledges extreme downward ramps (to –61 MW in some hours) with greater outliers than upward ramps, suggesting a dedicated adjustment may be needed. ERCOT is also exploring whether to move solar/wind calculations from Historical Scheduled Load (HSL) to Gross Real-Time Power Potential (GRPP) to better capture intra-hour renewable ramps. The probabilistic reserve methodology is undergoing sensitivity analysis on risk thresholds (Watch/EEA1/EEA2/Load Shed vs. frequency of violations), look-ahead periods (1–6 hours), risk credits, and tail-event treatment of net load forecast errors. Stakeholder meetings continue through August 2026, with final board vote scheduled for September 15, 2026.

documents.ai_summary: ERCOT is refining its 2027 ancillary-services methodology with one material change: addition of a Large Load Adjustment factor to Regulation Service requirements to account for extreme 5-minute ramps from data-center and non-conforming loads that can exceed 400 MW and are currently underrepresented in the net-load-forecast-error (NLFE) term. Comparative interest: ERCOT's modeling of large-load variability and its probabilistic criteria tuning (probability of violation targets of 1-in-10-year to 1-in-1-year) show how an inflexible-load-heavy system approaches reserve adequacy differently from hydro-rich grids where demand variability is less extreme. documents.ai_summary: PJM's Interconnection Process Subcommittee presented market participation options for Mixed Technology Facilities (MTF)—facilities with multiple generation or storage types behind a single interconnection point. Resources can participate as independent Co-Located Resources (each a separate market unit) or as a Hybrid Resource (single market unit with unit-specific accreditation). A closed-loop hybrid with storage can charge from grid; an open-loop hybrid cannot. Facilities with independent components can elect either model; those with significant interdependency (e.g., storage unable to charge from grid) must use the hybrid model. Classification must be declared 6 months before in-service date; capacity resources must choose the same model for both capacity and energy markets and must re-elect within RAA Schedule 9.2 deadlines; energy-only resources can change election once per calendar year with notice by May 30. For any MTF, the site Maximum Facility Output (MFO) cannot be exceeded in real time and capacity-must-offer obligations apply to the original Certified Interconnection Rights. The four use cases illustrate that inverter-gen + storage (like solar + battery or wind + battery) and non-inverter gen + storage (gas + battery) can form hybrids, while non-inverter gen + inverter gen (gas + solar) must participate as co-located resources. This framework directly affects pumped-storage hydro owners considering co-location with other generation or considering participation in paired-resource models, constraining how PSH state-of-charge management interacts with capacity accreditation and must-offer rules.

documents.ai_summary: The Independent Market Monitor (IMM) presents its interim reserve-redesign proposal for PJM's Reliability Committee, opposing PJM's parallel proposal. The IMM recommends three sequential implementation packages: (1) incorporating net load forecast uncertainty into reserve calculations (near-term priority); (2) reserve performance measurement and settlement changes; (3) reserve eligibility and market-clearing engine changes. The critical difference is the online/offline reserve mix: PJM proposes all 10-minute reserves be online-only, significantly raising production costs and clearing prices; the IMM proposes maintaining offline reserve capability (primary reserves) and synchronized (online) reserves separately. The IMM contends PJM's approach reduces market efficiency and jeopardizes reliability if current fast-start generators drop fast-start capability to avoid the online-reserve requirement. Solar generation in PJM has grown dramatically (14.3 GW maximum hourly output in 2026, 2.4% of annual generation), driving net-load uncertainty that both proposals address but with different reserve adequacy methods — the IMM's approach captures generator performance uncertainty in 30-minute reserves and includes demand response as eligible supply. No vote date or next-step deadline is stated; the presentation positions the IMM proposal as the operational-necessity baseline against PJM's preferred-design alternative.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE has established a Probabilistic Energy Adequacy Tool (PEAT) and Regional Energy Shortfall Threshold (REST) framework to conduct 5- and 10-year energy assessments (study years 2031 and 2036). The replacement strategy for retired resources uses interconnection-queue composition (70% batteries, 15% PV, 15% onshore wind) scaled by nameplate-to-capacity factors, not direct assumption of hydro replacement. For hydro and pumped-storage operators, the most material scenarios are the large-load and import-constrained sensitivities, which will reveal energy-shortfall risk periods and durations under high-scarcity conditions — data that affects seasonal accreditation exposure and the likelihood of sustained high-price regimes. The methodology explicitly excludes offshore wind from the replacement portfolio due to buildout uncertainty, leaving a net-generation gap in retirement scenarios that hydro supply could fill. No formal comment deadline or next action date is stated in this overview.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ proposes MIR81-R, which distinguishes 'Normal' MTIs (active in day-ahead, RUC, and pre-RTBM; then fixed in RTBM) from 'Dynamic' MTIs (active only in RTBM). A BA may register separate scheduling constraints for the same path using different transaction types, allowing it to restrict incremental real-time transfers independently of day-ahead commitment without disrupting the prior optimized dispatch plan. The mechanism allows BAs to limit swing in net scheduled interchange (NSI) between RTBM dispatch intervals while preserving the DA/RUC commitment. This affects transmission-constrained hydro by potentially reducing real-time flexibility access on congested paths and creating dynamic constraint shadow prices in RTBM that were previously zero or absorbed in DA/Pre-RTBM; hydro with limited upstream flexibility or PSH relying on real-time inter-BA transfers for arbitrage or reserve charging face higher exposure to binding Dynamic constraints. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in the presentation.

documents.ai_summary: Markets+ is establishing tariff and protocol language (MIR 9.2-R) to create a new "Dynamic Schedule Resource" participation type for dispatchable resources physically located in one participating BA but dynamically scheduled to serve load in another BA. The proposal addresses a double-counting problem in current power-balance accounting: when a dynamically scheduled resource is dispatched to a new output level, both the MTI (market transmission interface) and the dynamic NSI (net scheduled interchange) reflect the change, forcing both BAs to regulate separately. MIR 9.2-R introduces a Dynamic Schedule Resource Interface tied to each such resource, so only the interface — not both the output and the NSI — enters the attaining BA's power balance, eliminating double regulation. The framework allows resource-coupled dynamic schedules (Use Case 1a: participating BA to participating BA with a specific dispatchable resource) to remain under Markets+ dispatch control while transferring regulation responsibility to the attaining BA, with e-tagging requirements and registration mandates for market participants. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in the document; it appears to be a technical briefing of tariff and protocol changes already adopted or in final preparation.

documents.ai_summary: ERCOT's Retail Market Subcommittee is advancing two items related to a new Energy Attribute Certificate program (NPRR1264): an impact analysis (RMGRR182) and language review (LPGRR076) scheduled for vote on June 25, 2026. documents.ai_summary: CAISO has refined its generator on-peak deliverability study methodology, effective January 2024 and documented here as of June 2026, to address bottleneck risk as the generation fleet diversifies and solar penetration shifts peak net load. Hydroelectric facilities, particularly older reservoir-based units prone to becoming stranded as markets shift, may use this pathway to recover operating costs when transmission upgrades are pending; revenues from energy, capacity, and ancillary-services sales are credited against RMR charges, creating a hybrid cost-plus mechanism. The framework applies to units regardless of fuel type and is effective only upon FERC approval; PJM terminates the RMR when it determines the constraint is resolved. documents.ai_summary: PJM Part V tariff revisions (first read at June 24, 2026 MRC) govern generation deactivation notice, reliability-impact review, and continued operation under must-run arrangements. Generation owners must provide 12 months' notice; PJM then has 4–5 months to assess whether deactivation would harm transmission reliability. If reliability impacts are found, owners can elect either cost-of-service recovery or a Deactivation Avoidable Cost Credit (DACC) formula—a monthly payment that escalates from 110% in year one to 150% by year four of the deactivation-delay period, less actual net market revenues. The formula applies to generation (including hydropower) that continues operating beyond its desired retirement date to support grid reliability. Most relevant to aging hydro plants facing retirement but needed for transmission support or seasonal energy adequacy; the DACC structure and multiplier schedule directly determine whether an extended operating life is economically viable.

Key terms include: (1) Generation Owner may terminate only on Catastrophic Force Majeure, if PJM denies necessary Project Investment, or by exercising standard deactivation rights with 90 days' notice; (2) PJM may terminate on 61 days' notice if the RMR Resource is no longer needed, with full recovery of prudently incurred costs; (3) PJM may extend the term unilaterally, requiring Generation Owner response within 14 days and permitting renegotiation of compensation; and (4) PJM retains dispatch authority over the RMR Resource for transmission limits, system restoration, capacity emergencies, or operational testing, subject only to owner-disclosed operating limitations. The revisions require: (1) generators operate exclusively in automatic voltage-control mode unless documented exceptions are approved by PJM and the Transmission Owner; (2) define acceptable volt-VAR boundaries and VAR control ranges per MW output (32.87% of max MW capacity); and (3) establish a three-party investigative process (PJM, TO, and generator owner/operator) for reactive control performance issues, with PJM empowered to direct AVR and inverter settings changes. For conventional hydroelectric and pumped-storage facilities, this narrows operational flexibility in reactive-power dispatch—generators can no longer operate in constant-MVAR, constant power-factor, or manual modes without PJM/TO approval—potentially reducing the ability to optimize reactive output for revenue or water management. The mechanism locks storage owners into a single operational purpose (voltage/flow support) tied to planning-study assumptions, with tariff conforming language expected September–November 2026.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE has redlined Section II of its tariff to establish a formal Deactivation Notification process for permanent resource retirements, effective for the Capacity Commitment Period beginning June 1, 2028. Generators seeking to retire must file a deactivation notice by the first business day within 12 months of each CCP start; resources >20 MW are subject to a 90-day reliability review, after which ISO may delay deactivation if needed for local transmission reliability and offer net going-forward-cost compensation. Key mechanics: (1) resources that never held Capacity Network Resource Interconnection Service (CNR or equivalent) can deactivate by simple written notice; (2) resources inactive for three calendar years are deemed automatically deactivated unless repower-application protections apply; (3) Lead Market Participants must submit detailed cost workbooks and officer affidavits, subject to Internal Market Monitor audit. Most exposed are Northeast hydro owners contemplating retirement, especially run-of-river or peaking units currently holding CNR capacity — the reliability-review gate and potential delayed-deactivation obligation (with only net-going-forward-cost recovery) can trap owners in the market longer than planned, and the three-year automatic-deactivation clock creates planning urgency for units on extended outages.

documents.title: 2026-06-24 TC A05 NEPOOL Counsel Memo Summarizing FERC Show Cause Order to ISO-NE & PTOs (Docket No. EL26-72)
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: FERC's show-cause order to ISO-NE on large-load and co-located-load integration directly affects hydro's strategic options — co-location rules, new transmission service definitions, and generator interconnection pathways for resources serving co-located load will reshape how hydropower (especially pumped storage and run-of-river) can participate in transmission service markets and capture value from load-proximate generation.
documents.ai_summary: FERC issued a show-cause order (June 18, 2026, Docket EL26-72) to ISO-NE and Participating Transmission Owners, preliminarily finding the tariff unjust and unreasonable for lacking provisions on large-load and co-located-load integration. ISO-NE has 60 days to propose tariff changes addressing five categories: application procedures for large loads (defined as ≥50 MW peak at single site, ≥69 kV), cost transparency and cost-recovery agreements, rates and terms for co-location (co-located load defined as end-use customer load physically connected to a generating facility), new transmission services (interim NITS, firm and non-firm contract demand), and generator interconnection for resources serving electrically proximate or co-located load. The order defines three interconnection approaches for generators: new study process matching output to load forecast, use of existing service at existing POI, or load-limited service with no injection. ISO-NE must also file a 30-day informational report on resource adequacy for new large loads. This order parallels concurrent FERC actions in PJM and SPP and builds on Secretary of Energy ANOPR RM26-4-000 (October 2025). Hydro owners should note that co-location rules and new transmission service architecture will determine whether existing or new hydropower facilities can serve co-located or electrically proximate loads, and how ancillary services and BTMG netting are treated—directly affecting revenue models for pumped storage and run-of-river plants positioned near emerging data-center loads in New England.

documents.title: 2026-06-24 TC A05 FERC Show Cause Order to ISO-NE & PTOs (Docket No. EL26-72)

documents.ai_summary: FERC issued a Show Cause Order (Docket EL26-72, 195 FERC ¶ 61,215) finding ISO-NE's Tariff preliminarily unjust and unreasonable for lack of large-load integration provisions, with ISO-NE and PTOs required to respond by August 17, 2026, or request abeyance by August 3 to file a Section 205 tariff proposal by November 16. The Order identifies five deficiency categories: transmission-service application procedures, cost transparency and cost-shifting, co-location and behind-the-meter generation rules, new flexible transmission services, and generator interconnection for load-serving facilities. Most material to hydro and pumped storage: FERC mandates new interconnection service options for generators serving electrically proximate or co-located large loads (50+ MW) and requires tariff rules governing how behind-the-meter generation nets against load for transmission charges and ancillary-service cost allocation. This directly enables co-located storage/hydro at large industrial sites—including data-center clusters—to be studied and interconnected under expedited or load-limited frameworks, but requires ISO-NE to clarify which ancillary-service costs (regulation, black start) large loads cannot avoid and to ensure cost allocation does not shift to other wholesale customers. ISO-NE must also file an informational report on resource-adequacy proposals by July 20, 2026.

NPRR1329 allows two Resource Entities to jointly manage injection/withdrawal limits at a Point of Interconnection through shared QSE responsibility and attestation. documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Market Monitoring Unit analyzed the 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook to evaluate how market signals guide renewable and storage investment. Key finding: energy storage becomes cost-effective for curtailment mitigation only as wind and solar penetration increases and marginal curtailment rates rise; under the Index Storage Credit structure, storage has strong incentives to locate where curtailment risk is highest, but may be unprofitable near profitable renewable sites. The MMU also identifies nodal and technology discounts (differences between zonal average LBMP and generation-weighted LBMP at renewable sites), which reduce wind and solar net revenues below Index REC strike prices—a signal that affects both the competitiveness of all-renewable portfolios and the relative value of storage as a complementary product. For pumped-storage owners, this analysis quantifies the regional and temporal distribution of curtailment opportunities and implied net revenue costs of storage across three policy scenarios (Contract Case 2030, 100×44 High Load 2035, 95×44 Baseline Load 2035), directly informing where PSH investment is most economically justified under NYISO market rules.

No vote date or comment deadline is stated; the request is for stakeholder support to designate this as an FY2027 project. This particularly benefits reservoir-based hydropower and pumped storage that rely on schedule flexibility to optimize operations across interregional pricing signals; the change reduces a non-price scheduling constraint that previously limited their ability to respond to real-time conditions. Implementation is targeted for Q3 2026.

documents.ai_summary: MISO and PJM propose to retire the Coordinated Transaction Scheduling (CTS) product—a coordinated interchange optimization tool approved by FERC in 2016 and launched in 2017—due to minimal usage, underperformance ($740k in annual savings vs. $17–72M projected), and high migration costs ($1.4M to migrate to the new Market Clearing Engine, $0.8M to maintain over 5 years). Stakeholders submitted mixed feedback: some requested a modern replacement (e.g., SPP's Inter-Market Optimization) before retirement to avoid operational gaps, while others supported retirement given CTS inefficiencies. MISO responds that other interchange products (Fixed, Cleared Day-Ahead, and Dynamic schedules) already offer more granular, real-time scheduling (adjustable to 20 minutes before interval vs. 75 minutes for CTS), and MISO is open to pursuing replacement products with PJM and SPP after retirement. MISO and PJM intend to coordinate tariff and Joint Operating Agreement filings later in 2026 to remove CTS. Hydro owners on or serving the MISO-PJM interface lose a tool for optimizing interchange pricing and may see reduced locational value signals for flexibility; replacements under discussion are not yet defined.

documents.ai_summary: MISO is adopting enhanced meteorology-driven wind profiles for its PY2027–2028 Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) studies, replacing status-quo profiles with 30-year synthetic data that better capture low-wind conditions and seasonal variability. The new profiles increase wind ELCC values (especially in Spring, rising from 19.3% to 43.8%), but also shift the distribution of critical-event durations by season, causing storage DLOL accreditation to rise significantly in Fall (+12.7 percentage points) while falling in Winter and Spring (−11.2% and −20.0% respectively). Thermal resources' accreditation is affected primarily by shifts in which maintenance-outage hours overlap with newly identified critical hours. MISO plans to move forward with the enhanced profiles subject to final review and will maintain a hybrid approach (synthetic pre-2012, observed post-2012). documents.title: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 03 Refresher on Seasonal LOLE Targets.pdf
documents.filename: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 03 Refresher on Seasonal LOLE Targets.pdf

documents.ai_summary: MISO adopted a seasonal LOLE (Loss of Load Expectation) construct in 2023–2024, replacing a single annual 0.1 days/year target with per-season minima of 0.01 days/year. The framework accounts for seasonal variation in peak load (winter mornings, overnight cold events), forced-outage rates (thermal units fail more in extreme cold/heat), planned maintenance clustering (spring/fall), and ELCC values for wind and solar, which differ materially by season. MISO runs an annual LOLE study first, then upwardly adjusts any season falling below 0.01 days/year by adding perfect or proxy units. This document presents the construct as positioned between PJM's simple annual PRMR% approach and ISO-NE's proposed monthly granularity, and includes historical LOLE splits (PY25–26 all summer risk; PY26–27 split summer/winter/spring; PY29–30 nearly even summer/winter) showing how seasonal requirements dampen year-to-year volatility. Hydro operators are most affected because seasonal accreditation directly determines their RA contribution value in each quarter—winter peaking and spring outage windows matter independently rather than being smoothed into a summer-anchored requirement—and because the tariff filing referenced as of June 1, 2026 (adding a perfect positive unit to the LOLE algorithm) may change the study's outcome.

documents.title: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 04 LOLE Load Modeling Process and Results.pdf
documents.filename: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 04 LOLE Load Modeling Process and Results.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) study drives resource-adequacy requirements and seasonal capacity accreditation for all dispatchable units including hydro; unprecedented load growth and forecast-uncertainty revisions directly affect the capacity value and RA showing requirements hydro operators must meet, and seasonal peak-demand modeling shapes winter/spring reliability signals that influence hydro dispatch and scarcity pricing.
documents.ai_summary: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation Working Group is revising its load modeling process and load-forecast uncertainty assumptions for Planning Year 2027–2028, noting that actual loads have deviated from LOLE projections by 4% in shoulder seasons—exceeding current uncertainty bands. MISO is automating the load-development process (replacing NeuroShell with Histogram Gradient Boosting), standardizing extreme-temperature thresholds, and proposing to expand load-forecast error bands (e.g., from ±2% to a range including +3% to +4%) to reflect data-center and electrification-driven load growth. The key mechanism is that higher projected load peaks and wider uncertainty distributions increase the probability of scarcity conditions in LOLE runs, raising capacity-accreditation requirements for all dispatchable resources and making seasonal hydro availability more valuable in winter and shoulder months. MISO is requesting stakeholder feedback on model inputs and uncertainty-assumption options through July 7, 2026, via the Feedback Tool at misoenergy.org.

documents.filename: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 05 CIL CEL Model and Input File Overview.pdf

documents.ai_summary: MISO is conducting Capacity Import Limit (CIL) and Capacity Export Limit (CEL) studies for Planning Year 2027-2028 across four seasons (Summer 2027, Fall 2027, Winter 2027-2028, Spring 2028). CIL/CEL values constrain capacity transfers between MISO's Local Resource Zones in the Planning Resource Auction and are calculated using transfer-capability analyses that redispatch conventional generators and wind/solar (wind and solar are curtailed, not ramped up). The study uses PSSE power-flow models and contingency files now posted on ShareFile for stakeholder review. MISO requests stakeholder feedback on input files by July 7, 2026, with preliminary results expected in September 2026 and final values in October 2026. For hydro operators, tighter CIL/CEL values reduce their zone's ability to export capacity—lowering locational RA value and export revenue—while looser limits enhance those streams; the redispatch methodology's treatment of hydro as curtailable (not dispatchable) may understate the transfer capability available when hydro can flex output. Most exposed are multi-zone hydro fleets and pumped storage units in export-constrained Local Resource Zones.
