documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Large load interconnection and interim service step-up procedures materially affect hydro's strategic options for co-located load participation, transmission deliverability, and resource-adequacy obligations, and establish precedent for how RTOs structure partial-service pathways that could extend to storage and other dispatchable resources.
documents.ai_summary: MISO is formalizing a Firm Service Step Up process to allow large load customers to begin service on partial load blocks before full transmission upgrades are complete, using only interim available capacity. The process requires each partial load addition to pass NERC TPL-001 reliability studies (90-day cycle, quarterly submissions, first-ready-first-served prioritization) and mandates that the load-serving entity procure generation capacity in MISO's Planning Resource Auction to cover the interim load. Approved partial loads become effective at the start of the planning year and persist until the full load interconnection is operational; service is revoked if a load block fails to energize within 90 days of its approved date. For hydro and pumped-storage operators, this is strategically relevant: (1) co-located hydro can now supply large-load customers incrementally rather than waiting for full transmission readiness, shortening payback and improving investment returns; (2) the requirement that interim loads participate in the PRA means the resource-adequacy framework now extends to partial-service loads, establishing that generation must be procured at each step, a model that could define how storage and other flexible resources are accredited in segmented operations; (3) hydro deliverability and transmission-constraint management now explicitly account for multiple overlapping interim-service blocks, which affects zonal scarcity pricing and ramping-reserve demand. MISO requests stakeholder feedback on the prioritization methodology, submission granularity, study frequency, and generation-availability accounting by Monday, June 24, 2026, with tariff language to follow in August.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group is advancing three initiatives: (1) a zero-injection GIA framework (PAC-2024-2B) governing market participation and registration of co-located load and generation, with tariff review scheduled for June 10, 2026; (2) interconnection reliability requirements (LLWG-2026-3) including ramp capability, ride-through, and stability standards for large loads, with transitional language, data/modeling, and ride-through requirements under review; and (3) a large load firm service step-up study (LLWG-2026-1) with study-process design details due June 10. These establish the rules under which conventional hydro and pumped-storage hydro can compete to serve large loads co-located at or behind load centers, and define the operational obligations (ramp, stability, ride-through) that such service requires. The firm-service framework may create new contracting or capacity-accreditation pathways for dispatchable resources, particularly in load-growth regions where large loads are interconnecting.

documents.ai_summary: MISO is finalizing tariff language for Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements, targeting a June 30, 2026 filing. The framework distinguishes between Computational Loads (digitally driven, requiring advanced modeling, PMU, ramp, and ride-through requirements) and Non-Computational Loads (baseline data and telemetry only), with applicability triggered at 50 MW or expansions of 25+ MW. For hydro owners, this matters because (1) co-located data centers, cryptocurrency mining, and HPC workloads with which hydro may be sited or co-operate are now subject to detailed telemetry, PMU, dynamic modeling, and forecasting requirements that will flow upstream to the interconnecting hydro facility; (2) large-load definition and transition provisions now allow flexibility for in-flight projects, creating windows for strategic positioning; and (3) the distinction between computational and non-computational behavior may allow run-of-river or variable hydro paired with load to avoid some advanced-modeling burdens if properly characterized. Stakeholder feedback significantly shaped the revised language, particularly on applicability date, transition timelines, and load-type distinctions.

documents.ai_summary: MISO published a technical compendium establishing reliability requirements for large transmission-connected loads (data centers, AI computing, crypto mining) that are growing rapidly across its footprint. The framework mandates telemetry and PMU requirements, data/modeling disclosures, short-term load forecasting, ramp-rate limits, voltage and frequency ride-through standards, and transient-stability and oscillation assessments for new large loads. This affects hydro owners in two ways: (1) large-load behavior—rapid changes in power consumption and sudden disconnections during disturbances—will drive more volatile and unpredictable demand patterns that hydropower must balance in real time, potentially increasing the operational value of hydro's ramping and regulation services; and (2) ride-through and stability rules imposed on loads may shift grid-stability burdens away from demand-side and back onto traditional generation (including hydro), creating new obligations for synchronous units. The document does not indicate a comment deadline or vote schedule; it appears to be a draft technical standard (marked as compendium draft) with stakeholder-engagement appendix noted but not shown in excerpt.

documents.title: 05. NPRR1214_ERCOTComments_20260610 v6
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ERCOT's proposed changes to NPRR 1214 directly affect price formation (LMP and AS MCPC determination) and indifference-payment settlement mechanics that would apply to any dispatchable or storage resource participating in a similar market structure; the pricing and settlement innovations are instructive cross-market comparison points for how RTOs handle reliability deployments and the distortion between dispatch (actual) and pricing-run (counterfactual) awards.
documents.ai_summary: ERCOT proposes revisions to NPRR 1214 that eliminate energy and ancillary-service price adders by using SCED Pricing Run prices (LMPs and AS MCPCs) directly when a pricing run is active, rather than calculating adders as Pricing Run minus Dispatch Run prices. In parallel, ERCOT introduces an ancillary-services indifference payment (previously energy-only) using actual offer/bid curves instead of linear approximations, and extends indifference-payment consideration to RUC, RMR, and MRA resources whose real-time revenues were previously overlooked. The proposal also expands locational modeling of reliability deployments to Load and SOG resources under certain dispatch scenarios. Although ERCOT has no hydropower, the design—separating binding dispatch awards (from actual grid state) from binding prices (from hypothetical state absent reliability deployments), and compensating the resulting financial mismatch via indifference payments—illustrates an alternative settlement architecture that contrasts with how other RTOs (including those with hydro fleets) handle the same tension between dispatch realism and scarcity-signal accuracy.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes targeted adjustments to its day-ahead ancillary services (DA A/S) design, effective October 22, 2026, based on February 2026 Internal Market Monitor recommendations. The changes include: (1) reducing the Forecast Energy Requirement Demand Quantity (FER DQ) by expected uncleared front-of-the-meter wind and solar supply to better reflect actual reliability needs; (2) setting a daily floor for the DA A/S strike price (K) based on the marginal cost of an efficient, distillate-fired combustion turbine, including regional emissions costs; and (3) establishing a $3/MWh floor on the Impact Test Threshold. For hydro operators, the strike-price floor methodology is the key mechanic—it ties ancillary-services scarcity pricing to a fossil marginal-cost reference, which will raise the opportunity cost against which hydro's must-offer obligation is evaluated and may increase procurement volume during scarcity events when hydro's regulation and reserve products clear at higher prices. The FER DQ reduction for variable wind/solar will also shift the composition of reliability-based demand, potentially favoring the fast-ramping and continuous-availability profile that hydro supplies. ISO-NE Markets Committee votes on these changes June 9–10, 2026, with Participants Committee vote scheduled June 16–18, 2026.

documents.title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04k - CAR-SA: Capacity Bilaterals - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Capacity IBTs and exports rules directly affect how hydro and storage operators can hedge capacity-market revenues and manage export bids—both central to revenue optimization under ISO-NE's seasonal capacity market redesign (CAR-SA).
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes to implement Capacity Internal Bilateral Transactions (IBTs)—an ISO-administered financial instrument allowing participants to hedge capacity-market price risk by fixing capacity payments—and to simplify capacity-export rules under the seasonal Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA), effective Q2 2027. Under CAR-SA, capacity clearing occurs ~1 month before each 6-month season (vs. 40+ months ahead under the old FCM), shortening the forward-price visibility window and raising hedging demand. The Capacity IBT would allow a supplier and LSE to exchange fixed-for-floating swaps on capacity obligations, with the ISO settling the floating leg (pegged to seasonal clearing prices or CLO charge rates) and netting it within ISO settlement, while the fixed leg stays off-ISO books. Separately, ISO-NE would discontinue rarely-used export-bid curtailment exemptions (III.1.10.7(f) and III.15.8.1.2) and consolidate export functionality under simpler rules (III.1.10.7(i)), allowing capacity exporters to submit opportunity costs that determine MRIC eligibility. Hydro and PSH operators using export strategies or managing capacity revenues through bilateral hedges will see changes to both pricing instruments and export curtailment priority; the proposal suggests March 2027 implementation and is under stakeholder feedback.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE presents three approaches to cap the Balancing Ratio (BR) under its seasonal capacity auction reform (CAR-SA), addressing a FERC order requiring the BR cap at 1.0 to prevent resources from being obligated beyond physical capability. The migration from Qualified Capacity to Marginal Reliability Impact (MRI) accreditation will reduce total capacity supply obligations system-wide, raising BRs and causing the 1.0 cap to bind more frequently, which shrinks Capacity Performance Payments (CPPs) to overperformers due to funding deficiencies. ISO-NE's preferred Approach 3 would cap the BR at a seasonal ratio tied to net maximum capability divided by net MRIC (1.355 in summer, 1.444 in winter), preserving stronger performance incentives for overperformance while complying with FERC's logic. Additionally, ISO-NE proposes conforming the annual PFP stop-loss limit to a seasonal market by capping seasonal losses at two times (instead of three times) a resource's maximum monthly net loss. Stakeholder feedback is due to Jasleen Singh (jsingh@iso-ne.com) by June 24, 2026, with ISO-NE targeting July for its final proposal. Large-duration and seasonal-flexibility resources (including pumped storage and multi-week-capable reservoirs) are most exposed, as their value in CAR-SA depends on accreditation during scarcity hours; how the BR cap settles will determine whether they receive full or reduced CPP rates during performance.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes a Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) transition mechanism (target Q2 2027 effective date) that will gradually shift resource accreditation from current Qualified Capacity to proposed seasonal MRIC (Minimum Reliability Impact Contribution) values over two transition years (two summer and two winter seasons), with full phased design taking effect in Capacity Commitment Period 21. The transition uses a weighted-average approach: in Year 1, a 100 MW QC resource with 70 MW summer MRIC and 40 MW winter MRIC would be accredited at 90 MW (summer) and 80 MW (winter); by Year 3 it falls to the full MRIC floor (70/40 MW). Hydro owners will face material accreditation volatility during transition because MRIC values depend on seasonal performance during modeled Minimum Reliability Interest hours, potentially creating seasonal mismatches between what resources can offer and what demand curves procure. ISO-NE is still assessing demand-curve transition mechanics and whether to transition the winter gas constraint; comments and questions are due to Markets Committee Secretary Jasleen Singh (Jsingh@iso-ne.com) by June 24, 2026, with further stakeholder meetings scheduled through Q3 2026 before FERC filing.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is modeling accreditation outcomes under its proposed CAR-SA design using a 70-year weather-adjusted load dataset (weighted subset of years 2000/01–2022/23 for winter; 2007–2023 for summer) to capture long-term weather variability and peak-load scenarios. Sensitivity analysis shows that explicitly modeling all 70 years of winter hourly loads produces nearly identical net ICR, reliability metrics (LOLE, LOLH, EUE), and accreditation results (rMRI) across all resource types — including Daily/Weekly Hydro (96.1–96.2%), Energy Storage (20.9–21.7%), and IPR-Hydro (59.9–61.0%) — compared to the ISO's proposed weighted-year approach. The ISO assessed and rejected FirstLight Resource Management's alternate block-based weighting methodology, concluding it ignores inter-block weather correlations and temporal heterogeneity, understating the likelihood of severe winters and distorting the upper tail of the load distribution where resource adequacy is most critical. The proposed framework will remain in place for CAR-SA implementation targeting Q2 2027; FirstLight's alternative approach was a stakeholder submission rather than ISO proposal.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE presented seasonal offer construction methodology and seller-side market power mitigation rules for its Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) proceeding. The ISO proposes applying a Capacity Offer Price Threshold (COPT) methodology conformed from the FCA's Dynamic Delist Bid Threshold, capped at 25–75% of net Net CONE, plus a pivotal supplier test that automatically reduces bids above the threshold if the supplier is deemed pivotal. For the first seasonal auctions in CCP19, the ISO will use an initial COPT of 37% of annual Net CONE (derived from historical FCA16-18 ratios) rather than prior-auction pricing. The presentation illustrates offer formulation for generalized resources and gas-constrained resources by showing how next-best-alternative analysis drives capacity bids — resources whose NBA is temporary exit must cover netGFC plus expected PFP costs, while resources profitable in energy markets offer only the PFP common-value component. Hydro operators with seasonal revenue constraints (e.g., run-of-river or PSH facing winter/summer energy-market disparities) will need to validate whether their avoidable-cost calculations and PFP recovery assumptions survive the pivotal supplier test; if mitigated improperly, FERC cost-recovery procedures are available. Key findings: energy prices rose 66–79% in 2025 due to higher gas prices, peak loads, reduced OOM commitment, increased exports to Quebec, and reduced hydro availability; the MMU identifies $221M in misallocated costs annually, including $40M from statewide allocation of local reserve charges and $38M from largest contingencies not paying their impact on reserve requirements; the MMU recommends urgent reforms to shortage pricing (Rec #2017-2: raising NYCA 30-min ORDC to $2000/MWh up to 150% of largest contingency) to prevent economically unjustified exports to ISO-NE and PJM, and to dynamically adjust reserve requirements and model locational constraints in day-ahead commitment. Hydro operators benefit from higher scarcity pricing and better locational reserve signals, but face exposure to large downward corrections if demand-response baseline issues and cryptocurrency-miner over-consumption (paying full LMP despite uneconomic curtailment) are fixed; the report documents $34M annual uplift from paying demand response as if it generates electricity, which competes with traditional ramping and flexibility revenue.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's 2027 project-prioritization survey solicits stakeholder input on six initiatives, due July 15, 2026. Project 1 (5-Minute Transaction Scheduling) expands a 2020 study to develop market rules and mechanisms for scheduling interchange with Hydro-Québec at five-minute frequency, aligning with internal real-time dispatch and improving price convergence and ramping flexibility — directly increasing hydro's strategic options in cross-border trade and within-hour balancing. Project 3 (Aggregation System Integration) streamlines DER and aggregation enrollment processes via API integration, supporting Order 2222 participation pathways for small hydro. Project 4 (Demand Response Baseline Alignment) investigates whether demand-response baselines can be net suppliers of ICAP capacity, following MMU recommendations — the rules examined also govern how DSRs and storage interact with capacity markets. Project 5 (Automatic ICAP Surplus Offers) proposes automatic resale of unforced-capacity surplus to reduce market-clearing prices. These collectively reshape how hydro and storage interact with capacity, flexibility, and cross-border revenue mechanisms; survey responses and comments will be made public and posted with Budget & Priorities Working Group materials.

documents.ai_summary: MISO and PJM are conducting a coordinated Transmission and Market Enhancement Projects (TMEP) study to address ~$681 million in persistent congestion on Market-to-Market flowgates between the two RTOs (2024–2025 data). The study, initiated following a March 13, 2026 Issues Review IPSAC decision, will evaluate 23 flowgate candidates and assess whether non-transmission solutions (operator adjustments, market redesigns, or asset-owner flexibility) can relieve binding constraints more cost-effectively than capital projects. Study steps run June–November 2026, with outcomes informing which interregional bottlenecks impede hydro export capability and which may be solvable via operational or market changes rather than new wires. For hydro owners with resources near the MISO-PJM seam, the study outcomes determine whether transmission constraints limiting their revenue will be addressed via infrastructure investment, demand-response/flexibility products, or remain as persistent opportunity costs. The next IPSAC meeting is scheduled for August 17, 2026.

documents.ai_summary: MISO and PJM are jointly developing an expanded interregional transmission planning framework to overcome structural limitations in their Joint Operating Agreement's ability to identify and evaluate interregional solutions, with emphasis on long-range scenario-driven benefit identification under FERC Order 1920. They are stress-testing three benefit metrics (reliability, production-cost, and extreme-weather benefits) through an Interregional Transmission Coordinated Study (ITCS), with a compliance filing expected in Q4 2026 and ongoing coordination of planning assumptions and horizons across MTEP/RTEP cycles. This effort is material to hydro and PSH owners in the MISO-PJM seam because transmission expansion projects evaluated under the new framework could alter interregional transfer limits, change the economic value of storage flexibility across the seam, and shape how long-duration or seasonal hydro resource adequacy is credited in joint reliability studies — owners should monitor the Q4 2026 filing and the benefit-metric definitions MISO and PJM adopt, as they may reframe how interregional hydro exports and PSH cyclic operation are valued in future planning.

The RTOs assert their existing long-term regional planning processes (MISO LRTP, PJM Long-Term Planning) and interregional procedures are generally compliant; key reforms include explicit long-term transmission-needs posting, joint evaluation of interregional facilities, and allowance for any entity to propose interregional projects within regional planning processes. Stakeholder review (redlines July–August 2026, regional committee engagement through October–November 2026) precedes the December 2026 FERC filing. For hydro owners, interregional facility eligibility and transparent cost-benefit evaluation of cross-regional transmission solutions directly affect how PSH and reservoir hydro assets can be sited and valued for export; the expanded entity-proposal rights create a formal pathway for hydro interests to nominate interregional transmission solutions to meet long-term needs, with December 12, 2026 as the RTO filing deadline and stakeholder feedback windows in July–October 2026.

documents.title: Draft Final Proposal - Interconnection Service Capacity and Deliverability Retention for Non-Operating Generating Facilities - May 11, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Establishes mandatory timelines and conditions for retaining interconnection service capacity and deliverability rights when hydroelectric or pumped-storage facilities cease operations, mothball, or repower — directly affecting whether a hydro owner can preserve its grid position and capacity value during outages or strategic transitions.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Draft Final Proposal (May 11, 2026) codifies rules requiring non-operating generating facilities to either return to service, enter the generator interconnection queue, or begin repower construction within specified timeframes to retain deliverability allocations and interconnection service capacity rights; failure to act within these windows forfeits the rights, releasing capacity back to the system. MECHANISM: The proposal creates a hard-deadline retention regime that affects hydro owners planning extended maintenance, mothballing, or repowering. Facilities reaching physical derate (reduced maximum output) lose deliverability commensurate with the loss if the derate exceeds 3 years; those exiting wholesale markets to serve behind-the-meter load are treated as permanent retirements triggering reliability reviews and potential RMR (Reliability Must Run) obligations. SCOPE: All hydroelectric resources in CAISO territory, particularly those contemplating maintenance windows beyond 3 years, repower projects, or transitional mothball periods, are exposed. Generators choosing not to follow notification processes forfeit their rights, and the proposal strengthens ISO enforcement of 90-day advance notice and retirement affidavits. Next step: Draft Final Proposal status indicates Board action is pending (typical CAISO timeline ~Q3 2026); stakeholders should monitor for final tariff vote and implementation timeline.

documents.title: Item 04 – 1 Manual 14d – Revision 71 – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's revision to Manual 14d establishes binding reactive power control requirements for all generators, including hydroelectric units, affecting their compliance obligations and operational constraints on voltage support capability provision.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 14d Section 7.1.2 to clarify and strengthen reactive power (voltage support) control requirements for all generators in its footprint, driven by NERC's May 2026 lowering of IBR registration thresholds to 20 MVA and PJM's identification of increasing low-voltage risk (citing the 2025 Spain blackout). The revision mandates automatic voltage control mode as the default for all generators; defines volt-var control boundaries and reactive output ranges tied to MW output; specifies two new required reactive capability curve data points ('Maximum AVR capable MW Output' and 'Unit Minimum MW Output with Reactive Control'); and establishes a three-party investigative process (PJM, transmission owner, generator owner/operator) for reactive control performance issues. For hydroelectric owners, this tightens the operating envelope for reactive power supply: hydro units must now document and receive explicit approval for any AVR mode other than voltage control, and must define their reactive capability limits with new precision, constraining dispatch flexibility and potentially requiring retrofits or AVR reconfiguration on legacy units. The revision proceeds through SOS (June 15), MRC (July 1 and July 9), and OC endorsement (July 23), with education and Q&A sessions between June 4 and July 9. The compliance timeline is not yet stated in this first-read presentation.

documents.title: Item 04 – 2 Manual 14d – Revision 71 – Executive Summary
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: reactive power and voltage support obligations — PJM is clarifying VAR control requirements and AVR mode directives in Manual 14d, which directly affects how synchronous hydro and PSH units must operate their excitation systems and reactive-capability dispatch; this tightens an existing compliance obligation and may constrain flexibility in real-time volt-var/watt-var behavior.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 14d (Generator Operational Requirements), sections 7.1.2 and Attachment D, effective July 23, 2026, to add NERC Category 2 GO references, clarify allowable AVR (automatic voltage regulator) modes, specify acceptable volt-var and watt-var control ranges, and formalize PJM's monitoring and engagement authority over reactive-control behavior. The revision responds to NERC's May 2026 Category 2 GO initiative (expanding inverter-based resource reliability standards) and PJM's operational challenges from rising solar/IBR penetration and load growth outstripping generation, both elevating voltage risk. For synchronous hydro and PSH operators, this tightens the specification of reactive-capability dispatch and AVR operating ranges — reducing ambiguity about allowable volt-var curves but also narrowing operational flexibility in voltage control. Most affected are large reservoir hydro and PSH facilities with synchronous generators supplying reactive power in constrained voltage zones; smaller or run-of-river plants with limited reactive margin may face tighter conformance audits. MRC voting is scheduled for July 23rd, 2026.

documents.title: Item 04 – 3 Manual 14d – Revision 71 – Redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Manual 14D governs PJM generator operational and data-exchange requirements, metering standards, and dispatch procedures that directly affect hydro and storage operators' compliance obligations, participation pathways, and black-start procurement eligibility.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 14D (Revision 71, effective June 30, 2026) is a comprehensive operational and technical standard for all generating resources in PJM, including hydro, storage, and hybrid facilities. The redline reflects updates to control-center requirements, EMS data exchange and synchrophasor protocols, metering standards (with specific exhibits for energy-storage and hybrid resources), cold-weather resource preparation checklists for conventional and inverter-based units, black-start procurement processes, and behind-the-meter and microgrid business rules. Hydro and pumped-storage operators must comply with metering precision, reactive-capability testing and reporting (Attachments D–E), dispatch-instruction protocols, outage-scheduling, and cold-weather operational readiness (Attachment N) — and may be selected for black-start service under the revised incremental RFP and reliability backstop processes (Section 10). Mixed-technology facilities (solar–storage hybrids) now have dedicated marketing and metering rules (Section 13, Exhibit 7–8), setting a template that extends to other hybrid and co-located configurations. Revision 71 is already effective as of the meeting date, with no further comment period or vote indicated in the excerpt.

documents.title: Item 09 – Synchronous Reserve Update

documents.ai_summary: PJM's 2026 Q1 synchronized-reserve performance report shows 8 events (1 ≥10 minutes) with 48% average generation response to assignment and 66% demand-side response. March 1 event triggered $330K in penalties (first of the quarter), indicating tightened enforcement of reserve-response obligations. The report documents response-performance metrics by resource type (generation vs. demand-side resources) and region (RTO vs. MAD zone), establishing baseline compliance data that operators—particularly synchronous units like conventional hydro—must track for performance assessment and penalty exposure.

documents.title: Item 10 – Reliability Compliance Update
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NERC large-load interconnection guidance and inverter-based resource ride-through standards directly affect how synchronous hydropower (and competing generation) must operate during grid disturbances, and large computational loads affect hydro's strategic positioning in a scarcity-prone grid.
documents.ai_summary: NERC issued a Level 3 Essential Action Alert (due August 3, 2026) requiring registered entities to address risks from customer-initiated large load reductions and oscillations that threaten BPS reliability, alongside a Reliability Guideline recommending risk mitigation for emerging large loads. NERC also released implementation guidance for PRC-029-1 (inverter-based resource ride-through design), which sets standards hydro must comply with if required to operate in grid-support modes. The large-load alert is strategically relevant because rapid load swings create scarcity windows that reward flexible, synchronous resources like hydro; however, the ride-through standard applies primarily to inverter-based resources and does not directly change hydro's existing obligations. Hydro operators in PJM should monitor August 3 deadline compliance requirements and the June 5 MSPP Rules of Procedure webinar for any emerging standards that might extend ride-through or frequency-support mandates to synchronous units.

documents.title: Item 11 – Mtopoc Update
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MTOPOC coordinates major transmission outages that constrain interregional flows and affect generator dispatch flexibility and deliverability — directly impacting hydro owner outage scheduling options and revenue dependability during periods when transmission is constrained.
documents.ai_summary: PJM's Multi-TO Project Outage Coordination (MTOPOC) process manages ~$21 billion in transmission upgrades and associated major outages (230 kV and above, 20+ days) across 2026–2027 to minimize system reliability risk and construction conflicts. Generator outage coordination is becoming critical as load growth and generation retirements outpace new capacity additions; PJM is encouraging generators to submit outages early with detail and to maintain scheduling flexibility, as transmission constraints and emergent system conditions are triggering increased outage adjustments and recalls. Hydropower and pumped-storage operators in PJM face tightening outage windows and must coordinate outage timing with major transmission work affecting their deliverability corridors (Peach Bottom nuclear, northern Dominion, North-South flows); generators should engage with Emanuel Bernabeu and Joe Rushing early in the outage-planning cycle.

documents.title: Item 12 – Regulation Market Phase Ii Simulation Results
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: regulation market bifurcation (splitting single bidirectional product into separate RegUp and RegDown products) changes the offer, clearing, and settlement mechanics that hydro and PSH use to compete for and monetize regulation revenue in PJM, a major market where hydro operates.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is implementing Phase 2 of its Regulation Market redesign, effective October 1, 2026 (pending FERC approval), splitting the single bidirectional regulation product into two separate RegUp and RegDown products, each with its own requirement, clearing price, and settlement. The simulation, using FESTIV software across representative weeks in all four seasons, tested area control error performance, controller saturation, and generator movement under the bifurcated design versus the current unified product. Key findings show separate regulation products improve ACE (Area Control Error) performance and reliability metrics, though summer conditions remain challenging; improvements stem from changing resource mix and generator movement behavior. The implication for hydro and PSH operators is that the new product structure will change how their regulation capacity awards are determined and priced — previously a single award covered both up and down service; under Phase 2, RegUp and RegDown awards and prices are independently cleared, potentially altering the revenue profile for units providing regulation. The document does not contain comment deadlines or further implementation milestones beyond the October 1, 2026 effective date.

documents.title: Item 13 – Generation Operational Testing Update
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's Generation Operational Testing program establishes must-offer compliance obligations and performance penalties that directly affect dispatchable resource operators, including hydroelectric generators committed to RPM or FRR plans, through failure charges and retest requirements tied to start-time and minimum-run-time parameters.
documents.ai_summary: PJM's Performance Compliance team reported on the Generation Operational Testing program, which subjects all capacity resources (except variable resources) committed in RPM or FRR to unannounced real-time operational tests up to twice per season. Winter 2025 saw 54 total tests with a 40% failure rate (vs. 24% in summer 2024), driven mainly by delayed start times, mechanical issues, and telemetry errors; retests failed at 64% versus 36% for initial tests. PJM emphasized that generators face financial implications from failed retests and must proactively validate operational readiness and parameter accuracy (start-up time, minimum run time, notification delay) in Markets Gateway. Hydroelectric and pumped-storage operators committed as capacity resources in PJM fall squarely under this obligation; dispatchable hydro must maintain accurate start-time parameters and be capable of reliable real-time response or face test failure and associated penalties.

documents.title: Item 02 – Storage As A Transmission Asset – Sata – Phase 2 – Package Summary
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: SATA establishes a new participation model for energy storage as a regulated transmission asset in PJM, fundamentally altering how storage resources (including pumped-storage hydro) can be deployed and valued — either enrolled in SATA (transmission-only, cost-of-service recovery, no market participation) or remain in competitive markets, creating a strategic fork for PSH owners.
documents.ai_summary: PJM's Operating Committee reviewed the Phase 2 framework for Storage as a Transmission Asset (SATA), which allows energy storage (including pumped-storage hydro) to operate as regulated transmission facilities to address localized RTEP violations without participating in competitive markets. Under SATA Phase 2, eligible storage assets would discharge automatically to mitigate identified contingencies, charge via owner coordination afterward, and recover costs through transmission rates (Schedule 12 Transmission Enhancement Credits) rather than market revenue, with metering and telemetry matching standard energy-storage requirements. The framework explicitly prohibits SATA resources from queuing for interconnection or claiming capacity value, and expects assets to be small (≤10 MW) and short-duration (≤4 hours). The document advances to MRC review in July 2026, with FERC submission expected September–November 2026. This creates a new revenue pathway for pumped-storage owners willing to accept regulated-utility-like cost recovery in exchange for operational control and transmission-rate certainty, but forecloses market-participation optionality (energy, AS, capacity) for enrolled assets.

documents.title: Item 03 – 1 Manual 13 – Revision 98 – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Manual 13 governs PJM emergency operations procedures that directly affect hydro and other generating resources' obligations during system emergencies, capacity shortages, and transmission security events — particularly dispatch instructions, must-offer requirements, and emergency bid processes that touch hydro revenue and compliance.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 13 (Emergency Operations), Revision 98, underwent annual review with substantive changes to emergency procedure taxonomy and triggering thresholds effective July 23, 2026. Key changes separate transmission-security emergencies from capacity emergencies, clarify that transmission-security procedures do not trigger Energy Emergency Alerts (EEAs) or Persistent Advisories (PAIs), and add a new Capacity Advisory to provide advance notice when forecasted capacity approaches operating requirements. A new Attachment O codifies procedures for emergency use of backup generators under DOE 202(c) Orders. The revision also updates Advanced Scheduled Resources language for cold/hot-weather alerts and adds RCIS notification to Pre-Emergency Load Management procedures. For hydro operators, the distinction between transmission- and capacity-triggered emergencies affects when they will receive dispatch instructions and emergency bid solicitations — transmission emergencies no longer trigger EEAs, which may narrow the scope of emergency-reserve procurement that traditionally favors hydro's rapid-response capability; the Capacity Advisory may provide earlier signaling of system stress, allowing better strategic positioning. Most affected are large, flexible generators and storage operators participating in PJM's emergency-bid and reserve markets. Revision endorsed by Operating Committee June 4, 2026, with final approval timeline shown through June 24, 2026 (MRC second read).

documents.title: Item 03 – 2 Manual 13 – Revision 98 – Executive Summary
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Establishes procedures for emergency dispatch of large loads (data centers) on backup generation during capacity/transmission emergencies, creating new operational constraints and dispatch prioritization rules that affect hydro's role in reserve provision and emergency response.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 13 Revision 98 (effective July 23, 2026) introduces a new Emergency Use of Back-up Generators procedure allowing data centers and large loads to disconnect from the grid and operate on-site backup generation during capacity or transmission emergencies—after NERC EEA2 is declared and a DOE 202(c) Order is obtained. PJM will direct Transmission Owners to coordinate disconnection of large loads within 15 minutes, with capacity-deficient control zones exhausting all available large-load capacity before requesting disconnection in zones with excess capacity. This reshapes hydro's strategic value during emergencies: where previously all generation resources (including hydro's full output) would be called to meet contingency reserves, large-load disconnection now becomes an alternative resource, potentially reducing dispatch calls on conventional generators and changing the economic incentive structure for hydro emergency participation. Most exposed are reservoir and pumped-storage operators supplying contingency reserves in constrained zones; run-of-river hydro with fixed output faces less direct impact. The manual becomes effective immediately; no comment deadline is stated.

Key changes include addition of a Capacity Advisory level to the emergency-level structure (Section 2.3), updated language for Advanced Schedule Resources during cold and hot weather alerts, clarification that transmission security procedures do not trigger PAIs or EEAs, and a new Attachment O on emergency use of backup generators. For hydro operators, these procedures determine obligations during system stress (e.g., must-offer and minimum generation requirements), affect the timing and magnitude of scarcity-pricing events and emergency bidding, and establish the dispatch scenarios in which hydro's flexibility is most valued or constrained. All hydro-owning utilities in PJM footprint must comply with these operating standards.

documents.title: 11. PDCWG-Report-to-ROS_060426
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ERCOT frequency response and inertia management, particularly FFR procurement and PFR performance monitoring, demonstrate a market-design approach to frequency support that contrasts with hydro-rich RTOs and informs NHA's cross-market analysis of how different regions value synchronous and fast-response capability.
documents.ai_summary: ERCOT's Primary Frequency Response (PFR) performance monitoring under BAL-001-TRE has stalled due to too few Frequency Measurable Events (FMEs) — the criteria used to evaluate PFR performance are generating only fewer than the desired 20–35 events per year. ERCOT has proposed revised FME selection criteria to increase event counts and improve oversight of Responsive Reserve Service providers; revised criteria have been shared with the PDCWG and ERCOT has begun using them immediately while retaining discretion in selection. The ERCOT system inertia trends show a structural decline: synchronous inertia at minimum-load points has fallen from 143 GW·s in 2016 to 114.7 GW·s in March 2026, while non-synchronous generation has grown to 81% of system load and Fast Frequency Response procurement has expanded from zero to 430 MW. This illustrates a cross-market contrast — whereas hydro-rich RTOs rely on synchronous hydro for inertia and primary frequency response, ERCOT's low-inertia, high-renewable grid is increasingly dependent on FFR procurement and stricter frequency-event metrics to maintain reserve adequacy and response capability.

documents.ai_summary: PJM is implementing Manual 11 revisions (Phase 1) to formalize advance scheduling of resources with notification or start-up times exceeding 24 hours, triggered by lessons from Winter Storm Elliott. Resources pre-scheduled in advance of the Day-ahead Market on binding cost-based offers will have their offer prices locked and the 'Switch to Cost Schedule' flag set by PJM; they cannot update to price-based schedules for the locked days. Resources with start-up/notification <24 hours may update cost-based offers only through the Day-ahead bid period and during real-time rebidding windows. The rule prevents advance-scheduled units from exercising price-based flexibility once committed. Implementation is scheduled for June 2026, with MIC first read May 26 and second read/endorsement in June.

documents.title: Informational Only – PJM Esr Model Enhancements Position Paper
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's proposed enhancements to energy storage resource market participation rules—particularly opportunity-cost offer methodology, state-of-charge management, and must-offer requirements—directly affect how pumped-storage hydro and battery storage compete for energy and ancillary-services revenue and how their dispatch is constrained by SOC accounting, setting precedent that will shape storage treatment across RTOs.
documents.ai_summary: PJM staff proposes enhancements to its Energy Storage Resource Participation Model to accommodate rapid battery-storage growth (4,800 MW expected by 2030). The proposal addresses four issue areas: (1) a standardized opportunity-cost calculation for real-time energy offers capping cost at max(incremental energy cost, maximum DA LMP) up to $2,000, with emergency override to $2,000; (2) SOC accounting in day-ahead dispatch (rolling calculation to prevent infeasible dispatch) and ancillary-services clearing (recognizing SOC depletion from AS deployment), but explicit rejection of centralized SOC optimization; (3) no change to inter-day offer rules; and (4) complementary work via the Reserve Certainty Senior Task Force. A stakeholder process begins July 2026. The opportunity-cost cap directly affects how pumped storage (and batteries) offer into real-time markets—tying the cap to max DA LMP rather than real-time conditions or a multiplier makes cost-based offers more predictable but may suppress PSH discharge bids during high-priced hours when SO-C is low. SOC accounting prevents infeasible dispatch but stops short of RTO-led optimization, preserving operator discretion. documents.ai_summary: ERCOT proposes to eliminate separate energy and ancillary-service price adders by using SCED Pricing Run prices (LMPs and AS MCPCs) directly as binding prices when reliability deployments are active, replacing a previous approach that added the difference between pricing and dispatch runs. ERCOT also refines indifference-payment calculations to use actual offer/bid curves instead of linear approximations, and extends indifference payments to ancillary services and RUC/RMR/MRA resources. The proposal addresses a settlement inconsistency: dispatch-run awards (reflecting real-time conditions) paired with pricing-run prices (reflecting a hypothetical grid absent deployments) can financially harm participants and create perverse incentives to chase prices. This represents ERCOT's approach to neutralizing distortions from out-of-market actions — a design problem that hydro-rich markets handle differently (e.g., PJM's opportunity-cost framework, CAISO's reliability-deployment uplift). No explicit comment deadline or vote date is stated in the slides.

documents.ai_summary: ERCOT proposes reforms to NPRR1214 that modify how reliability deployments (out-of-market dispatchable loads, reserve curtailments, and generation adjustments) are priced and compensated. The proposal replaces energy and ancillary-service price adders with direct use of SCED pricing-run locational marginal prices and market clearing prices, and introduces ancillary-service indifference payments to offset the gap between binding dispatch-run awards (reflecting actual reliability actions) and hypothetical pricing-run prices (reflecting the counterfactual absent those deployments). ERCOT positions this as more accurate than prior approximations and states it will be discussed at the Wholesale Market Subcommittee; no vote or implementation date is stated in this draft. Although ERCOT has no significant hydropower fleet, this precedent is relevant to NHA members in other RTOs (especially CAISO, NYISO, and PJM) where similar tensions arise between must-run or must-offer generation commitments and competitive pricing, and where storage and hydro operators increasingly face indifference-payment regimes to offset scarcity pricing or out-of-market dispatch.

documents.title: Item 03 – 1 Manual 14h Revisions Ieee 2800 – Presentation

The revision adds Section 9.15 and new Attachment K, specifying mandatory ride-through times (e.g., 6 seconds at 0.70–0.90 p.u. voltage) and default frequency-response parameters (droop 5%, dead-band 0.06% × fnom). For hydropower and pumped-storage operators, the key provisions include: Section 9 sets requirements for generating facilities (power factor, capacity vs. energy resource status elections, behind-the-meter generation, inverter-based resource rules); Section 12 covers surplus interconnection service, the mechanism by which existing hydro plants can access previously-allocated but unused interconnection capacity for uprates or expansion; and Sections 1–5 establish the phased study and agreement process that determines project viability and cost allocation. Scenario B.1 models state RPS targets and battery storage targets, including policy-driven generator deactivations; Scenario A.1 does economic resource-stack optimization without specific RPS modeling. The capacity expansion model assumes 218.3 GW summer and 204.5 GW winter peak load in 2034, forcing addition of solar, wind, gas, battery storage, and nuclear uprates. Storage targets (modeled in Sensitivity A.3 and Scenario B.1) and clean energy policies via generator retirements (Illinois CEJA, New Jersey CO₂ Rule, Virginia Clean Economy Act) reshape the assumed generation fleet PJM uses for transmission needs assessment, altering the scarcity and reserve conditions hydro will operate in and the competing resources for RA accreditation. This is the planning foundation for 2026–2034 transmission and resource-adequacy decisions across PJM.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO Installed Capacity Working Group meeting (June 2, 2026) will address four rule changes: DER market-participation enhancements, ICAP Manual Attachment N updates, revised treatment of intermittency in capacity accreditation, and improved duct-firing modeling for fossil units. The intermittency revisions are most material — they modify how NYISO accredits variable and run-of-river hydro in the capacity market, and how storage is modeled in the reserve-margin calculation. Manual updates will be presented by Sushant Varghese and Vijay Kaki; Potomac Economics will discuss 2025 State of the Market findings, which often include capacity-accreditation trends and hydro-performance analysis. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this agenda.

documents.title: 2 DER Market Enhancements
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: DER aggregation participation rules directly affect small hydropower owners' ability to participate in NYISO markets under Order 2222 frameworks; the DADSR concept and proposed telemetry/accreditation changes alter the strategic options and compliance burden for hydro resources enrolled in DER aggregations.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO proposes a Day-Ahead Demand-Side Resource (DADSR) variant within its existing DER & Aggregation participation model, designed to accommodate DSR with longer start-up times and limited real-time flexibility. DADSR would bid day-ahead, lock to a fixed real-time schedule, and be ineligible for operating reserves or regulation service; it would qualify for ICAP participation with 2–24-hour energy duration limitations and potentially reduced telemetry requirements (6-second with 30-second scan rates for sub-1 MW facilities versus current standards for 1+ MW). Small hydropower and run-of-river resources enrolled in DER aggregations face a strategic choice: participation under current DER rules (with full telemetry/ancillary-service obligations) or under DADSR (simpler telemetry, day-ahead certainty, but loss of regulation/reserve revenue and real-time flexibility upside). NYISO is also evaluating MNBT and ECBL enhancements and the 10 kW threshold; stakeholder discussion continues at the July ICAPWG/MIWG meeting.

documents.title: 3 ICAP Manual Attachment N Revisions
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO is revising Attachment N methodology for calculating translation factors that convert nameplate capacity to unforced capacity (UCAP) for intermittent and run-of-river hydro resources, directly affecting hydro accreditation in resource adequacy and capacity-requirement studies.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO proposes revisions to ICAP Manual Attachment N to implement seasonal (summer and winter) translation factors for intermittent resources and limited-control run-of-river hydro, replacing the current summer-only methodology. The change responds to observed winter Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) beginning in the 2026–2027 IRM study and supports the Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements proposal (filed with FERC 2/18/2026, target implementation 5/1/2027 for the 2027–2028 Capability Year). The proposal also corrects the availability-factor formula to apply proper weighted averaging, aligning calculation with current implementation in IRM, LCR, and deliverability studies. For run-of-river hydro owners, this means winter availability will now drive a separate winter UCAP translation factor based on December–February production patterns weighted by winter LOLE distribution, potentially improving winter accreditation if winter production is high relative to winter scarcity hours, or reducing it if winter is a dry season; the revision will be presented to the Business Issue Committee on 6/10/2026.

documents.title: 4 Balancing Intermittency Manual Updates
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's Uncertainty Reserve Requirement (URR) design directly affects how intermittent resources and ramping/flexibility are procured and priced in both day-ahead and real-time markets, creating new reserve products that hydro will be called upon to supply and creating new demand curves that establish payment terms for flexibility hydro traditionally provides.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO is finalizing manual revisions to implement its Uncertainty Reserve Requirement (URR), a new 24-hour reserve product designed to hedge forecast uncertainty for net load, land-based wind, offshore wind, and front-of-meter solar. The design was accepted by FERC in July 2025 (ER25-1998) and is scheduled for deployment in August 2026. The updated manuals clarify URR calculation methodology (incorporated in new Attachment D to the Ancillary Services Manual), specify that URR can be met using 30-Minute Reserve in the day-ahead market, introduce locational demand curves with a new Long Island requirement row (270 MW and 540 MW separately), and refine operating-capacity accounting for seasonal differences. Stakeholder votes are scheduled for June 10–11, 2026 (BIC and OC); comments can be submitted at the June 4 SOAS meeting. For hydro owners, URR creates both a revenue opportunity (new procurement of a flexibility product hydro naturally supplies) and a compliance obligation (must-offer rules in the 30-minute reserve product that backs URR); pumped-storage facilities are particularly positioned to capture value from locational reserve requirements, especially on Long Island where the demand curve now explicitly separates 270 MW and 540 MW tiers.

documents.title: 5 Improve Duct Firing Modeling Manual Updates
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Duct-firing modeling for combined-cycle gas turbines is a gas-generation-specific technical improvement with no direct application to hydropower revenue, obligations, or strategic options.

documents.title: 6 2025 State of the Market Report
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's 2025 State of the Market Report addresses capacity-market design, seasonal accreditation, resource-adequacy signals, and locational pricing — all mechanisms that directly shape revenue for hydro and pumped-storage resources in NYISO and influence investment and retention decisions.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Market Monitoring Unit (Potomac Economics) identifies structural gaps in the capacity market that undervalue reliability contributions and distort investment incentives. Key findings: (1) demand curves based on 2-hour battery cost understate Net CONE, risking premature retirements even as load grows; (2) seasonal incentives are misaligned—firm fuel/UDR elections locked 16 months in advance don't respond to winter market prices, and elected capacity for 2026/27 (15.2 GW) exceeds planning assumptions (12.3 GW), creating cost-allocation risk; (3) transmission security is undercompensated—downstate LCRs increasingly bind at floor, overpaying bottled generation (SCRs, large units) and underpaying non-firm gas units while creating $74M annual inefficiency post-CHPE. Recommendations filed or pending include raising the demand-curve floor (Rec. 2025-1a), moving seasonal-election deadlines closer to winter (Rec. 2022-2), introducing locational CAFs (Rec. 2025-2), and expanding capacity zones. These touch pumped-storage accreditation (2-hour battery CONE undermines longer-duration PSH value), seasonal energy adequacy (firm fuel elections timing), and locational value recognition (hydro deliverability and transmission-security contribution). No formal comment deadline is stated in this highlights presentation, but the full 2025 SOM Report (posted May 19, 2026) and tariff filing ER26-1431 are the operative documents.

documents.title: 4c Ancillary Services Manual Revisions
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's Ancillary Services Manual revisions directly govern how hydropower and pumped storage are compensated and must perform for regulation, frequency response, voltage support, and operating reserves — the core revenue streams and operational obligations for dispatchable hydro and PSH.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO issued a draft Ancillary Services Manual (v10.0, effective May 1, 2026) with revisions to regulation and frequency response service, voltage support, operating reserves, and energy imbalance rules. The manual specifies qualification criteria, performance-tracking methods, settlement mechanics, and testing procedures for generators, synchronous condensers, HVDC with voltage-source converter (VSC) technology, and energy storage resources providing these services. Hydro and PSH operators must comply with reactive capability testing protocols (section 3.6), regulation service prequalification and performance audits (section 4.11), and operating-reserve supplier eligibility and day-ahead/real-time bidding rules (sections 6.2–6.4). This is a working draft for discussion at the Installed Capacity Working Group (committee acceptance 04/15/2026, OC acceptance 04/16/2026); the effective date is May 1, 2026, making this a compliance-critical update for all NYISO hydro and storage participants.

documents.title: 4b Day Ahead Scheduling Manual Revisions

documents.ai_summary: NYISO has issued revisions to its Day-Ahead Scheduling Manual (Manual 11, effective 10/29/2024, accepted by BIC 08/14/2024 and OC 08/15/2024). The manual governs SCUC initialization, unit commitment of dispatchable resources including hydropower, energy storage resource constraint evaluation, ancillary service demand curves, and bilateral transaction evaluations that directly shape day-ahead market dispatch and pricing. For hydro owners, key mechanics documented include scheduling of 'must run' resources, multiple response rates for resources, energy storage limits constraints, and limiting participation constraints—all of which define the operational envelope within which hydro's dispatch and AS offerings are optimized. Hydro and PSH operators rely on these rules to understand how their bids enter unit commitment and how their flexibility is valued in the scheduling process.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Installed Capacity Manual Attachment N specifies the methodology for calculating translation factors that convert nameplate capacity into unforced capacity (UCAP) for intermittent power resources and limited-control run-of-river hydro. This accreditation procedure determines how much capacity credit variable hydro can claim in NYISO's ICAP auctions and capacity showings. The document also references Attachment M (Energy Limited Resource and Energy Duration Limitation procedures) and Attachment D (Dependable Maximum Net Capability test procedures including a hydro-generation form), indicating NYISO uses performance-data-driven methods to credential hydro's contribution to resource adequacy. For run-of-river and variable-output hydro operators in NYISO, the translation-factor calculation directly sets the capacity value realized in auctions and affects their RA contribution and revenue.

Changes to these translation factors directly alter the megawatt-accreditation—and thus auction revenue—that run-of-river and variable hydro operators can claim. documents.ai_summary: NYISO is issuing a revised Transmission and Dispatch Operations Manual (Manual 12) effective May 1, 2026, following committee acceptance on April 15–16, 2026. The manual covers operational monitoring (real-time data, security assessment, reserve and regulation requirements), transmission operations (operating limits, voltage control, phase angle regulators), real-time commitment and mitigation processes, and scheduling procedures. Hydro operators must comply with the manual's reserve calculation methodology, regulation-requirement definition, outage scheduling processes, and real-time dispatch instruction protocols—changes to any of these affect when hydro units are called on, how their output is metered and settled, and the operational flexibility they must maintain. The document's status as draft-for-discussion suggests revisions are still in circulation; the June 2, 2026 Installed Capacity Working Group meeting will likely discuss final language.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's MTEP26 transmission planning cycle, entering subregional planning meetings in June 2026, targets 574 new Appendix A projects (190 in the Central region) with $4 billion in Expedited Project Review (EPR) investment as of May 2026. The planning process uses NERC reliability standards (TPL-001-5, FAC-013/014, PRC-023) across six analytical dimensions: steady-state, transient, voltage stability, transfer capability, nuclear plant, and deliverability assessment for 2/5/10-year and 20+ year horizons. For hydro owners, the scope is material: load-growth-driven transmission projects directly alter export pathways and scarcity signals that determine when hydro units clear energy and ancillary-services markets; interconnection of new generation (especially in Central region with a sharp uptick in Generator Interconnection requests) shifts locational marginal prices and ramping needs; and large-load additions (data centers, electrification) raise baseline energy scarcity and extend the value horizon for flexible dispatchable resources. The MTEP Portal is the single source of project data; stakeholder feedback windows close September 15 and October 27, with final Board approval by December 3, 2026.

SPM2 is scheduled for June 2, 2026. documents.title: Item 02 – 1 Manual 13 – Revision 98 – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Manual 13 Revision 98 establishes emergency operating procedures affecting how hydropower and other dispatchable resources participate in PJM's capacity and transmission emergency protocols, plus introduces a new Capacity Advisory mechanism that signals resource scarcity — both touch hydro operators' obligations to respond to emergency directives and may alter revenue opportunities during stress periods.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 13 (Emergency Operations) to clarify its roles as Reliability Coordinator, Balancing Authority, and Transmission Operator under NERC EOP-011. The revision introduces a new Capacity Advisory (Section 2.3) to provide advance notice when forecasted available capacity approaches the operating requirement — designed to address gaps in temperature-based emergency triggers and expected to increase in frequency as demand growth outpaces generation interconnection. Revision 98 also establishes Attachment O, a conditional procedure to mobilize backup generation at large data-center loads during extreme emergencies (triggered only if the DOE issues a Section 202(c) order); this procedure was activated during Winter Storm Fern (January 2026) but not implemented. The revision cleanly separates transmission-security emergency procedures from capacity-based procedures, removes capacity-related actions from transmission protocols, and updates language for Advanced Scheduled Resources in cold/hot weather alerts. Endorsement is sought before the summer operating period; the timeline shows second reads at the MRC on June 24, 2026. The Capacity Advisory may increase call frequency for emergency ramping from dispatchable hydro, while data-center load growth (now formally recognized in procedures) creates both scarcity signals that favor hydro dispatch and potential operational constraints if backup-gen mobilization competes for transmission or reserve capacity.

documents.title: Item 02 – 2 Manual 13 – Revision 98 – Redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Manual 13 governs PJM emergency operations including load-shedding procedures, transmission security emergencies, and resource-limitation reporting that directly affect how dispatchable hydro and pumped-storage resources must respond to system stress and what operating obligations they face.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 13 Revision 98 (effective July 23, 2026) updates emergency-operations procedures across capacity emergencies, weather/environmental events, and transmission security. Key changes include: restructured transmission-security emergency procedures that no longer trigger PAIs or EEAs; split of Maximum Generation Emergency into separate Transmission Security–Local Maximum Generation Emergency Alert and Load Management Alert; addition of Capacity Advisory to Section 2.3; updated Advanced Schedule Resources language for cold and hot weather alerts; and new Attachment O on emergency back-up generator use. For hydro and pumped-storage operators, the procedure changes govern mandatory response protocols during transmission constraints (Section 5.2) and capacity shortages (Section 2), and clarify which emergency triggers obligate generation or discharge (e.g., load-shedding directives, transmission relief actions). The removal of PAI/EEA linkage to transmission-security procedures may reduce frequency of certain dispatch signals to storage resources during local constraints. Pumped-storage operators should review Section 2 (reserve and capacity procedures), Section 5.2 (transmission-security load and generation actions), and Attachments E–F (manual load-dump allocation) to confirm charging/discharging obligations under updated protocols.

documents.title: 2026-05-29 IPSAC A02.2 ISO-NE Regional Planning Needs and Solutions
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: transmission-planning decisions and constraint analyses affect hydro deliverability, resource adequacy valuation, and revenue-generating scarcity conditions; Loss of Source study baseline, LTTP RFP evaluation, and area studies (Connecticut 2034, daytime minimum load) directly shape transmission availability and locational scarcity signals that determine hydro's economic dispatch and reserve deployment value.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE's May 2026 regional planning update covers several transmission-planning initiatives affecting New England hydro deliverability and resource adequacy: (1) Loss of Source study with PJM and NYISO concluded without achieving full objectives but established new baseline for system constraints in neighboring RTOs; report anticipated Q2/Q3 2026. (2) 2025 Longer-Term Transmission Planning (LTTP) RFP evaluation ongoing, final determination by September 2026; stakeholder discussions on FERC Order 1920 compliance (interregional transmission coordination) paused pending RFP completion, resuming Q3 2026 with June 14, 2027 compliance-filing deadline. (3) Connecticut 2034 Solutions Study underway with preferred solution anticipated late 2026; 2035 Daytime Minimum Load Needs Assessment begins post-May 2026 CELT report release, base-case library Q3 2026. These constraint-relief and long-lead-time transmission projects directly affect hydro's ability to deliver reserve and energy products into neighboring markets and hydro's valuation in resource-adequacy showings; owners relying on New England hydro for interregional exports or RA accreditation should monitor LTTP RFP vendor evaluation (financial viability, construction feasibility) and Order 1920 stakeholder discussions resuming Q3 2026.

documents.title: 2026-05-29 IPSAC A02.1 PJM Regional Transmission Expansion Planning Process
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: TRANSMISSION PLANNING: PJM's 2025 RTEP window selected backbone transmission projects (765 kV lines, 500 kV HVDC) and load-growth driver analysis affecting interregional transfer capability and hydro deliverability in Mid-Atlantic, South/Dominion, and PJM West regions; hydro owners exporting or operating within these zones depend on these backbone routes for revenue realization.
documents.ai_summary: PJM completed evaluation of 134 proposals (57 greenfields, 77 upgrades) submitted in its 2025 Reliability Window 1 and selected regional backbone solutions totaling ~$11.7 billion: a 222-mile 765 kV line from Kammer–Buttermilk–Juniata (Mid-Atlantic), a 185-mile 500 kV HVDC line from Heritage–Mosby (South/Dominion), and three 765/345 kV lines in PJM West (Greentown–Teddy–Marysville, Guernsey–Conesville–West Millersport–Adkins, and 345 kV laterals). The primary drivers are load growth in PPL zone (~5–8.5 GW cumulative), data-center load external to Dominion, and southbound generation flowing to northern VA load centers, all creating 500 kV capacity violations on north–south corridors by 2030–2032. The next FERC 1000 window opens July 2026 with proposal close August/September 2026 and board approval targeted October 2026–February 2027. For hydro operators exporting from the South or West into load-heavy Mid-Atlantic, these backbone augmentations directly increase transmission import capacity and firm locational revenue signals; conversely, the selection of HVDC on the Heritage–Mosby corridor (rather than purely AC) creates a new constraint on traditional hydro exports via 500 kV AC paths.

documents.title: 2026-05-29 IPSAC A02.3 NYISO Updates on Comprehensive System Planning Process
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's system planning process and reliability assessments directly affect hydro and storage dispatch needs, transmission-constrained resource valuations, and generator deactivation/RMR decisions that reshape the market environment for peaking and flexible resources.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO presented its 2026–2027 Reliability Planning Process cycle, including the 2026 Reliability Needs Assessment (covering 2030–2036) and the 2027–2036 Comprehensive Reliability Plan. The 2025 Q3 and 2026 Q1 Short-Term Reliability Assessments (STARs) identified persistent deficiencies in New York City (Zone J) and Long Island (Zone K) that depend on continued operation of fossil peakers (Gowanus, Narrows, Far Rockaway, Danskammer) until transmission solutions energize or demand-side/storage alternatives materialize. Generator deactivations are being withdrawn or held in Interim Service Provider status pending solution entry. These assessments directly affect which generation assets receive RMR contracts or withdrawal approval, which in turn shapes the scarcity pricing, transmission congestion, and reserve-procurement environment in which hydro and storage must compete. Any expansion of transmission or storage-as-transmission alternatives in the planning scenarios could displace fossil peakers and alter the revenue drivers for hydro ramping and energy supply in the constrained zones.

documents.title: 2026-05-29 IPSAC A05 IPSAC NCSP25
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Interregional transmission planning and coordination directly affect hydro deliverability, resource adequacy needs assessment, and the strategic question of whether interregional transmission investments (vs. regional solutions) will shape hydro's revenue opportunities and grid export capacity in the Northeast.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE, NYISO, and PJM completed their 2025 coordinated interregional transmission planning cycle under FERC Order 1000, with draft results posted in early April 2026 and stakeholder comments due April 20–27, 2026. The planning process found no interregional transmission projects that are more efficient or cost-effective than separate regional solutions, meaning each ISO will pursue its own system needs independently rather than jointly. This outcome is significant for hydro owners because it confirms the near-term transmission topology will remain within existing regional footprints; interregional transmission constraints will not be relaxed by new joint projects, and the value of existing hydro resources for intraregional scarcity and export will depend on each ISO's separate needs assessments and queue development. The final NCSP25 report is pending posting.

documents.title: 2026-05-27 PAC A05.0 2025 LTTP RFP – RFP Objective Follow-up
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: TRANSMISSION PLANNING: ISO-NE's 2025 Longer-Term Transmission Planning (LTTP) RFP evaluation directly affects hydro export capability and interregional transfer limits (Maine–New Hampshire and Surowiec–South interfaces), which constrain the locational value and revenue of New England hydropower and determine whether transmission upgrades will be required to relieve scarcity.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE evaluated six Longer-Term Transmission Plan proposals submitted in response to NESCOE's RFP; two proposals (A1, A2) passed RFP Objectives testing (thermal, voltage, and transient stability at ≥3000 MW Maine–New Hampshire and ≥3200 MW Surowiec–South transfer limits) and proceed to No Adverse Impact Screening and Benefits Calculation, while four proposals (B1, C1, D1, D2) failed stability or voltage criteria and remain excluded. After follow-up reviews requested by proposal sponsors, ISO-NE confirmed that C1 failed transient stability testing due to insufficient dynamic reactive support, and D1/D2 sponsors acknowledged instability under single-fault scenarios; both determinations remain unchanged. ISO-NE expects to present its preliminary preferred Longer-Term Transmission Solution to PAC by September 2026. For hydro owners, the outcome determines which transmission projects advance to benefits evaluation — projects that increase Maine–New Hampshire or Surowiec–South transfer limits would reduce congestion and increase the marginal value of New England hydro's energy sales southward; rejection of four proposals may delay relief of these critical constraints.

documents.title: Draft Transmission Planning Technical Guide Rev 8.5 (clean)
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Transmission planning technical guide directly affects hydropower deliverability, interconnection modeling, and system planning study treatment of conventional hydro and energy storage resources — foundational to how hydro assets are rated, tested, and accommodated in the network.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE has issued Revision 8.5 of its Transmission Planning Technical Guide, effective September 30, 2025. The guide establishes modeling requirements and study protocols for the region's resource mix, including dedicated sections on conventional hydro generation (2.3.7) and energy storage systems (2.3.8), along with steady-state, transient stability, and short-circuit criteria used in transmission needs assessments. Changes to modeling conventions, reactive power requirements, stability test protocols, or resource-rating methodologies in this revision directly impact how existing hydro plants and new storage projects are characterized in interconnection studies, deliverability analyses, and system planning — affecting both operational flexibility valuations and accreditation inputs to New England's capacity market. The guide is now in effect; any comments on the revision history or requests for clarification should be directed to ISO-NE Planning.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is conducting its 2026 Economic Study to model New England's resource needs, transmission limitations, and emission profiles over a 10-year horizon. The benchmark scenario (preliminary results Q3 2026, final by December 2027) uses 2025 historical hydro operations data integrated into PLEXOS to determine monthly max/min capacity and energy availability; pumped storage is modeled at 74% efficiency with a $3/MWh VOM cost, and both hydro and storage are assigned reserve capabilities (10-minute spinning, 10-minute non-spinning, 30-minute operating reserves). The study will also examine potential System Efficiency Needs through competitive solicitation, which could affect transmission interconnection and deliverability. Stakeholders may submit requests for additional sensitivity analyses by June 2026.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE has updated its Transmission Planning Technical Guide (TPTG) to formally document Storage as a Transmission Only Asset (SATOA) — energy storage devices at 115 kV or higher used to address transmission reliability needs post-N-1-1 contingencies and to provide continuous reactive power support like synchronous condensers. SATOA treatment was accepted by FERC on October 19, 2023, and is now being incorporated into planning-study methodology in TPTG Section 2.3.8.1, with conforming changes to Section 2.3.8. This formalizes a pathway for storage (including pumped storage) to compete as a transmission solution in ISO-NE's competitive solutions process alongside traditional wires and other non-wires alternatives, potentially creating revenue streams for PSH owners who can locate facilities to address identified transmission needs. Comments on the draft TPTG are due by June 10, 2026.

documents.title: Joint Letter on LTTP Solicitation to the PAC
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: HVDC transmission expansion and black-start capability affect hydro's regional transmission access, cost recovery, and operational flexibility value; this RFP dispute touches the governance process through which major transmission investments that reshape hydro's market are selected.
documents.ai_summary: A coalition including National Grid Ventures, New England Power Company, and PowerBridge submitted two HVDC-based transmission proposals to ISO-NE's inaugural Longer-Term Transmission Planning (LTTP) solicitation but was excluded from further evaluation after failing stability analysis in March 2026. The coalition disputes ISO-NE's rejection of technical mitigation measures (adding an isolated circuit and transformer to the converter station), arguing the tariff allows non-material modifications and that iterative refinement is standard practice. The broader stakes: all expanded HVDC solutions were eliminated, leaving only HVAC alternatives—eliminating HVDC's claimed benefits of black-start capability, bi-directional power-flow control, and future cost reduction. For hydro owners, HVDC transmission expansion directly affects regional scarcity pricing, deliverability of remote hydro resources, and operational flexibility value; the coalition's exclusion narrows the solutions competitive set and may reduce the scope of future regional investments in transmission features that benefit dispatchable resources.
